`MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Preferences/ApiUserPreferenceReader.cs:22`, `:21-31`). The write is strictly
best-effort: the cookie is the device-local runtime channel and a failed persist never breaks the
in-page switch. Best-effort has a cost, though, and both sides guard it, first by refusing to send
when the token is missing, unreadable or within 30 seconds of expiry via `JwtTokenInfo.IsFresh`
(`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:35`, `:93`; `ApiUserPreferenceReader.cs:21`, `:31`), and second by
remembering the exact token the API last answered 401 to, so a revoked session costs one failed
request rather than one per toggle (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:41-47`, `:98-104`, `:116-119`).
Comparing the token rather than setting a latch is what lets a fresh sign-in resume writing with no
reset step. Saves are also sent one at a time in call order, each waiting at most five seconds for the one before it: a theme toggle followed quickly by a language switch otherwise sent two concurrent PUTs, and the switcher's force-reload either cut off the theme write or let the two race on the user row's concurrency token, so the next sign-in applied the old theme (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:56`, `:58-74`, `:76-84`). That is a `[Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]` detail as much as a `[Rubric §19,
State Management]` one: at low traffic, one 401 per theme toggle is enough on its own to trip a
failed-request alert rule.

**Pluggable UI modules.** The module system that organizes the back end
([`IModule`](group-14-module-system-composition.md#imodule), chapter 14) has a front-end counterpart in
[`IUIModule`](#iuimodule) (`MMCA.Common.UI/Common/Interfaces/IUIModule.cs:11`). A module descriptor
exposes its navigation entries as [`NavItem`](#navitem) values, the `Assembly` holding its Razor pages
so the host can add it to `AdditionalAssemblies` for route discovery, and five defaulted collections of
component types to render: in the app bar for a signed-in user, in the app bar for every visitor (a site search box, or a cart a signed-out shopper also uses), at the root layout, at the top of the main content region, and in the layout footer (`IUIModule.cs:5-40`, the footer collection documented from `:41`). The
registration prologue is shared too: `AddUIModule<TModule>()` runs one Scrutor scan that picks up
every `IEntityService<,>` implementation in the module's assembly as scoped, then registers the
descriptor as a singleton (`MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:487-496`), so a module's own
`Add{Module}UI()` no longer carries its own copy of that scan and can still register services that
must win afterwards. [`UIModuleConfiguration`](#uimoduleconfiguration) lets a host switch a module off
through `Modules:{name}:Enabled`, defaulting to enabled when the section is absent
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Common/Settings/UIModuleConfiguration.cs:28-35`), and
[`IHomePageContent`](#ihomepagecontent) is the per-app landing-page hook behind the shared `/` route,
naming the component type and the page title
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Common/Interfaces/IHomePageContent.cs:8-15`). Adding a feature module therefore wires
its pages, its services and its menu entries into the shell with no edit to the shell.
`[Rubric §18, UI Architecture]` and `[Rubric §1, SOLID]` (open/closed).

**A complete vertical slice shipped inside the framework: notifications.** Unlike the rest of the
package, which is base classes consumers extend, the `Notifications` area is a finished feature an app
switches on with one call. [`NotificationUIModule`](#notificationuimodule)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Notifications/NotificationUIModule.cs:15`) contributes a user-facing inbox nav entry
plus a push-notification entry gated on the `NotificationPermissions.Manage` permission rather than on
a role name (`:17-21`, the permission facet at `:20`), the app-bar
[`NotificationBell`](#notificationbell) (`:23`) and a root-layout listener component (`:25`);
[`NotificationInbox`](#notificationinbox), [`NotificationList`](#notificationlist) and
[`NotificationSend`](#notificationsend) (with its [`NotificationSendModel`](#notificationsendmodel)
form model) render it; [`NotificationInboxService`](#notificationinboxservice) and
[`PushNotificationService`](#pushnotificationservice) (behind
[`INotificationInboxUIService`](#inotificationinboxuiservice) and
[`IPushNotificationUIService`](#ipushnotificationuiservice)) call the API; and
[`NotificationHubService`](#notificationhubservice)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Notifications/NotificationHubService.cs:45`) holds the **SignalR**
connection to the API's [`NotificationHub`](group-10-notifications.md#notificationhub). A dropped
connection reconnects for as long as the service is alive: the internal
[`UnboundedReconnectPolicy`](#unboundedreconnectpolicy)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Notifications/UnboundedReconnectPolicy.cs:21`, wired at
`NotificationHubService.cs:207`) walks a 0, 2, 5 and 10 second warm-up and then retries every 30
seconds, where the SignalR default gives up after about 42 seconds and leaves live notifications dead
until a page reload (`UnboundedReconnectPolicy.cs:6-20`, `:24-32`, `:44-46`). A connection that still
closes with an error is restarted under the same 30-second cap, a deliberate stop or dispose is never
restarted, and a 401 or 403 handshake ends both loops, since an expired session cannot recover by
retrying (`NotificationHubService.cs:32-42`, `:281`). The same connection
carries ephemeral **live channel** events
([ADR-039](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/039-live-channel-push.html)): components join through
`JoinChannelAsync` (`NotificationHubService.cs:320`), membership is reference-counted per key by
[`ChannelReferenceCounter`](#channelreferencecounter)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Notifications/ChannelReferenceCounter.cs:16`) so one subscriber leaving does
not cut the channel off for the others, handlers are multicast through disposable
[`ChannelSubscription`](#channelsubscription) handles (`NotificationHubService.cs:772`), and every held
channel is re-joined on `Reconnected` because SignalR group membership does not survive a new
connection (`NotificationHubService.cs:227`). On a WebAssembly client whose host runs the same-origin
proxy, the hub connects through it and sends the proxy's CSRF header instead of an access token
(`NotificationHubService.cs:100-110`, `:541`). Which notifications a user sees can be narrowed by
[`INotificationScopeProvider`](#inotificationscopeprovider), an app-supplied scope key such as
`"event:2"` that both HTTP services consume so a send and the reads that follow agree, defaulting to
the unscoped [`NullNotificationScopeProvider`](#nullnotificationscopeprovider) and contractually
forbidden from throwing, with the further instruction to fail *closed* (return the last known key)
rather than degrade to null, since a null silently widens the view to every notification
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Notifications/INotificationScopeProvider.cs:9-22`). Shared unread state
lives in [`NotificationState`](#notificationstate)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Notifications/NotificationState.cs:18`), which stamps when the count was
last established so a subscriber can ask `IsStale` instead of re-fetching on every trigger (`:7-12`)
and arbitrates a single active-poller slot by **owner reference** rather than a counter, so a teardown
that never unregisters cannot strand the slot for the life of the circuit (`:23-29`). Both of the
badge's timings are configuration rather than compiled-in constants:
[`NotificationBellOptions`](#notificationbelloptions)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Common/Settings/NotificationBellOptions.cs:12`) binds a 30-second default
`PollInterval` and a 30-second `NavigationRefreshMaxAge`, so a deployment paying per API call widens
the poll and a page change within the window keeps the count it has (`:22`, `:29`), read by the bell
through `IOptions` and a `TimeProvider`
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Notifications/NotificationBell.razor.cs:34`, `:36-37`). The bell also
registers strictly symmetrically, because hosts render it twice inside `<AuthorizeView>` and a routine
token refresh tears both instances down and rebuilds them (`NotificationBell.razor.cs:22-29`). The
whole feature is wired by its own `AddNotificationUI()`
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Notifications/DependencyInjection.cs:12`, `:20-42`), kept separate so an app that does
not want real-time notifications never pays for the SignalR plumbing. A host that skips it can also set
`HideNotificationPagesWhenUnregistered` (`MMCA.Common.UI/Common/Settings/LayoutSettings.cs:49`), and
[`NotificationPageGate`](#notificationpagegate)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Notifications/NotificationPageGate.cs:11`) then has the router answer the three
notification pages with the not-found page whenever no `NotificationUIModule` is registered
(`:14-31`). The router places the internal
[`NotificationPageNotFoundStatus`](#notificationpagenotfoundstatus)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Notifications/NotificationPageNotFoundStatus.cs:11`) beside that not-found page; it
renders nothing and calls `NavigationManager.NotFound()` on initialization, so a server render
answers 404 rather than 200 (`:5-10`, `:18`). The pages themselves declare the
`mmca:notification-pages` policy instead of a bare `[Authorize]`, because `[Authorize]` is endpoint
metadata and the authorization middleware would challenge a signed-out visitor to sign in before the
router's gate ever ran, for a page that does not exist on this host
([`NotificationPageRequirement`](#notificationpagerequirement),
`MMCA.Common.UI/Notifications/NotificationPageRequirement.cs:18`, `:23`, rationale at `:14-19`).
[`NotificationPageAuthorizationHandler`](#notificationpageauthorizationhandler)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Notifications/NotificationPageAuthorizationHandler.cs:16`) passes an authenticated
caller, and every caller while the host hides the pages, reusing the gate's own predicate so the two
cannot disagree (`:26-30`); `AddUIShared` registers the policy and the handler for every host
(`MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:78-85`).

**Administration screens ship as components, not pages.** Identity administration is the second
finished feature in the package
([ADR-116](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/116-identity-completions-opt-in.html)), and it is
delivered as components an app routes itself: [`UserAdminList<TUser>`](#useradminlisttuser)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Administration/UserAdminList.razor.cs:44`), [`RoleAdminList`](#roleadminlist)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Administration/RoleAdminList.razor.cs:28`) and
[`RoleAdminEdit`](#roleadminedit) (`MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Administration/RoleAdminEdit.razor.cs:36`)
carry no `@page` directive, so the route, the authorization attribute and the links between them stay
the app's decision (`UserAdminList.razor.cs:17-22`, `RoleAdminList.razor.cs:12-14`,
`RoleAdminEdit.razor.cs:13-14`). The account roster is the one shipped screen that derives from the
list-page base itself (`MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Administration/UserAdminList.razor:4`) and it is generic
over the app's own DTO, constrained only to `IUserAdminDTO` (`UserAdminList.razor.cs:47-48`). It has
two data paths: by default it reads through
[`IUserAdminUIService<TUserDto>`](#iuseradminuiservicetuserdto)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Administration/IUserAdminUIService.cs:17`), whose endpoint takes a search
term and a role rather than the grid's per-column filter syntax
(`IUserAdminUIService.cs:11-16`, `:27-32`), while an app whose roster lives on its own filtered
endpoint passes a `FetchPage` delegate instead and the service is never resolved for reads, with the
free-text box injected under the `SearchFilterKey` filter key (`UserAdminList.razor.cs:32-39`,
`:50-55`). The three account actions always go through
[`IUserAdminActionsUIService`](#iuseradminactionsuiservice)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Administration/IUserAdminActionsUIService.cs:16`), the non-generic half so a
component that only acts on an account never names the DTO, and they are hidden on the signed-in
operator's own row: an operator who locked or demoted themselves would lose the very capability needed
to undo it, and the API has no notion of "the caller" (`UserAdminList.razor.cs:40-44`). `SetRoleAsync`
is its own member rather than a default interface implementation over `SetRolesAsync`, because a
default implementation is not virtual on the interface a mock proxies, so a test could neither stub
nor verify it (`IUserAdminActionsUIService.cs:40-54`).

Role administration is non-generic throughout, since a role and a permission are both strings the
framework already owns ([`IRoleAdminUIService`](#iroleadminuiservice),
`MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Administration/IRoleAdminUIService.cs:22`, rationale at `:11-15`). The roster
reports the permissions a role's code grants and the permissions stored rows grant as two separate
counts, because only the stored half is editable and a single total would hide that removing a
compiled permission is a code change (`RoleAdminList.razor.cs:16-20`). The editor offers only what the
server's catalog declares, so nothing it can submit is a permission no endpoint checks, and it locks
two kinds of checkbox: one the host compiled in for this role, and `ManageRoles` itself, which guards
this very screen and which the server refuses to store, so offering it would be offering an action
guaranteed to fail (`RoleAdminEdit.razor.cs:17-29`). The rest are grouped by the area before the first
colon of an `area:capability` name through the private [`PermissionGroup`](#permissiongroup) record,
with un-prefixed permissions filed under a localized "General" (`RoleAdminEdit.razor.cs:39`, `:245-247`,
`:338-340`). Wording stays the app's: every string these three render is looked up in an app-supplied
`IStringLocalizer` **first** and falls back to the framework's
[`UserAdminListResources`](#useradminlistresources),
[`RoleAdminListResources`](#roleadminlistresources) and
[`RoleAdminEditResources`](#roleadmineditresources) markers, so "Deactivate" instead of "Lock" costs
no parameter per word (`UserAdminList.razor.cs:24-31`,
`MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Administration/RoleAdminListResources.cs:9-14`). Both implementations,
[`UserAdminService<TUserDto>`](#useradminservicetuserdto)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Administration/UserAdminService.cs:26`) and
[`RoleAdminService`](#roleadminservice)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Administration/RoleAdminService.cs:24`), derive from
[`AuthenticatedServiceBase`](#authenticatedservicebase) rather than the entity-service base, because
these endpoints are not CRUD over an entity resource, and they read every answer back through
[`ProblemDetailsResultReader`](group-08-auth.md#problemdetailsresultreader) inside
[`HttpResultExecutor`](#httpresultexecutor) so only the caller's own cancellation still propagates
(`UserAdminService.cs:15-22`, `RoleAdminService.cs:64-78`, `:89-101`). `[Rubric §18, UI Architecture &
Component Design]` again: the framework ships the screen, the app keeps the route, the vocabulary and
the DTO.

**Two-factor and permission-gated pages follow the same opt-in shape.** Two-factor authentication
ships on the notification pattern. [`TwoFactorUIModule`](#twofactoruimodule)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/TwoFactor/TwoFactorUIModule.cs:16`), registered by `AddTwoFactorUI()`, contributes
the account page's navigation item and the layout listener that sends a session refused for want of
a second factor to that page, and a host that never registers it has no page, no nav item and no
listener (`TwoFactorUIModule.cs:10-15`). [`TwoFactorPageGate`](#twofactorpagegate)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/TwoFactor/TwoFactorPageGate.cs:12`) has the router answer the page with the
not-found page whenever the module is absent, because the page needs a client and API endpoints such
a host does not have (`:6-11`), and the page declares the policy behind
[`TwoFactorPageRequirement`](#twofactorpagerequirement)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/TwoFactor/TwoFactorPageRequirement.cs:14`) instead of a bare `[Authorize]`, so on
such a host every caller reaches the router and gets a 404 rather than a sign-in challenge for a page
that does not exist, the same rule the notification pages follow (`:5-13`), evaluated by
[`TwoFactorPageAuthorizationHandler`](#twofactorpageauthorizationhandler). A permission-gated page
needs no registration at all: [`HasPagePermissionAttribute`](#haspagepermissionattribute)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/HasPagePermissionAttribute.cs:19`) requires a signed-in caller whose
token carries the named `permission` claim, in every head, and checks it with the same
`HasPermissionClaim` as `NavItem.RequiredPermission`, so a menu entry and the page it opens cannot
disagree; it reads the claim only, since a UI head has no permission registry, so a role-only token
never passes (`:5-17`). [`PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator`](#pagepermissionpolicyconfigurator)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator.cs:16`) registers one policy per
permission declared in `MMCA.Common.UI` or in a registered UI module's assembly when the
authorization options are first built, after the host has registered its modules, and keeps any
policy the host already registered under the same name (`:8-14`). `[Rubric §26, Front-End Security]`
and `[Rubric §18, UI Architecture]`.

**Writes made offline, and a log the app can show.** [`IOfflineWriteQueue`](#iofflinewritequeue)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/IOfflineWriteQueue.cs:11`), registered scoped by
`AddOfflineWriteQueue` (`MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:417`), is a durable queue in the
device's local store: each entry belongs to the user signed in when it was queued and is replayed
through the [`IOfflineWriteHandler`](#iofflinewritehandler) registered for its kind, matched ordinally
(`IOfflineWriteQueue.cs:5-10`, `MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/IOfflineWriteHandler.cs:5-9`).
[`OfflineWriteQueue`](#offlinewritequeue) (`MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/OfflineWriteQueue.cs:47`)
keeps the whole queue as one list under one semaphore, so concurrent callers of one instance never
lose a write, while two tabs or two circuits over one store are not coordinated (`:14-20`). A replay
walks the user's entries oldest first: an entry older than `MaxAge` is discarded as `Expired` without
being sent, an entry with no handler is skipped and kept, a transport failure, a timeout, or an
unexpected, too-many-requests or unauthorized answer keeps the entry with one more attempt and stops
the pass, a conflict discards it as `Conflict` and any other failure as `Rejected` (`:22-29`, the
outcomes being [`OfflineWriteOutcome`](#offlinewriteoutcome)). A replay starts when the device comes
back online, on the notifier component's first interactive render, and from a single retry timer on
the injected `TimeProvider` whose delay doubles after each pass that settled nothing; the timer is
removed when nothing is left to retry, when the device goes offline and on dispose (`:30-42`).
Signing out clears the local store and the queue with it (`:43-45`; the clear is the optional
`ILocalCacheStore` in [`AuthUIService`](#authuiservice), `MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthUIService.cs:54`,
`:599`). Separately, `AddInAppDiagnostics` registers [`InAppLogBuffer`](#inapplogbuffer)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Diagnostics/InAppLogBuffer.cs:11`), a bounded, thread-safe in-memory ring
buffer filled by [`InAppLoggerProvider`](#inapploggerprovider) and read by the `InAppDiagnosticsLog`
component, held only in process memory so nothing is written to disk or sent anywhere and the entries
are gone on restart (`:5-10`); its size and lowest recorded level are
[`InAppDiagnosticsOptions`](#inappdiagnosticsoptions)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Diagnostics/InAppDiagnosticsOptions.cs:6-10`). `[Rubric §29, Resilience]`
and `[Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]`.

**One composed Blazor web host.** The registration list, the request pipeline and the
additional-assembly list every Blazor Server plus WebAssembly head repeats are three calls on
[`BlazorWebHostExtensions`](#blazorwebhostextensions)
(`MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Hosting/BlazorWebHostExtensions.cs:44`, `:32-39`). `AddMmcaBlazorWebHost(options)`
registers, in a fixed order, the service defaults, Razor components with interactive server
components, bounded circuits and the UI rate limiter, MudBlazor, the shared UI services, the session
cookie pair, the trusted-caller header, session-cookie authentication, server token storage, the
same-origin proxy, the web form factor, the Blazor CSP and finally the security headers (`:50-61`,
`:75`). `UseMmcaBlazorWebPipeline` puts the UI rate limiter ahead of the exception handler and the
not-found re-execute, so a throttled request answers 429 without re-rendering a page, adds the
authenticated no-store header, and maps the client-config, session-cookie, same-origin proxy,
culture, static-asset and service-worker endpoints (`:166-173`, `:181`, `:203`), and
`GetMmcaRazorComponentAssemblies` supplies the head's additional assemblies (`:225`). What differs
between heads arrives through [`MmcaBlazorWebHostOptions`](#mmcablazorwebhostoptions) and
[`MmcaBlazorWebPipelineOptions`](#mmcablazorwebpipelineoptions); render-mode registration stays per
head, so the package takes no WebAssembly server dependency (`:35-38`), and a head must not register
`ITokenRefresher` or `ISessionCookieSync` after the call, because the same-origin proxy replaces both
and fails the boot when displaced (`:62-67`).

**How it wires up at startup.** A host's `Program.cs` calls `AddUIShared(configuration)` once, a C#
`extension(IServiceCollection)` member (see
[primer §4](00-primer.md#4-c-build-and-code-style-conventions)) on
[`DependencyInjection`](#dependencyinjection) (`MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:35`, `:43`).
In order it binds and **validates on start** [`ApiSettings`](#apisettings), so a missing endpoint
fails the host rather than the first request (`:42-45`; the read-only face of those options is
[`IApiSettings`](#iapisettings), whose `WasmApiEndpoint` lets the server call an internal URL while
the browser is handed an external one, `MMCA.Common.UI/Common/Settings/IApiSettings.cs:11-17`); binds
[`LayoutSettings`](#layoutsettings), `LegalSettings`, `RegistrationSettings`, [`SignInSettings`](#signinsettings) and
`NotificationBellOptions` *without* validation, deliberately optional so a host that configures none
of them keeps the compiled-in defaults; `TryAdd`s `TimeProvider.System` as the clock those
staleness policies are measured against; registers the
notification pages' authorization policy and its handler (`:81-85`); sets up localization, the
pseudo/Mud localizer decorators and the MudBlazor localization interceptor (`:88-110`); registers the
auth and culture delegating handlers and the named
`"APIClient"` whose base address comes from `ApiSettings` and whose timeout is pinned to
[`HttpResilienceDefaults`](group-16-aspire-orchestration.md#httpresiliencedefaults)`.TotalRequestTimeout`
rather than the BCL's arbitrary 100s, so the transport never pre-empts the resilience budget
(`:118-147`; when `Api:SameOriginApiEndpoint` is configured the base address is that proxy endpoint
and [`SameOriginProxyRequestHandler`](#sameoriginproxyrequesthandler) joins as the innermost handler,
`:120-121`, `:136`, `:149-154`); calls `AddCommonUiFacades()` for the toast and dialog pair (`:159`);
then `TryAdd`s [`AuthUIService`](#authuiservice), the email-confirmation client (`:166`), the
terms-acceptance client (`:170`), the [`OAuthFlowStateStore`](#oauthflowstatestore) (`:174`),
the two list-page state services,
[`NavigationHistoryService`](#navigationhistoryservice), [`ThemeService`](#themeservice),
[`EndpointCultureApplier`](#endpointcultureapplier), `ViewerTimeZone` (`:190`),
[`NavigationPublicLinkBuilder`](#navigationpubliclinkbuilder) behind
[`IPublicLinkBuilder`](#ipubliclinkbuilder) (share-sheet and QR links resolved against the browser
origin, which a MAUI head replaces because its WebView origin is a virtual host nobody else can open,
`MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Navigation/IPublicLinkBuilder.cs:9`,
`MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Navigation/NavigationPublicLinkBuilder.cs:11`), the preference reader and writer, and a
default [`IOAuthUISettings`](#ioauthuisettings) ([`DefaultOAuthUISettings`](#defaultoauthuisettings))
that downstream apps override with
[`ConfigurationOAuthUISettings`](#configurationoauthuisettings), which reads provider availability
from the `OAuth` section for a server host and from pre-computed `Enabled` flags for a WASM client
(`:161-204`, `MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/OAuth/ConfigurationOAuthUISettings.cs:19`, `:24-30`); and finally
calls `AddDeviceCapabilityDefaults()` so every capability contract resolves on every head (`:208`,
[ADR-042](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/042-device-capability-abstraction.html), chapter 26).
The `TryAdd*` discipline is what lets a consumer pre-register its own implementation and win. Browser
hosts add `AddClientAuthSessionCookieSync()` (`:240-242`) and `AddWasmFormFactor()` (`:252`); a
Blazor Server head adds `AddCommonServerTokenStorage()`, `AddCommonBlazorCsp()` (before
`AddCommonSecurityHeaders`, so it beats the `TryAdd`ed static provider) and
`AddCommonWebFormFactor()` from `MMCA.Common.UI.Web`
(`MMCA.Common.UI.Web/DependencyInjection.cs:41`, `:67`, `:85`; the first also registers `BrowserOriginHandler`, `:47-48`) plus the
`UseAuthenticatedNoStore()` middleware. A Blazor Web host that should install as a web app with an offline page also maps `MapCommonServiceWorker()` from [`ServiceWorkerEndpointExtensions`](#serviceworkerendpointextensions) (`MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Pwa/ServiceWorkerEndpointExtensions.cs:15`, `:60-70`): an anonymous `GET /service-worker.js` at the root so the worker's scope covers the whole site, excluded from the OpenAPI description and served `no-cache` (`:17-18`, `:34-37`), while the host supplies the app identity (manifest, icons, `theme-color`, `:10-14`). The worker never caches pages or data, because a server-rendered page carries the signed-in user's data: it sends every GET navigation to the network and falls back to the offline page only when the network fails, leaving every other request to the browser (`:40-46`). The package version is written into the embedded script, so each framework release is a byte change the browser installs on its next update check (`:48-51`, `:73-84`), and setting `Pwa:ServiceWorker:Enabled` to `false` serves a retired worker with no fetch handler that deletes the offline cache, so retiring a bad worker is a configuration change rather than a release (`:24`, `:52-57`, `:64-66`). The administration screens are opt-in on the same pattern:
`AddUserAdministrationUI<TUserDto>()` registers the generic service and **forwards** the non-generic
actions contract to that same instance, so the roster and the actions it performs go through one
object and one substitute in a test (`MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:321-328`), and
`AddRoleAdministrationUI()` registers the role client (`:295-297`); nothing in the framework calls
either, so an app serving no administration endpoints registers nothing and the components are
simply never rendered. An
SSR host behind the gateway also calls `AddTrustedCallerHeader(configuration)`, which composes
[`TrustedCallerHandler`](#trustedcallerhandler)
(`MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Security/TrustedCallerHandler.cs:35`) onto **every** `HttpClient` the host creates,
inserted at index 0 so the origin gate judges the authority the caller wrote rather than one Aspire's
service-discovery handler has already rewritten (`MMCA.Common.UI.Web/DependencyInjection.cs:121`,
`:143-156`), and registers nothing at all when no secret, header name or parseable gateway origin is
configured (the early return at `:137`). The breadth is the point: the call that suffers most from the gateway's per-IP
limiter partition, the cookie-session token refresh, is created by the framework under a name a host
cannot reach, while the handler itself stays narrow, stamping the secret only on a request whose
scheme, host and port match the gateway origin and replacing rather than appending the header, because
the gateway compares one single-valued header in constant time (`TrustedCallerHandler.cs:9-27`,
`:67-79`). [`UISharedAssemblyReference`](#uisharedassemblyreference)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:502`) is the marker other assemblies scan against.

**How a WebAssembly client learns its API address.** The WASM bundle is static, so the API base
address is fetched at runtime rather than baked in. On the server side,
[`ClientConfigEndpointExtensions`](#clientconfigendpointextensions)
(`MMCA.Common.UI.Web/ClientConfig/ClientConfigEndpointExtensions.cs:19`) adds
`MapClientConfigEndpoint`, an anonymous `GET /client-config` excluded from the OpenAPI description
whose framework-owned `Api` section carries `Api:WasmApiEndpoint` (`:17`, `:52-81`). It
**fails closed**: with that key missing it throws rather than fall back to `Api:ApiEndpoint`, which is
the server head's service-discovery name a browser cannot resolve, so the client fails to start
instead of pointing at the wrong API (`:32-38`, `:53-59`). When the host runs the same-origin proxy,
the same `api` section also carries `sameOriginApiEndpoint`, the proxy prefix with a trailing slash,
which is what moves the client's `"APIClient"` onto it (`:84-99`). The endpoint declares `AllowAnonymous`
itself, because the client fetches the document before it can hold a session and a host's fallback
policy would otherwise gate it (`:40-44`, `:80`). A host adds its own sections through a per-request
[`ClientConfigBuilder`](#clientconfigbuilder)
(`MMCA.Common.UI.Web/ClientConfig/ClientConfigBuilder.cs:19`), whose `Add` refuses a blank name, the
reserved `Api` section and a duplicate, and whose remarks warn that everything added is served to
every browser before sign-in, so only public values belong there (`:12-16`, `:45-62`). The client
half is [`MmcaClientConfigBootstrap`](#mmcaclientconfigbootstrap)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Common/Settings/MmcaClientConfigBootstrap.cs:28`), whose `LoadAsync` fetches the
document from the app's own origin with a 15-second per-attempt timeout and a single retry after one
second (for the cold-start case where the Server host is still warming), then rethrows a second
failure on purpose, and returns a buffered stream because browser fetch streams do not support the
synchronous reads `AddJsonStream` performs (`:12-22`, `:30`, `:33`, `:44-85`). Only the timeout it
did not ask for is retried, never the caller's own cancellation (`:87-90`). ADC wires both halves, the server half through the `ClientConfig` callback it hands
`UseMmcaBlazorWebPipeline`
(`MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web/Program.cs:128`,
`MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web/Program.cs:170`,
`MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web.Client/Program.cs:31`).

The small Level-0 supporting cast fills in the rest: [`NotificationRoutePaths`](#notificationroutepaths)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Common/NotificationRoutePaths.cs:8`), whose deep-link builder formats invariantly
because the route's `:int` constraint is the validation boundary (`:14-20`);
[`QrErrorCorrectionLevel`](#qrerrorcorrectionlevel), the framework's own enum for `QrCodeImage` so the
component's public API does not pin consumers to QRCoder's `ECCLevel`
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Sharing/QrErrorCorrectionLevel.cs:9`);
[`RatingStars`](#ratingstars) (`MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Ratings/RatingStars.razor.cs:13`), five
read-only stars out of a `MaxValue` of 5 rendered as one `role="img"` element whose required
`AriaLabel` carries the numeric figure, so the stars stay decorative rounding (whole stars fill, a
half star shows at .5 and above, `:6-11`, `:16`, `:31-33`, `:46-54`), which the ADC feedback and
speaker dashboards render
(`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.UI/Pages/Feedback/OrganizerSessionFeedback.razor:67`);
[`ApiFileDownloadButton`](#apifiledownloadbutton)
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Forms/ApiFileDownloadButton.razor.cs:16`), which gives browsers a plain download
link and native heads a fetch-stage-share flow, stripping directory segments from the supplied file
name so a value built from entity data cannot steer the write out of the temp directory (`:21-30`);
and [`MauiBackNavigationBridge`](#mauibacknavigationbridge) with its
[`BackNavigationResult`](#backnavigationresult) for MAUI hardware-back handling, which reports both
whether `history.back()` fired and whether the WebView is at the root of its stack so a host can decide
to exit (`MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Navigation/MauiBackNavigationBridge.cs:19`, `:28`). Form-factor
detection has graduated into its own device-capability layer
([`IFormFactor`](group-26-device-capability-layer.md#iformfactor) and friends, chapter 26). The
presentational helper [`MoneyExtensions`](#moneyextensions) formats
[`Money`](group-02-domain-building-blocks.md#money) for display, grouping a mixed collection by
currency so unrelated amounts never collapse under whichever symbol came first
(`MMCA.Common.UI/Extensions/MoneyExtensions.cs:14`, the single-price form at `:29-30` and the
collection form at `:33`), keeping a display concern out of the
domain value object, exactly where Clean Architecture wants it.

Read the per-type sections that follow for the mechanics. The consumer-side module UIs live in the ADC
module-UI chapter ([chapter 21](group-21-conference-ui.md)), and the bUnit component tests plus the
Playwright/axe-core E2E suite that exercise this package are covered in the testing chapter
([chapter 27](group-29-testing-infrastructure.md)), which is where `[Rubric §28, Front-End Testing]`
lives.

### PagePermissionPolicy

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Authorization` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/PagePermissionPolicy.cs:9` · Level 0 · class (static)

- **What it is**: the naming rule for the page permission policies. It turns a permission name such as `conference:sessions:manage` into the policy name a [HasPagePermissionAttribute](#haspagepermissionattribute) asks for.
- **Depends on**: nothing.
- **Concept introduced, a policy name as a shared contract.** ASP.NET Core authorization looks a policy up by string, so the attribute that names a policy and the code that registers it must agree on the exact string. Putting the format in one static class makes that agreement a compile-time reference rather than two copies of a literal. `[Rubric §26, Front-End Security]` assesses whether client-side route guards are consistent and hard to get wrong; one builder used by both sides is how this code keeps the guard and its registration from drifting.
- **Walkthrough**: `Prefix = "page-perm:"` (`PagePermissionPolicy.cs:12`) and `NameFor(string permission) => Prefix + permission` (`PagePermissionPolicy.cs:17`). Nothing else.
- **Why it's built this way**: the class doc comment (`PagePermissionPolicy.cs:3-8`) records why the prefix differs from the API's `perm:`: the API's policy provider, which a web host may install by replacement, intercepts every `perm:` name, while a `page-perm:` name falls through to the default provider and so reaches the policy `AddUIShared` registered. A distinct prefix is what lets the page guard coexist with [ADR-020](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/020-permission-based-authorization.html)'s API policies on a Blazor Web head that hosts both.
- **Where it's used**: the [HasPagePermissionAttribute](#haspagepermissionattribute) constructor passes `NameFor(permission)` to its base (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/HasPagePermissionAttribute.cs:24`), and [PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator](#pagepermissionpolicyconfigurator) registers under the same name (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator.cs:35`). The permission-coverage fitness rule strips the same prefix to recover the permission from an `[Authorize(Policy = ...)]` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Rules/Api/ArchitectureRules.PermissionCoverage.cs:16`, `:140-142`).
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: the fitness rule keeps its own `"page-perm:"` literal (`ArchitectureRules.PermissionCoverage.cs:16`) rather than referencing `Prefix`, so the two strings agree by convention, not by the compiler.

### PagePermissionRequirement

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Authorization` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/PagePermissionRequirement.cs:11` · Level 0 · record (internal, sealed)

- **What it is**: the authorization requirement behind every page permission policy: the caller's token carries a `permission` claim equal to `Permission`.
- **Depends on**: `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization.IAuthorizationRequirement` (`PagePermissionRequirement.cs:1`).
- **Concept**: the requirement/handler split of ASP.NET Core authorization, the same shape as [NotificationPageRequirement](#notificationpagerequirement) in this group: a requirement is pure data, and a separate handler decides whether it is met.
- **Walkthrough**: one positional record, `internal sealed record PagePermissionRequirement(string Permission) : IAuthorizationRequirement;` (`PagePermissionRequirement.cs:11`). The doc comment (`PagePermissionRequirement.cs:5-10`) names its evaluator, [PagePermissionAuthorizationHandler](#pagepermissionauthorizationhandler).
- **Why it's built this way**: internal, because nothing outside the framework constructs one; a host only writes the attribute. A record gives value equality for free, which is all a requirement needs.
- **Where it's used**: constructed once per declared permission by [PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator](#pagepermissionpolicyconfigurator) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator.cs:40`). The shipped nav-guard contract base recognizes it by type name to model what a guarded page demands (`MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.UI/Navigation/NavItemGuardContractTestsBase.cs:50`, `:313-315`), which is why it can stay internal.

### UISharedAssemblyReference

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:502` · Level 0 · class

- **What it is**: an empty marker class whose only job is to give code a compile-checked `typeof(...).Assembly` handle on the shared UI assembly.
- **Depends on**: nothing.
- **Concept introduced, the assembly-marker type.** Reflection over an assembly needs an `Assembly` instance, and there are two ways to get one: a string (`Assembly.Load("MMCA.Common.UI")`, which fails at run time when someone renames the project) or a type reference (`typeof(UISharedAssemblyReference).Assembly`, which fails at compile time and is carried along by a rename refactoring). Every layer of the framework ships an equivalent marker; this is the UI layer's. `[Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality]` assesses exactly this kind of refactor-safety over stringly-typed lookups.
- **Walkthrough**: a single declaration using the semicolon type body, `public class UISharedAssemblyReference;` (`DependencyInjection.cs:502`), with its doc comment on line 217. It shares a file with [DependencyInjection](#dependencyinjection) but is declared at namespace scope **beneath** it, outside that static class, because a type nested inside a static class could not serve as a public marker the same way. It carries no members, so nothing can accidentally depend on state it does not have.
- **Why it's built this way**: type-only, public and empty is the whole point. It is the assembly's identity expressed as a symbol the compiler tracks.
- **Where it's used**: the architecture fitness suite is the real consumer. `CommonArchitectureMap` registers the assembly as the framework's UI layer with `Framework(Layer.Ui, typeof(Common.UI.UISharedAssemblyReference).Assembly)` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Common.Architecture.Tests/CommonArchitectureMap.cs:27`), which is what lets the shared layer-dependency rules know which assembly *is* the UI layer; `AnonymousEndpointTests` includes it in the assemblies it scans (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Common.Architecture.Tests/Api/AnonymousEndpointTests.cs:19`); and `NavigationContractTests` enumerates its types with `typeof(UI.UISharedAssemblyReference).Assembly.GetTypes()` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.Common.Architecture.Tests/Ui/NavigationContractTests.cs:105`). `[Rubric §34, Architecture Governance & Documentation]` applies: this one-line type is what makes a layer boundary machine-checkable.
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: the doc comment (`DependencyInjection.cs:346`) offers "e.g., for Scrutor scanning" as the motivating case, but no Scrutor registration in this repo takes its scan root from this marker. `AddUIModule<TModule>()` scans `FromAssemblyOf<TModule>()` (`DependencyInjection.cs:491`), taking the root from the module descriptor's own assembly instead. Trust the call sites: the current consumers are the architecture tests.

### HasPagePermissionAttribute

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Authorization` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/HasPagePermissionAttribute.cs:19` · Level 1 · class (sealed attribute)

- **What it is**: the attribute a Blazor page puts on itself to require a signed-in caller whose token carries a given permission claim, in every UI head (web, WebAssembly and MAUI), for example `@attribute [HasPagePermission(ConferencePermissions.ActivitiesManage)]` (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.UI/Pages/Activities/ActivityList.razor:2`).
- **Depends on**: [PagePermissionPolicy](#pagepermissionpolicy); `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization.AuthorizeAttribute` (`HasPagePermissionAttribute.cs:1`, `:19`).
- **Concept introduced, the page-side twin of a menu permission.** The doc comment (`HasPagePermissionAttribute.cs:5-10`) states the design goal: the attribute and [NavItem](#navitem)'s `RequiredPermission` check the claim with the same `HasPermissionClaim` ([ClaimsPrincipalExtensions](group-08-auth.md#claimsprincipalextensions), `MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:95`), so a menu entry gated on a permission and the page it opens cannot disagree; the menu runs that check at `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Layout/NavMenu.razor.cs:127`. `[Rubric §25, Navigation & IA]` assesses whether navigation and route access are consistent; here the two derive from one predicate. `[Rubric §26, Front-End Security]` assesses route guards: the attribute derives from `AuthorizeAttribute`, so the Blazor router's standard `[Authorize]` handling applies it, rather than each page checking in code. The server-side counterpart is [ADR-020](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/020-permission-based-authorization.html)'s API permission policy; this attribute is a UI guard only, and the API still authorizes every call itself.
- **Walkthrough**: `[AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Class, AllowMultiple = true, Inherited = true)]` (`HasPagePermissionAttribute.cs:18`). The constructor passes `PagePermissionPolicy.NameFor(permission)` to the base as the policy name and keeps the raw permission (`HasPagePermissionAttribute.cs:23-24`), exposed as `Permission` (`HasPagePermissionAttribute.cs:27`) so the configurator can read it back by reflection.
- **Why it's built this way**: the second paragraph of the doc comment (`HasPagePermissionAttribute.cs:11-16`) gives the two decisions. No registration is needed, because `AddUIShared` registers one policy per permission declared on a component in `MMCA.Common.UI` or in any registered UI module's assembly (see [PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator](#pagepermissionpolicyconfigurator)). And the check reads the claim only, because a UI head has no permission registry, so it suits a host whose token issuer stamps permission claims; a role-only token never passes.
- **Where it's used**: ADC's Conference management pages (for example the activity, category and event list, create and detail pages, `MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.UI/Pages/Events/EventList.razor:2`); the module descriptor notes that its nav items require the same permissions so an editor sees exactly the entries its grant opens (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.UI/ConferenceUIModule.cs:27`). The permission-coverage fitness rule reads the attribute by full name and its `Permission` value (`MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Rules/Api/ArchitectureRules.PermissionCoverage.cs:9`, `:120`).

### PagePermissionAuthorizationHandler

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Authorization` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/PagePermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:12` · Level 1 · class (internal, sealed)

- **What it is**: the handler that decides a [PagePermissionRequirement](#pagepermissionrequirement): it succeeds when the principal carries the permission claim.
- **Depends on**: [PagePermissionRequirement](#pagepermissionrequirement), `HasPermissionClaim` from [ClaimsPrincipalExtensions](group-08-auth.md#claimsprincipalextensions) (`PagePermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:2`); `AuthorizationHandler<TRequirement>`.
- **Concept**: cross-reference [NotificationPageAuthorizationHandler](#notificationpageauthorizationhandler), which uses the same `HasPermissionClaim` for its optional permission (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Notifications/NotificationPageAuthorizationHandler.cs:39`).
- **Walkthrough**: `HandleRequirementAsync` (`PagePermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:15-28`) guards both arguments (`:19-20`), calls `context.Succeed(requirement)` only when `context.User.HasPermissionClaim(requirement.Permission)` (`:22-25`), and returns `Task.CompletedTask` (`:27`). It never calls `Fail`, so a missing claim simply leaves the requirement unmet.
- **Why it's built this way**: the doc comment (`PagePermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:6-11`) calls `HasPermissionClaim` the framework's single definition of a token-granted permission and the same check the nav menu runs, so page and menu entry cannot disagree. The handler does not test authentication itself: the policy adds `RequireAuthenticatedUser()` (`PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator.cs:39`), so an unauthenticated principal never passes.
- **Where it's used**: registered by `AddUIShared` through `TryAddEnumerable` as a transient `IAuthorizationHandler` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:112-113`).

### PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Authorization` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Authorization/PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator.cs:16` · Level 3 · class (internal, sealed)

- **What it is**: an `IConfigureOptions<AuthorizationOptions>` that discovers every permission a [HasPagePermissionAttribute](#haspagepermissionattribute) declares and registers one policy for each, so a host adds a guarded page with no registration call of its own.
- **Depends on**: [IUIModule](#iuimodule) (primary constructor, `PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator.cs:16`), [PagePermissionPolicy](#pagepermissionpolicy), [HasPagePermissionAttribute](#haspagepermissionattribute), [PagePermissionRequirement](#pagepermissionrequirement); `System.Reflection` and `Microsoft.Extensions.Options` (`PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator.cs:1-3`).
- **Concept introduced, options configuration as late discovery.** An `IConfigureOptions<T>` runs when the options instance is first built, not when it is registered. The doc comment (`PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator.cs:8-14`) relies on exactly that: it runs after the host has registered its modules, so the module list it scans is complete regardless of whether `AddUIShared` was called before or after the `Add{Module}UI()` calls. `[Rubric §33, Developer Experience]` assesses how many steps a common change takes; adding a guarded page here is one attribute.
- **Walkthrough**: `Configure` (`PagePermissionPolicyConfigurator.cs:20-43`) builds the permission set as one LINQ pipeline (`:24-31`): every module's `Assembly` (`:25`), plus the framework's own UI assembly (`:26`), deduplicated (`:27`), flattened to their types through `LoadableTypes` (`:28`), each type's `HasPagePermissionAttribute`s read with `inherit: true` (`:29`), projected to `Permission` (`:30`) and deduplicated ordinally (`:31`). For each permission it computes the policy name (`:35`) and, only when `options.GetPolicy(name)` is null (`:36`), adds a policy that requires an authenticated user and a [PagePermissionRequirement](#pagepermissionrequirement) (`:38-40`). `LoadableTypes` (`:47-57`) returns `assembly.GetTypes()` and, on a `ReflectionTypeLoadException`, the types that did load (`:53-55`); its comment (`:45-46`) explains that a module assembly referencing something the head does not load would otherwise fail the whole scan.
- **Why it's built this way**: keeping an existing policy of the same name (`:36`) leaves the host the last word, consistent with the `TryAdd` convention of [DependencyInjection](#dependencyinjection). Scanning the registered modules, rather than every loaded assembly, bounds the reflection to the assemblies that can contribute routable pages.
- **Where it's used**: registered by `AddUIShared` through `TryAddEnumerable` as a transient `IConfigureOptions<AuthorizationOptions>` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:110-111`); its module list comes from the `AddSingleton<IUIModule, TModule>()` that `AddUIModule<TModule>()` performs (`DependencyInjection.cs:496`).
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: the framework assembly is scanned too (`:26`), but no `.razor` or `.cs` file under `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation` applies the attribute today, so in practice the policies come from module assemblies.
