### ListPageQueryStateService

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/ListPageQueryStateService.cs:28` · Level 2 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the two-way translator between a [ListPageState](#listpagestate) and the browser
  address bar, so browser back/forward, a refresh and a link pasted into chat all restore the same
  filtered, sorted, paged view.
- **Depends on**: [ListPageState](#listpagestate), [ColumnFilterState](#columnfilterstate) and
  [QueryStringCodec](#querystringcodec), which parses and appends query strings, so the UI package
  takes no query-helper dependency; externals `NavigationManager` and `StringValues`.
- **Concept introduced, the URL as shareable state.**
  `[Rubric §25, Navigation & Information Architecture]` assesses whether the address bar reflects what
  the user is looking at; this class is that contract for every list page. The remarks
  (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:13-27`) document the reserved keys and why they are terse (they end up
  in shareable links): `p` (0-indexed desktop page), `ps` (page size), `mp` (1-indexed mobile page),
  `s` (sort column), `sd` (`desc` only, since ascending is the default), `d` (`1` only, since
  comfortable density is the default), `q` (free-text search), `f:<name>` for any other named
  filter and `c:<property>` for a grid column filter, written `<operator>:<value>` because MudDataGrid
  operators never contain a colon (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:24`). Defaults are omitted entirely,
  so a pristine list page has a clean URL.
  `[Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow]` applies because this is the second of the three
  transports the same record travels over.
- **Walkthrough**
  - The key names are private constants (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:30-42`), including the
    `"search"` filter name that maps to `q` by convention, the `c:` prefix and its `:` separator
    (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:38-39`), and the `desc`/`1` markers. A separate
    `MaxPageSize` constant of `1000` (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:47`) caps the page size a URL may
    ask for; its summary (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:44-46`) ties it to the same ceiling
    `KeysetPageRequest.MaxPageSize` states.
  - `ReadCurrent()` (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:52-56`) is the instance entry point: it resolves the
    absolute URI from the injected `NavigationManager` and hands the query to the parser.
  - `ParseQueryString` (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:63`) is deliberately `static` and public,
    documented as a pure helper exposed for unit testing without a `NavigationManager`
    (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:58-62`). It parses through `QueryStringCodec.Parse`
    (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:65`), then reads the three integers through `TryGetInt`
    (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:273-283`, which parses with `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` and falls
    back to the supplied default rather than throwing). Out-of-range values get the same fallback as
    unparsable ones (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:67-71`): the page is floored at `0`, the mobile page
    at `1`, and a page size outside `1..1000` collapses to `0`, the page default, through
    `ClampPageSize` (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:271`). The inline comment states the reason: a
    hand-edited or stale link with `p=-3` or `ps=5000` must not leave the list stuck on a failing
    fetch. It then treats a blank sort value as no sort
    (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:74-81`), matches `desc` case-insensitively
    (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:86`) but the dense marker `1` ordinally
    (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:92`), then hands the rest to `ParseFilters`
    (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:95`, body at `ListPageQueryStateService.cs:191-220`), which skips
    empty values, folds `q` into the `search` filter, strips the `f:` prefix off named filters and
    turns each `c:` key into a [ColumnFilterState](#columnfilterstate)
    (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:212-216`). Both dictionaries land on the returned state
    (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:105-106`).
  - `TryParseColumnFilter` (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:256-268`) splits the value at its first
    colon. A value with no colon or no operator (`separator <= 0`, `ListPageQueryStateService.cs:259`)
    is a hand-edited link and is ignored, and an empty value after the colon becomes a `null` value
    for an operator that takes none, such as `is empty` (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:251-255`).
  - `BuildPath` (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:115`) is the inverse, and the omission rules are visible
    one by one: page only when `> 0` (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:122`), page size only when `> 0`
    (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:127`), mobile page only when `> 1`
    (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:132`), `sd` only when a sort column exists and is descending
    (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:137-144`), `d` only when dense
    (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:146-149`). Filters go through `AddFilterParameters`
    (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:151`, body at `ListPageQueryStateService.cs:223-249`), which writes
    `q`, the `f:` keys and one `c:<property>` key per column filter that has an operator
    (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:242-248`). With no parameters at all it returns the bare base path,
    otherwise it appends them with `QueryStringCodec.AddQueryString`
    (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:153-155`).
  - `ReplaceState` (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:174`) writes the URL back using
    `NavigationOptions { ReplaceHistoryEntry = true }` (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:187`) so filter
    changes do not pollute the back stack.
- **Why it's built this way**: the most instructive part is the guard in `ReplaceState`
  (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:179-184`), which drops the write when the current path no longer
  matches the owning `basePath`. The remarks (`ListPageQueryStateService.cs:164-173`) record the
  diagnosed defect: a grid-state write is inherently deferred (a debounced search, a late `ServerData`
  completion), so it can land after the user has already navigated away. Building from the then-current
  URI used to stamp grid parameters onto the next page's URL and issue a spurious navigation that
  disposed it mid-load, and detail pages reached by clicking a list row had their first data fetch
  canceled about 66ms in, leaving them stuck on their loading state.
- **Where it's used**: registered `TryAddScoped` (`DependencyInjection.cs:217`) and injected into
  [DataGridListPageBase<TDto>](#datagridlistpagebasetdto)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Common/DataGridListPageBase.cs:30`), which
  reads the URL on initialization and on parameter changes (`DataGridListPageBase.cs:266` and
  `DataGridListPageBase.cs:337`) and writes it back after a grid or filter change
  (`DataGridListPageBase.cs:1720` and `DataGridListPageBase.cs:1797`).

### ListPageStateService

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/ListPageStateService.cs:70` · Level 2 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the per-circuit memory of list-page state, keyed by route, with an optional
  write-through to `sessionStorage` so the state survives things a circuit-scoped dictionary cannot.
- **Depends on**: [ListPageState](#listpagestate) and [LazyJsModule](#lazyjsmodule); externals
  `IJSRuntime`, `IJSObjectReference` and the `nav-interop.js` module shipped in the package's
  `wwwroot`.
- **Concept introduced, a synchronous fast path with an asynchronous durable path.**
  `[Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow]` assesses how state survives lifecycle boundaries; this
  class answers with two tiers. The class comment (`ListPageStateService.cs:62-69`) names exactly what
  the durable tier buys: state survives circuit teardowns, `forceLoad: true` navigations and the SSR to
  WASM render-mode transition. The synchronous dictionary matters just as much, because it is safe to
  read from `OnInitialized` during prerender, when JS interop does not exist yet.
- **Walkthrough**
  - Two constants set the contract: the module path `./_content/MMCA.Common.UI/nav-interop.js`
    (`ListPageStateService.cs:72`) and the `mmca.lps:` session-key prefix
    (`ListPageStateService.cs:73`). State is a plain `Dictionary<string, ListPageState>`
    (`ListPageStateService.cs:75`) plus one [LazyJsModule](#lazyjsmodule)
    (`ListPageStateService.cs:76`).
  - `GetState` (`ListPageStateService.cs:83-84`) is a `GetValueOrDefault` and is documented as safe to
    call during SSR prerender (`ListPageStateService.cs:78-82`). `SaveState`
    (`ListPageStateService.cs:91-92`) stores in memory only.
  - `UpdateScrollPosition` (`ListPageStateService.cs:99-102`) is the fast path for scroll events: it
    uses a `with` expression to preserve every other field, and creates a minimal entry when none
    exists yet, for the case where the user scrolls before the grid has fired its first save.
  - `HydrateFromSessionAsync` (`ListPageStateService.cs:110`) invokes `sessionGet` on the JS module
    (`ListPageStateService.cs:120`, the export at
    `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/wwwroot/nav-interop.js:12`) and adopts any
    persisted snapshot (`ListPageStateService.cs:121-124`).
  - `PersistToSessionAsync` (`ListPageStateService.cs:137`) does the reverse through `sessionSet`
    (`ListPageStateService.cs:152`, `nav-interop.js:24`), returning early when there is nothing in
    memory to write (`ListPageStateService.cs:139-142`).
  - `ClearAsync` (`ListPageStateService.cs:169`) forgets every list page's state: it clears the
    in-memory dictionary first (`ListPageStateService.cs:171`), then calls `sessionRemoveByPrefix` with
    the `mmca.lps:` prefix (`ListPageStateService.cs:181`, the export at `nav-interop.js:45`), leaving
    the tab's other `sessionStorage` keys alone. Its summary (`ListPageStateService.cs:161-168`) gives
    the reason: the search and filters belong to the account that typed them, `sessionStorage` outlives
    the session in the same tab, and clearing memory before the first await means a caller that cannot
    await still drops it at once.
  - All three interop methods share one exception filter, `catch (Exception ex) when
    (IsInteropUnavailable(ex))` (`ListPageStateService.cs:126`, `ListPageStateService.cs:154` and
    `ListPageStateService.cs:183`). `IsInteropUnavailable` (`ListPageStateService.cs:212-213`) matches
    `InvalidOperationException` (prerender), `JSDisconnectedException` (a torn-down circuit),
    `JSException` (a browser-side failure such as Safari Private mode or an exceeded quota) and
    `TaskCanceledException` (an interop timeout or cancellation); the comment above it
    (`ListPageStateService.cs:209-211`) notes it is the same set
    [PendingToastService](#pendingtoastservice) swallows. The catch in `PersistToSessionAsync`
    (`ListPageStateService.cs:156-157`) records why it matters there: the call is fire-and-forget from
    the grid page, so an escaping exception would be an unobserved fault.
  - The private `GetModuleAsync` (`ListPageStateService.cs:190-204`) converts an unavailable runtime
    into a `null` module rather than an exception, which is what makes the public methods' early
    returns read cleanly. `DisposeAsync` (`ListPageStateService.cs:207`) simply forwards to the module
    wrapper.
- **Why it's built this way**: the degradation contract here is "never let storage failures break the
  calling page", which is why this class swallows what [LazyJsModule](#lazyjsmodule) deliberately does
  not. Scoped registration means one instance per circuit, so the in-memory dictionary is naturally
  per-user without any keying by identity.
- **Where it's used**: registered `TryAddScoped` (`DependencyInjection.cs:216`) and injected into
  [DataGridListPageBase<TDto>](#datagridlistpagebasetdto) (`DataGridListPageBase.cs:29`), which reads
  it during state restore (`DataGridListPageBase.cs:268`), hydrates from session on first render
  (`DataGridListPageBase.cs:503`), records scroll offsets (`DataGridListPageBase.cs:688`), and
  saves plus persists after grid and density changes (`DataGridListPageBase.cs:1699-1726` and
  `DataGridListPageBase.cs:1792-1801`). [JwtAuthenticationStateProvider](#jwtauthenticationstateprovider)
  takes it as an optional dependency
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/JwtAuthenticationStateProvider.cs:43`)
  and calls `ClearAsync` on sign-in and sign-out (`JwtAuthenticationStateProvider.cs:141`,
  `JwtAuthenticationStateProvider.cs:149` and `JwtAuthenticationStateProvider.cs:153-154`); the
  session-ended handler cannot await, so it relies on the synchronous in-memory clear
  (`JwtAuthenticationStateProvider.cs:147-148`).

### MudToastService
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/MudToastService.cs:33` · Level 2 · class (internal sealed)

- **What it is**: the MudBlazor-backed [IToastService](#itoastservice). It is one of only two types in
  the framework that name a component-library service, the other being its sibling
  [MudAppDialogService](#mudappdialogservice).
- **Depends on**: [IToastService](#itoastservice) (the contract implemented at
  `MudToastService.cs:33`) and [ToastSeverity](#toastseverity) (the vendor-neutral level, taken as a
  `Show` parameter at line 56 and switched over at lines 180-186); MudBlazor's `ISnackbar` (held in a
  private field, line 35), `Snackbar`, `Severity`, `Variant`, `Color` and `SnackbarOptions`, and
  `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Rendering.RenderTreeBuilder` (ASP.NET Core) for the one method that
  renders markup (lines 63-69).
- **Concept introduced, the vendor boundary.** `[Rubric §20, Design System, Theming & UI Consistency]`
  assesses whether the app depends on its own design vocabulary rather than on a specific component
  library's API. Every page, component and `Result` helper in both applications depends on
  `IToastService`; only this class and `MudAppDialogService` know that MudBlazor exists, and the DI
  comment says so outright
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:225-230`).
  `[Rubric §14, Testability & Test Strategy]` is the practical payoff: a test records toasts against
  the interface without rendering a snackbar host, which is how
  [ResultUiExtensions](#resultuiextensions)`.NotifyOnFailure` can be tested at all
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Common/ResultUiExtensions.cs:255,267`).
  `[Rubric §1, SOLID Principles]` covers the shape: an internal implementation behind a public
  interface means no consumer can name the concrete type even by accident. The class doc comment also
  states why toast text is not duplicated into a second screen-reader channel: `MmcaThemeProviders`
  hosts MudBlazor's `MudSnackbarProvider` inside a `role="status" aria-live="polite"` element, so the
  rendered toast is itself the live-region content, and pushing the same sentence through a second
  channel would announce it twice and make every text locator ambiguous.
- **Walkthrough**
  - The class holds `ISnackbar` in a private field (`_snackbar`, line 35) set by an explicit
    constructor (line 41) rather than a primary-constructor parameter; the two are behaviorally
    identical, only the field-access syntax changed. Beside it sit the pinned-toast bookkeeping, a
    `List<Snackbar>` (`_pinned`, line 38) and a `Lock` (`_pinnedSync`, line 39).
  - Four one-liners cover the common levels: `Success`, `Info`, `Warning` and `Error` (lines 44, 47,
    50, 53), each a direct `_snackbar.Add(message, Severity.X)`. `Show(message, severity)` (line 56) is
    the same call with the level chosen at runtime. None of these is pinned, so they never touch the
    tracking list.
  - `ShowPersistent(title, body, severity)` (line 59) is the push-notification shape. It renders a
    two-line body through a `RenderTreeBuilder` (a bolded title, a line break, then the body,
    lines 63-69) and sets `RequireInteraction = true` with `Variant.Filled` (lines 75-76). The comment
    states the rule (lines 73-74): the message arrived unprompted, so it must survive until the user
    has actually looked at the screen rather than expiring on the default timer. The whole `Add` call
    is wrapped in `AddPinned(...)` (line 60) so the toast is tracked and capped.
  - `ShowAction(message, actionText, onAction, severity, requireInteraction)` (line 80) is the
    undo-style toast. A local `Configure` function (line 96) sets `Action` and `ActionColor` (lines
    98-99) and adapts MudBlazor's click signature to the caller's parameterless delegate by discarding
    the `Snackbar` instance MudBlazor passes (line 103). `requireInteraction` is opt-in: when false the
    toast goes straight to `_snackbar.Add` (line 93) so the host's own snackbar timing applies and the
    toast is not tracked; when true it goes through `AddPinned` (line 89) and `Configure` states both
    `RequireInteraction` and `Variant.Filled` outright rather than relying on MudBlazor's null default
    (comment at lines 107-110, values at lines 111-112).
  - `AddPinned(Func<Snackbar?> add)` (line 122) is the pinned-toast cap. MudBlazor shows at most
    `SnackbarConfiguration.MaxDisplayedSnackbars` at once and queues the rest out of sight, and a
    pinned toast never expires, so a burst of pushes would fill every slot and each newer toast would
    wait invisibly. Under the lock (line 124), when tracked toasts have reached the cap
    (`_snackbar.Configuration.MaxDisplayedSnackbars`, line 130) it removes the oldest one this service
    raised (lines 131-136), then adds the new one and subscribes `ForgetPinned` to its `OnClose`
    (lines 141-146). The newest is therefore always the one on screen. The class comment states the
    scope: only toasts this service added are ever removed, timed toasts and snackbars raised
    elsewhere are untouched (`MudToastService.cs:18-27`), and the tracking is per circuit or per app
    because the service is scoped, with a lock because close events arrive on timer threads (lines
    28-31). A null return from `add()` means the host's duplicate prevention suppressed the toast, so
    there is nothing to track (comment at line 140).
  - Two helpers keep the list honest. `ForgetPinned` (line 165) drops a toast from the list when its
    `OnClose` fires, under the same lock. `ForgetRemovedPinned` (line 156) catches removals that raise
    no event (`ISnackbar.Remove`, `RemoveByKey`, `Clear`): when fewer snackbars are shown than the cap,
    nothing is queued, so any tracked toast absent from `ShownSnackbars` is gone and is pruned (lines
    158-161).
  - `Map(ToastSeverity)` (line 178) projects the neutral enum onto MudBlazor's with an explicit switch
    over all five members plus a `Normal` default (lines 180-186). It is written out rather than cast on
    purpose: the two enums agree numerically today, and an implicit dependency on that would break
    silently the day either side gains a member (comment at lines 173-177).
  - The cap behavior is pinned by `MudToastServicePinnedCapTests`, which builds the service over a
    `SnackbarConfiguration` with `MaxDisplayedSnackbars = Cap`
    (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/MudToastServicePinnedCapTests.cs:124`).
  - Nothing wraps `onAction`. The absence is a documented contract, pinned by a test that asserts a
    throwing callback propagates
    (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/MudToastServiceTests.cs:49-59`): a
    caller whose work can fail guards it instead of discovering the failure as a swallowed no-op.
- **Why it's built this way**: keeping the vendor type behind a facade is what makes the component
  library swappable in principle and mockable in practice, and it is the reason the framework ships
  `AddCommonUiFacades()` as its own registration
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:278-284`), factored out so a
  bUnit harness can register exactly these three services (toast, dialog and pending toast) without
  pulling in the whole shared-UI surface (comment at lines 165-166). Every method returns `void`: a
  toast is fire-and-forget by design, and MudBlazor's `ISnackbar.Add` is synchronous. The pinned-toast
  eviction exists because a notification burst is the one case where fire-and-forget silently loses
  the newest message.
- **Where it's used**: registered by `AddCommonUiFacades` with `TryAddScoped`
  (`DependencyInjection.cs:280`), which `AddUIShared` calls for every host
  (`DependencyInjection.cs:187`). Consumers resolve `IToastService`, never this type: the framework's
  `NotificationListener` raises an incoming push as a persistent toast
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Notifications/NotificationListener.razor:49`),
  [ResultUiExtensions](#resultuiextensions)`.NotifyOnFailure` turns a failed
  [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result) into one
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Common/ResultUiExtensions.cs:267`), and ADC's
  [LiveEventListener](group-22-engagement-module.md#liveeventlistener) uses the action shape for its
  reconnect prompt
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Components/LiveEventListener.razor.cs:191,332`).
  Its own behavior is pinned by
  [MudToastServiceTests](group-29-testing-infrastructure.md#per-project-test-rollup), which captures the
  options lambda and applies it to a fresh `SnackbarOptions` carrying MudBlazor's defaults, so the
  assertions see exactly what a rendered snackbar would
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/MudToastServiceTests.cs:163`).
- **Caveats**: `ShowPersistent` renders the title and body as content in a render fragment, so both are
  escaped by the renderer, but neither string is length-bounded in source: a long push body produces a
  correspondingly tall toast. `Show`, `Success` and the rest pass the caller's string straight to
  MudBlazor, so any localization has to happen before the call; the facade does not touch
  `IStringLocalizer`. The pinned-toast cap evicts only toasts this class raised and tracks them per
  scope, so two scopes (two circuits) never evict each other's toasts.

---

### PendingToastService

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/PendingToastService.cs:13` · Level 2 · class (internal sealed)

- **What it is**: the `sessionStorage`-backed [IPendingToastService](#ipendingtoastservice), the toast that
  survives a full page reload. A toast raised through [MudToastService](#mudtoastservice) lives in the
  current circuit or WebAssembly runtime, so one raised just before
  `NavigateTo(url, forceLoad: true)` dies with the page; this service parks it instead.
- **Depends on**: [IPendingToastService](#ipendingtoastservice) (implemented) and `IAsyncDisposable`
  (`PendingToastService.cs:13`), `IJSRuntime` via the primary constructor, a [LazyJsModule](#lazyjsmodule)
  over `./_content/MMCA.Common.UI/nav-interop.js` (lines 18, 20), [ToastSeverity](#toastseverity), and
  the nested [PendingToast](#pendingtoast) payload.
- **Concept introduced, best-effort persistence across a reload.** `[Rubric §20, Design System, Theming & UI Consistency]`
  covers consistent user feedback: a confirmation that vanishes because the page reloaded reads as
  silence. The service reuses the `nav-interop.js` module (`sessionSet`, `sessionGet`, `sessionRemove`)
  that [ListPageStateService](#listpagestateservice) already uses (class comment, lines 6-12), under one
  fixed key, `mmca.pendingToast` (`StorageKey`, line 16). One toast is held at a time: queueing again
  overwrites it (`IPendingToastService.cs:11`).
- **Walkthrough**
  - `QueueAsync(severity, message, ct)` (line 23) returns early for a blank message (lines 25-28),
    otherwise imports the module lazily and calls `sessionSet` with a new [PendingToast](#pendingtoast)
    (lines 32-33).
  - `TakeAsync(ct)` (line 42) reads with `sessionGet` (line 47), returns `null` when nothing is parked,
    and removes the entry with `sessionRemove` before returning it (line 55). The comment (lines 53-54)
    gives the reason: removing first means a second render, or a second tab restoring the session,
    cannot show the same toast twice. A blank message or an undefined severity is discarded as `null`
    (lines 57-59), so a tampered entry cannot reach the toast host.
  - Both methods swallow interop failure through `IsInteropUnavailable` (lines 72-73): prerender
    (`InvalidOperationException`), a torn-down circuit (`JSDisconnectedException`), a browser-side
    failure (`JSException`) and an interop timeout or cancellation (`TaskCanceledException`). The comment
    at line 37 of the queue path says why: the toast is a courtesy and must not fail the action that
    raised it.
  - `DisposeAsync` (line 68) forwards to the lazy module.
- **Why it's built this way**: parking in `sessionStorage` rather than a cookie or server state keeps it
  per tab and off the wire. The interface also warns callers not to pass the page's lifetime token when
  the same action signs the user out of an `[Authorize]` page, because the re-render disposes the page
  and cancels that token, silently dropping the toast (`IPendingToastService.cs:24-29`).
- **Where it's used**: registered by `AddCommonUiFacades` with
  `TryAddScoped<IPendingToastService, PendingToastService>()` (`DependencyInjection.cs:282`). The shared
  layout renders `PendingToastHost` (`Layout/MainLayout.razor:19`), which calls `TakeAsync` on its first
  interactive render (`Components/Notifications/PendingToastHost.razor:18`) and shows the result through
  [IToastService](#itoastservice). ADC's `Profile` page queues through it before a forced reload
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.UI/Pages/Users/Profile/Profile.razor.cs`). Tests:
  `MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/PendingToastServiceTests.cs`.

  (`options.Sources = [.. options.Sources, .. sources]`, `DependencyInjection.cs:463-464`), so two calls

  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Administration/FeatureFlagAdmin.razor.cs:76`),
  and the page shows a source column only when more than one source is in play (line 79).
- **Where it's used**: configured by [DependencyInjection](#dependencyinjection-2)
  (`DependencyInjection.cs:463`); injected into [FeatureFlagAdmin](#featureflagadmin)
  (`FeatureFlagAdmin.razor.cs:74`); ADC's Conference UI module registers its sources
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:58`); pinned by
  `FeatureFlagAdminTests.cs`.

### IFeatureFlagAdminUIService

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Administration` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Administration/IFeatureFlagAdminUIService.cs:16` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the typed client contract for the feature-flag admin page: list one source's flags,
  set one flag's override, clear one flag's override. Every member takes the `source` route prefix
  first, so one client serves every service's flag endpoints.
- **Depends on**: [FeatureFlagStatusResponse](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#featureflagstatusresponse)
  (the per-flag read shape), [SetFeatureFlagOverrideRequest](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#setfeatureflagoverriderequest)
  (the override payload), and [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result) / `Result<T>` for
  every return. Its sole implementation is [FeatureFlagAdminService](#featureflagadminservice).
- **Concept**: like [IRoleAdminUIService](#iroleadminuiservice), each member's XML doc names the wire
  call it makes (`GET {source}`, `PUT {source}/{name}`, `DELETE {source}/{name}`, lines 18, 26, 38), so
  the contract is also the endpoint map. The source parameter is what makes it multi-service: the
  doc gives `Admin/FeatureFlags` as an example prefix (line 19). `[Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]`
  assesses whether a client contract mirrors its server surface cleanly; here the three members map
  one-to-one onto the three verbs of the feature-flags controller.
- **Walkthrough**: `GetAllAsync(source, ...)` (lines 22-24) returns
  `IReadOnlyList<FeatureFlagStatusResponse>`. `SetOverrideAsync(source, name, request, ...)` (lines
  32-36) returns the flag's state afterwards. `ClearOverrideAsync(source, name, ...)` (line 43) returns
  a bare `Result`.
- **Why it's built this way**: the opt-in UI half of reloadable feature flags
  ([ADR-031](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/031-feature-flag-management.html)); an app that calls
  no `AddFeatureFlagAdministrationUI` registers nothing (`DependencyInjection.cs:445-458`).
- **Where it's used**: registered with [FeatureFlagAdminService](#featureflagadminservice) by
  [DependencyInjection](#dependencyinjection-2) (`DependencyInjection.cs:462`); injected into
  [FeatureFlagAdmin](#featureflagadmin) (`FeatureFlagAdmin.razor.cs:70`); mocked in
  `FeatureFlagAdminTests.cs`.

### IMachineClientAdminUIService

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Administration` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Administration/IMachineClientAdminUIService.cs:10` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the typed client contract for the machine-client admin page: list every client
  (revoked ones included), create one, rotate, promote and revoke its secret.
- **Depends on**: [MachineClientResponse](group-08-auth.md#machineclientresponse),
  [MachineClientSecretResponse](group-08-auth.md#machineclientsecretresponse) (the create and rotate
  result, which carries the secret), [CreateMachineClientRequest](group-08-auth.md#createmachineclientrequest),
  and [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result) / `Result<T>`. Client ids are plain `Guid`
  (lines 27, 33, 39). Its sole implementation is [MachineClientAdminService](#machineclientadminservice).
- **Concept, a secret shown once.** `CreateAsync` and `RotateAsync` return
  `MachineClientSecretResponse` and their docs say the secret comes back once (lines 17, 23); every other
  member returns the secret-free `MachineClientResponse`. Rotation is two-step: `RotateAsync` issues a
  secondary secret and `PromoteAsync` makes it the primary, so a caller can deploy the new secret before
  the old one stops working. `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses credential handling; the return types keep
  a secret off every read path after the one that minted it.
- **Walkthrough**: `GetAllAsync` (line 15), `CreateAsync(request, ...)` (line 21), `RotateAsync(clientId,
  ...)` (line 27), `PromoteAsync(clientId, ...)` (line 33), `RevokeAsync(clientId, ...)` (line 39).
- **Why it's built this way**: the UI opt-in of machine clients
  ([ADR-140](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/140-machine-clients-oauth-client-credentials.html)),
  registered only by `AddMachineClientAdministrationUI` (`DependencyInjection.cs:354-367`).
- **Where it's used**: registered with [MachineClientAdminService](#machineclientadminservice) by
  [DependencyInjection](#dependencyinjection-2) (`DependencyInjection.cs:364`); injected into
  [MachineClientAdmin](#machineclientadmin)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Administration/MachineClientAdmin.razor.cs:50`);
  mocked in `MachineClientAdminTests.cs`.

### IRoleAdminUIService

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Administration` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Administration/IRoleAdminUIService.cs:22` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the typed client contract for the role-admin editor: read every role's compiled and
  stored permissions, read one role, read the catalog an editor renders from, and replace one role's
  stored permission set.
- **Depends on**: first-party: [RolePermissionsResponse](group-08-auth.md#rolepermissionsresponse) (the
  per-role read and write shape), [PermissionCatalogResponse](group-08-auth.md#permissioncatalogresponse)
  (the closed sets a role editor may choose from), and [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result)
  / `Result<T>` (`IRoleAdminUIService.cs:30,36,44,54`) for every member's return type. Its sole
  implementation is [RoleAdminService](#roleadminservice).
- **Concept**: each member's XML doc names the exact endpoint it calls (`GET Admin/Roles`,
  `GET Admin/Roles/{role}`, `GET Admin/Roles/catalog`, `PUT Admin/Roles/{role}/permissions`, lines
  27,32,40,47-48), so the contract doubles as the wire map for the role-admin surface without a
  separate reference. `[Rubric §1, SOLID Principles]` reads this as a small, role-scoped interface:
  it names only what a role editor needs and nothing a user editor would, the mirror decision to the
  split between [IUserAdminActionsUIService](#iuseradminactionsuiservice) and
  [IUserAdminUIService<TUserDto>](#iuseradminuiservicetuserdto) one member table below.
- **Walkthrough**: `GetAllAsync` (line 30) and `GetAsync(string role, ...)` (line 36) are the two reads
  that feed the role list and role-detail pages. `GetCatalogAsync` (line 44) reads the roles-plus-
  permissions catalog a role editor renders its checkboxes from. `SetStoredPermissionsAsync(role,
  permissions, ...)` (lines 54-57) replaces the complete stored permission set for one role in a single
  PUT, not an incremental add/remove, so the caller always sends the full desired set.
- **Why it's built this way**: this is an ADR-116 opt-in surface
  ([ADR-116](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/116-identity-completions-opt-in.html)): the admin app
  can wire role management by registering [RoleAdminService](#roleadminservice) against this contract
  without the framework hard-wiring an admin UI into every consumer.
- **Where it's used**: implemented by [RoleAdminService](#roleadminservice) and registered against it in
  [DependencyInjection](#dependencyinjection-2) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs`);
  consumed by `RoleAdminEdit.razor.cs` and `RoleAdminList.razor.cs`; its ADC identity pages carry the
  behavior-pinning tests
  (`MMCA.ADC/Tests/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.UI.Tests/Pages/Roles/RoleEditTests.cs`,
  `RoleListTests.cs`).

### IUserAdminActionsUIService

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Administration` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Administration/IUserAdminActionsUIService.cs:16` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the account-mutation contract for user admin: lock, unlock, and two shapes of
  role-replacement, a full-set `SetRolesAsync` and a single-role convenience `SetRoleAsync`.
- **Depends on**: first-party: [SetUserRolesRequest](group-08-auth.md#setuserrolesrequest) (implied wire
  shape behind `SetRolesAsync`), [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result)
  (`IUserAdminActionsUIService.cs:22,26,33,41,56,58`); `UserIdentifierType` (the module's identifier
  alias) names every account parameter. Extended by
  [IUserAdminUIService<TUserDto>](#iuseradminuiservicetuserdto).
- **Concept, a member that exists only because a mock cannot proxy a default interface method.** The
  remarks on `SetRoleAsync` (lines 108-111) give the reasoning directly: the obvious shape would have
  been a default interface implementation over `SetRolesAsync` that wraps the single role in a
  one-element list, but a default implementation on an interface is not virtual to a mock proxy, so a
  test could neither stub nor verify it if it were written that way. Declaring `SetRoleAsync` as its
  own interface member keeps it mockable at the cost of one more line on the contract.
  `[Rubric §14, Testability]` is the rubric this decision serves.
- **Walkthrough**: `LockAsync(userId, ...)` (line 84) and `UnlockAsync(userId, ...)` (line 90) are the
  two session-revoking actions. `SetRolesAsync(userId, roles, ...)` (lines 97-100) replaces the complete
  role set an account holds. `SetRoleAsync(userId, role, ...)` (line 116) is documented as sending a
  one-element set to the same replacement endpoint (lines 102-106), the shape both shipped consumers
  need because each holds exactly one role per account.
- **Why it's built this way**: separated from the read/page surface in
  [IUserAdminUIService<TUserDto>](#iuseradminuiservicetuserdto) so the mutating actions have one
  narrow, generic-free contract a page or a test can depend on without also depending on the DTO type
  parameter.
- **Where it's used**: extended by [IUserAdminUIService<TUserDto>](#iuseradminuiservicetuserdto);
  implemented by [UserAdminService<TUserDto>](#useradminservicetuserdto); called directly from
  `UserAdminList.razor.cs` for the lock/unlock/role actions on the user-admin grid, and pinned by
  `UserListTests.cs` (ADC) and `UserAdminListTests.cs` (Common).

### FeatureFlagAdminService

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Administration` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Administration/FeatureFlagAdminService.cs:22` · Level 4 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the HTTP implementation of [IFeatureFlagAdminUIService](#ifeatureflagadminuiservice):
  a GET, a PUT and a DELETE against whatever route prefix the caller passes as `source`.
- **Depends on**: [AuthenticatedServiceBase](#authenticatedservicebase) (base class, lines 22-25),
  [HttpResultExecutor](#httpresultexecutor) (lines 34, 58, 77),
  [ProblemDetailsResultReader](group-08-auth.md#problemdetailsresultreader) (lines 42, 66, 85),
  [FeatureFlagStatusResponse](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#featureflagstatusresponse) and
  [SetFeatureFlagOverrideRequest](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#setfeatureflagoverriderequest);
  `IHttpClientFactory` and [ITokenStorageService](#itokenstorageservice) are the primary-constructor
  parameters (lines 23-24).
- **Concept**: the same executor-outside, retry-middle, reader-innermost composition as
  [RoleAdminService](#roleadminservice). All three calls, including the PUT and the DELETE, run inside
  the inherited `RetryPolicy` (lines 38, 62, 81): setting or clearing an override is a replace, so a
  repeat lands in the same state.
- **Walkthrough**: `GetAllAsync(source, ...)` (lines 28-46) guards `source` with
  `ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace` (line 32) and GETs the prefix itself. `SetOverrideAsync` (lines 49-70)
  null-checks the request (line 55) and PUTs it as JSON to the flag URL (line 63).
  `ClearOverrideAsync` (lines 73-88) DELETEs the flag URL (line 82) and reads a bare `Result`. The
  private `FlagUrl(source, name)` (lines 90-96) guards both arguments and returns
  `{source without trailing slash}/{escaped name}` (line 95), so a prefix written with or without a
  trailing `/` and a flag name with reserved characters both round-trip.
- **Why it's built this way**: taking the prefix per call instead of fixing one endpoint constant is what
  lets one registered client serve every service listed in
  [FeatureFlagAdminUIOptions](#featureflagadminuioptions)
  ([ADR-031](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/031-feature-flag-management.html)).
- **Where it's used**: registered against [IFeatureFlagAdminUIService](#ifeatureflagadminuiservice) by
  [DependencyInjection](#dependencyinjection-2) (`DependencyInjection.cs:462`), and reached by
  [FeatureFlagAdmin](#featureflagadmin) through that interface.

### IUserAdminUIService<TUserDto>

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Administration` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Administration/IUserAdminUIService.cs:17` · Level 4 · interface

- **What it is**: the read-plus-actions contract a user-admin page depends on: a single-account read
  generic over the consumer's own user DTO, a read of the account's live sessions, a read of its
  sign-in history, plus every mutation from
  [IUserAdminActionsUIService](#iuseradminactionsuiservice) via interface inheritance. The roster
  is deliberately not a member: it is the app's generic paged entity endpoint, read through the standard
  entity service and handed to `UserAdminList` as its `FetchPage` delegate (type doc comment).
- **Depends on**: extends [IUserAdminActionsUIService](#iuseradminactionsuiservice) (line 17); its
  read is generic over `TUserDto`, the consumer-supplied user row shape. `UserIdentifierType` names
  the account parameter of `GetAsync` (line 23), `GetSessionsAsync` (lines 32-34), which returns
  [RefreshSessionSummaryResponse](group-08-auth.md#refreshsessionsummaryresponse) rows (line 32), and
  `GetSignInsAsync` (lines 43-45), which returns
  [SignInSummaryResponse](group-08-auth.md#signinsummaryresponse) rows (line 43).
  Implemented by [UserAdminService<TUserDto>](#useradminservicetuserdto).
- **Concept, the type parameter is the boundary between a shared service and an app-specific DTO.** ADC
  and Store each ship their own user row shape (different columns for the admin grid), so the interface
  is generic rather than fixed to one DTO, and only the single-account read needs the parameter (the
  sessions and sign-ins reads return fixed framework responses): the write half in
  [IUserAdminActionsUIService](#iuseradminactionsuiservice) takes only an id and never returns a DTO, so
  it carries no type parameter of its own. `[Rubric §1, SOLID Principles]` reads the split as interface
  segregation again: a caller that only needs to lock or re-role an account depends on the narrower,
  non-generic interface.
- **Walkthrough**: `GetAsync(userId, ...)` (line 23) reads one account, including its lock state, from
  `GET Admin/Users/{userId}`. `GetSessionsAsync(userId, ...)` (lines 32-34) reads the account's live
  (signed-in) sessions, newest first, from `GET Admin/Users/{userId}/sessions`; it is view only (doc
  comment, lines 25-28). `GetSignInsAsync(userId, ...)` (lines 43-45) reads the account's sign-in
  history from `GET Admin/Users/{userId}/sign-ins`: one row per sign-in, ended ones included, newest
  first, at most 50, also view only (doc comment, lines 36-39). The cap of 50 is stated by the doc
  comment; the client passes no limit, so it is the server's to enforce.
- **Why it's built this way**: generic over `TUserDto` rather than one fixed shape keeps the
  single-read plumbing in the framework while each consumer app supplies its own admin row DTO; the
  roster reuses the generic entity paging instead of a parallel admin-only listing.
- **Where it's used**: implemented by [UserAdminService<TUserDto>](#useradminservicetuserdto),
  registered against it by [DependencyInjection](#dependencyinjection-2); consumed by
  `UserAdminList.razor.cs` and ADC's `UserDetail.razor.cs`
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.UI/Pages/Users/UserDetail/UserDetail.razor.cs`),
  and pinned by `UserAdminListTests.cs` (Common) and `UserDetailTests.cs` (ADC). ADC's `UserDetail`
  renders the sign-in history through [SignInHistoryTable](#signinhistorytable)
  (`UserDetail.razor.cs:174`).

### MachineClientAdminService

  and `GetCatalogAsync` are each a one-line call into it with a different URL and response type (lines

  and the private read return the executor's task directly rather than awaiting it (lines 64, 90), so
  they are not `async` methods themselves.

  [HttpResultExecutor](#httpresultexecutor) outside, `RetryPolicy` in the middle,

  Every method builds a relative URL under `Admin/Users`, then runs an executor-outside,
  retry-middle, reader-innermost lambda. The methods return the executor's task directly instead of
  awaiting it, so only the inner lambda is `async` (lines 40, 61, 82, 119, 142).

  `GetSignInsAsync(userId, ...)` (lines 76-94) has the identical shape against
  `{Endpoint}/{userId}/sign-ins` and reads an `IReadOnlyList<SignInSummaryResponse>`, which feeds
  [SignInHistoryTable](#signinhistorytable). `LockAsync` and `UnlockAsync`
  (lines 97-102) both delegate to the private `PostLockChangeAsync(userId, action, ...)` (lines

### ISessionCookieSync
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/ISessionCookieSync.cs:8` · Level 0 · interface

- **What it is**: a two-method contract for mirroring the client's in-memory tokens into the browser's
  HttpOnly auth cookies, and for clearing them again on logout. Both methods report whether the
  cookie jar was actually updated.
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party. Implemented by
  [`JsFetchSessionCookieSync`](#jsfetchsessioncookiesync) and, on a Blazor Server host that enabled
  the same-origin proxy, by [`HandoffSessionCookieSync`](#handoffsessioncookiesync)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/SameOriginProxy/HandoffSessionServices.cs:52`);
  consumed by
  [`WasmTokenStorageService`](#wasmtokenstorageservice) and by
  [`ServerTokenStorageService`](#servertokenstorageservice)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Services/ServerTokenStorageService.cs:51`).
- **Concept introduced, the prerender visibility gap.** A Blazor Web App renders a server-side pass
  before the interactive circuit exists. During that pass there is no `Authorization` header and no
  way to read the interactive client's in-memory access token, so an `[Authorize]` page opened by a
  deep link, an F5, or right-click "open in new tab" would bounce to `/login` even for a signed-in
  user. The interface doc says exactly that (`ISessionCookieSync.cs:3-7`). The cookie is the one thing
  both sides can see, so keeping it in step with the in-memory token is what makes fresh GETs work.
  - `[Rubric §26, Front-End Security]` assesses where browser credentials live. The target is an
    HttpOnly cookie, unreadable from JS, rather than `localStorage`.
  - `[Rubric §25, Navigation, Routing & Information Architecture]` assesses whether deep links behave.
    This contract is the reason a bookmarked authorized route renders instead of redirecting.
- **Walkthrough**: two members, both returning `Task<bool>`: `true` when the cookie jar was
  updated, `false` when the write failed or could not be attempted (a non-2xx answer, a dropped
  connection, JS interop unavailable).
  `SyncAsync(accessToken, refreshToken)` writes the pair (`ISessionCookieSync.cs:15`) and
  `ClearAsync()` removes it (line 20). The two callers treat the answers differently on purpose.
  A failed sync is surfaced: [`WasmTokenStorageService`](#wasmtokenstorageservice) throws
  `InvalidOperationException` when `SyncAsync` returns `false`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/WasmTokenStorageService.cs:153-156`),
  so [`AuthUIService`](#authuiservice) reports `Auth.TokenStorageUnavailable` instead of a sign-in
  that silently ends at the first access-token expiry, when no cookie exists to refresh from
  (comment at lines 64-67; [`ServerTokenStorageService`](#servertokenstorageservice) does the same at
  `ServerTokenStorageService.cs:216`). A failed clear is discarded (`_ = await
  sessionCookieSync.ClearAsync()`, `WasmTokenStorageService.cs:167`), because sign-out proceeds
  locally whatever the cookie endpoint answered.
- **Why it's built this way**: the shape is the client half of
  [ADR-022](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/022-browser-session-cookie-auth.html), which decided
  the BFF-style `mmca_auth_access` / `mmca_auth_refresh` HttpOnly cookie pair and the
  `/auth/session/token` hydration endpoint. Keeping it an interface (rather than calling JS interop
  inline from token storage) is what lets a bUnit or unit test drive the storage services with a mock
  and no browser, which `WasmTokenStorageServiceTests` does
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/WasmTokenStorageServiceTests.cs:30`).
- **Where it's used**: registered by the dedicated extension
  `AddClientAuthSessionCookieSync()`, which `TryAddScoped`s
  [`JsFetchSessionCookieSync`](#jsfetchsessioncookiesync)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:291-295`); the doc there
  records that both the Blazor Server host and the WebAssembly client call it (lines 165-169).

### SameOriginProxyHeaders
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/SameOriginProxyHeaders.cs:11` · Level 0 · class (static)

- **What it is**: two constants naming the fixed CSRF request header the same-origin API proxy
  requires on every state-changing request: `CsrfHeaderName = "X-CSRF"`
  (`SameOriginProxyHeaders.cs:14`) and `CsrfHeaderValue = "1"` (line 17).
- **Depends on**: nothing. It lives in `MMCA.Common.UI` rather than `MMCA.Common.UI.Web` so the
  client that stamps the header and the server that checks it share one definition.
- **Concept introduced, a custom header as a CSRF signal.** A cross-site page can make a browser send
  a simple POST carrying the user's cookies, but it cannot add a custom header without a CORS
  preflight. The proxy answers `OPTIONS` itself with no CORS grant and refuses any request whose
  `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site` names another origin, so the header is defense in depth behind that
  origin check; the value carries no secret (`SameOriginProxyHeaders.cs:3-10`).
  - `[Rubric §26, Front-End Security]` assesses cookie-borne credentials against cross-site request
    forgery. Once the bearer moves into an HttpOnly cookie, a header the browser will not attach on a
    cross-site request is what distinguishes the app's own calls.
- **Walkthrough**: two `const string` members and no behavior. Being `const`, both values are baked
  into each caller at compile time.
- **Why it's built this way**: one shared type instead of a literal per call site keeps the stamp
  and the check from drifting apart. The proxy design is
  [ADR-131](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/131-same-origin-api-proxy.html).
- **Where it's used**: stamped by [`SameOriginProxyRequestHandler`](#sameoriginproxyrequesthandler)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/SameOriginProxyRequestHandler.cs:19-20`)
  and by [`NotificationHubService`](#notificationhubservice) on the SignalR connection options
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Notifications/NotificationHubService.cs:374`);
  checked by [`SameOriginApiProxyEndpoint`](#sameoriginapiproxyendpoint) in `HasCsrfHeader`, which
  demands exactly one value equal to `CsrfHeaderValue`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/SameOriginProxy/SameOriginApiProxyEndpoint.cs:125-128`);
  stripped before forwarding by [`SameOriginProxyTransformer`](#sameoriginproxytransformer)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/SameOriginProxy/SameOriginProxyTransformer.cs:78`).
  Covered by `SameOriginProxyClientTests`
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/SameOriginProxyClientTests.cs:27`).

### JsFetchSessionCookieSync
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/JsFetchSessionCookieSync.cs:13` · Level 1 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the [`ISessionCookieSync`](#isessioncookiesync) implementation. It calls two small JS
  helpers that issue a browser-side `fetch`, so the resulting `Set-Cookie` lands in the user's cookie
  jar on both Blazor Server and WebAssembly.
- **Depends on**: [`ISessionCookieSync`](#isessioncookiesync) (the contract) and `IJSRuntime`
  (`Microsoft.JSInterop`), plus the `mmcaAuthCookie` object defined in the package's static web asset
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/wwwroot/mmca-auth-cookie.js:4`.
- **Concept introduced, why the fetch has to come from the browser.** On Blazor Server the code runs on
  the server, so a server-issued HTTP call would put the cookie in the server's own handler, not the
  user's browser. Routing the call through JS interop makes the browser the one issuing the request,
  which is the only way the `Set-Cookie` reaches the right cookie jar
  (`JsFetchSessionCookieSync.cs:6-8`).
  - `[Rubric §26, Front-End Security]` again: the tokens transit JS only for this one same-origin POST
    and are never persisted anywhere JS can read afterwards.
  - `[Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity]` assesses degradation. Every interop failure is
    caught and turned into a `false` answer, so a prerender pass or a disconnected circuit cannot throw
    out of a cookie write, yet the caller still learns the write did not happen.
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `IsInteropUnavailable(ex)` (`JsFetchSessionCookieSync.cs:15-16`) is the shared exception filter,
    naming the four types that mean "there is no live JS runtime right now":
    `InvalidOperationException`, `JSDisconnectedException`, `JSException` and
    `OperationCanceledException`.
  - `SyncAsync(accessToken, refreshToken)` (line 19) returns
    `InvokeAsync<bool>("mmcaAuthCookie.set", accessToken, refreshToken)` (line 23): the script itself
    reports whether the endpoint answered 2xx. An interop failure returns `false`, the comment noting
    nothing was written (lines 25-29).
  - `ClearAsync()` (line 33) returns `InvokeAsync<bool>("mmcaAuthCookie.clear")` (line 37) under the
    same filter, and an interop failure again returns `false` because the cookie was not cleared by
    this call (lines 39-43). The class doc records that the script tries the clear twice
    (`JsFetchSessionCookieSync.cs:9-11`).
- **Why it's built this way**: a shared static filter rather than two duplicated `when` clauses keeps
  the definition of "interop unavailable" in one place. Reporting rather than swallowing silently is
  what lets the token storage services refuse a sign-in whose cookie never landed (see
  [`ISessionCookieSync`](#isessioncookiesync)). The cookie contract itself
  belongs to [ADR-022](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/022-browser-session-cookie-auth.html).
- **Where it's used**: `TryAddScoped` behind [`ISessionCookieSync`](#isessioncookiesync) by
  `AddClientAuthSessionCookieSync()`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:293`); consumed by
  [`WasmTokenStorageService`](#wasmtokenstorageservice) and
  [`ServerTokenStorageService`](#servertokenstorageservice).
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: the `mmcaAuthCookie.set` / `.clear` JS implementations live in
  `mmca-auth-cookie.js`, outside this unit; only the C# side is described here.

### SameOriginProxyRequestHandler
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/SameOriginProxyRequestHandler.cs:11` · Level 1 · class (internal, sealed)

- **What it is**: the innermost handler of the `"APIClient"` pipeline on a WebAssembly client whose
  host runs the same-origin API proxy. It removes any `Authorization` header and stamps the proxy's
  CSRF header on every request (`SameOriginProxyRequestHandler.cs:3-10`).
- **Depends on**: [`SameOriginProxyHeaders`](#sameoriginproxyheaders) for the header name and value;
  external `DelegatingHandler`.
- **Concept introduced, the browser holds no usable bearer.** Behind the proxy the client only ever
  holds a claims-only token; the proxy attaches the real bearer server-side from the HttpOnly session
  cookie. Any `Authorization` header the outer handlers (such as
  [`AuthDelegatingHandler`](#authdelegatinghandler)) or a service's `DefaultRequestHeaders` attached is
  therefore noise at best, so this handler clears it rather than trusting every caller to know.
  - `[Rubric §26, Front-End Security]` assesses whether a usable credential is reachable from browser
    code. Here it is not, and the transport enforces that for every request.
- **Walkthrough**: one override. `SendAsync(request, cancellationToken)`
  (`SameOriginProxyRequestHandler.cs:14`) guards `request` with `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull`
  (line 16), sets `request.Headers.Authorization = null` (line 18), removes any existing CSRF header
  and adds exactly one with `TryAddWithoutValidation` (lines 19-20), then delegates to
  `base.SendAsync` (line 21). Removing first guarantees a single value, which is what the proxy's
  check demands.
- **Why it's built this way**: registering it innermost means it sees the request after every other
  handler and service has had its say, so one place decides what reaches the proxy. It is
  registered only when `Api:SameOriginApiEndpoint` is configured, so every other client (Blazor
  Server, MAUI, a WebAssembly client of a host that did not opt in) keeps its pipeline unchanged
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:144-149`). The proxy design is
  [ADR-131](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/131-same-origin-api-proxy.html).
- **Where it's used**: `AddTransient` and `AddHttpMessageHandler` inside `AddUIShared()` behind the
  `usesSameOriginProxy` check (`DependencyInjection.cs:178-183`), after the auth and culture handlers
  (lines 124-125). The proxy side that reads the CSRF header is
  [`SameOriginApiProxyEndpoint`](#sameoriginapiproxyendpoint).

### JwtAuthenticationStateProvider
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/JwtAuthenticationStateProvider.cs:24` · Level 2 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the custom `AuthenticationStateProvider` that turns the stored JWT into the
  `ClaimsPrincipal` Blazor's `AuthorizeView` and `[Authorize]` read, pushes a new state
  immediately on login and logout, signs the shell out when the token storage reports that the
  session ended on the server, and forgets the list pages' persisted search and filters on every
  sign-in and sign-out.
- **Depends on**: [`ITokenStorageService`](#itokenstorageservice) (required constructor parameter),
  [`ListPageStateService`](#listpagestateservice) (optional constructor parameter, defaulted to
  `null`) and [`ISessionAwareTokenStorage`](#isessionawaretokenstorage) (an optional capability it
  probes the storage for); externals `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Authorization.AuthenticationStateProvider`,
  `System.Security.Claims` and `JwtSecurityTokenHandler`.
- **Concept introduced, Blazor's auth-state contract.** Blazor does not know about JWTs; it asks an
  `AuthenticationStateProvider` for an `AuthenticationState` and re-renders every
  `CascadingAuthenticationState` consumer when the provider says the state changed. This class is the
  adapter between "there is a token in storage" and that framework contract.
  - `[Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow]` assesses how a cross-cutting piece of UI state
    propagates. Notifying rather than reloading is the whole point: a sign-in updates the navbar and
    every guarded fragment without a page refresh (lines 96-99). The class doc also makes this the
    one place per-tab list state is forgotten, because every sign-out passes through it
    (`JwtAuthenticationStateProvider.cs:18-22`).
  - `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses the trust boundary, and the class doc draws it: claims are
    extracted client-side without server validation to keep the UI responsive, and the WebAPI performs
    full token validation on every request (lines 9-11). The same doc records the second half of
    that boundary (lines 12-17): a session revoked from another device, or ended by account deletion,
    flips the shell to anonymous instead of leaving it signed in behind 401s (A-34).
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `AnonymousState`, a single static `AuthenticationState` over an empty `ClaimsIdentity`
    (`JwtAuthenticationStateProvider.cs:26-27`). Because a `ClaimsIdentity` with no authentication
    type reports `IsAuthenticated == false`, this one shared instance is the "signed out" answer.
  - One constructor, `(ITokenStorageService tokenStorageService, ListPageStateService? listPageState = null)`
    (line 41). It null-guards the storage (line 45), stores both into `_tokenStorageService` and
    `_listPageState` (fields at lines 29-30), and, when the storage is an
    `ISessionAwareTokenStorage`, subscribes `OnSessionEnded` to its `SessionEnded` event
    (lines 50-53). The comment at line 49 explains why no unsubscribe is needed: the provider shares
    the storage's DI scope and lifetime, so the subscription never outlives either. The parameter doc
    gives the reason the list state is taken at all: it is mirrored to `sessionStorage`, which
    outlives the session in the same tab, so without the clear the next account signing in on that
    tab saw the previous account's search applied (lines 36-40).
  - `GetAuthenticationStateAsync()` (line 61) reads the token (line 65) and returns the anonymous
    state on a blank token (lines 66-69), an unreadable token (lines 72-75), or an expired one
    (`ValidTo < DateTime.UtcNow`, lines 78-81). On success it builds a `ClaimsIdentity` from the
    token's claims with the authentication type `"jwt"`, and the comment at line 83 records why that
    string matters: naming an authentication type is what makes the identity `IsAuthenticated`. A
    bare `catch` under an annotated `CA1031` suppression ("an unreadable token is an anonymous user,
    never a broken authentication state", lines 88-93) turns any remaining failure, including JS
    interop being unavailable, into anonymous rather than an exception inside a render.
  - `NotifyUserAuthentication(token)` (line 100) rebuilds the principal the same way and calls the base
    `NotifyAuthenticationStateChanged` (line 106). It does not consult storage, because the caller has
    just been handed the token.
  - `NotifyUserLogout()` (lines 112-113) pushes `AnonymousState` back out.
  - `SignOutAsync()` (line 121, `internal`) is the sign-out every [`AuthUIService`](#authuiservice)
    path ends in: it awaits the list-state clear, then calls `NotifyUserLogout()`. It is awaited so the
    `sessionStorage` removal lands before the caller's `forceLoad` navigation to the sign-in page
    tears the page down (doc at lines 115-120).
  - `SignInAsync(token)` (line 139, `internal`) is the sign-in counterpart: it awaits the list-state
    clear, then calls `NotifyUserAuthentication(token)`. The doc (lines 127-137) records why it clears
    on EVERY sign-in, the same account's included: in WebAssembly a session revoked from another
    device while the tab was not running ends without `SessionEnded`, so a different account can sign
    in over a tab that still looks signed in, and telling accounts apart would need an identity that
    case no longer has. A token refresh is not a sign-in and keeps the state.
  - `OnSessionEnded` (lines 145-151), the private event handler, starts the list-state clear without
    awaiting it (`_ = ForgetListPageStateAsync()`, line 149), because an event handler cannot await
    and the in-memory state clears synchronously inside the call (comment at lines 147-148), then
    calls `NotifyUserLogout()` (line 150). Per
    `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/ISessionAwareTokenStorage.cs:3-10,14-18`
    the event fires once, only on a definitive "no session" refresh answer (never on a transient
    failure), and the stored access token is already cleared when it does.
  - `ForgetListPageStateAsync()` (lines 153-154) is `Task.CompletedTask` when no list state was
    supplied, otherwise `_listPageState.ClearAsync().AsTask()`.
- **Why it's built this way**: falling back to anonymous on every failure is the safe direction for a
  UI gate, since the API rejects anything the client wrongly let through. Keeping the notify methods
  public and adding the `internal` `SignInAsync` / `SignOutAsync` pair is what lets
  [`AuthUIService`](#authuiservice) drive the state transition at the exact moment tokens change; it
  does so behind an `is JwtAuthenticationStateProvider` type test
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthUIService.cs:201,483,544`),
  so a host that registered a different provider still works. Putting the list-state clear here
  rather than in each sign-out path means the server-ended session (driven by the storage event)
  and the client-driven sign-outs cannot disagree about what is forgotten. Both the list state and
  the session-aware capability are optional (a defaulted parameter and a type test), so a storage
  that does not implement `ISessionAwareTokenStorage` behaves exactly as before.
- **Where it's used**: registered with `AddScoped<AuthenticationStateProvider, JwtAuthenticationStateProvider>()`
  by the shared Blazor Server host wiring
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Hosting/BlazorWebHostExtensions.cs:144`) and by
  the WebAssembly and MAUI heads (`MMCA.Store/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.Store.UI.Web.Client/Program.cs:54`,
  `MMCA.Store/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.Store.UI/MauiProgram.cs:130`,
  `MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web.Client/Program.cs:53`,
  `MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI/MauiProgram.cs:178`). Covered by
  `JwtAuthenticationStateProviderTests`
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/JwtAuthenticationStateProviderTests.cs:16`),
  whose `WhenTheStorageReportsTheSessionEnded_NotifiesAnonymous` (line 137) and
  `WhenTheStorageReportsTheSessionEnded_ForgetsTheListPageStateAndNotifiesAnonymous` (line 152)
  drive the session-ended path through a fake session-aware storage (its `EndSession`, line 178).
  `AuthUIServiceTests` constructs a real one rather than a double, precisely because the type test
  above would not match a mock
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/AuthUIServiceTests.cs:80`, and
  with a list state at line 609); the shared token-storage tests do the same
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Shared/UI/TokenStorageServiceTestsBase.cs:316`).
  ADR-051 (client auth token lifecycle) mentions it.

### TokenOwner
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:344` · Level 2 · record (private, sealed, nested in [`AuthDelegatingHandler`](#authdelegatinghandler))

- **What it is**: the value type of the handler's owner map: which storage attached a bearer, and
  when (`AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:343-344`). Two positional members,
  `WeakReference<ISessionAwareTokenStorage> Storage` and `long TrackedAt`.
- **Depends on**: [`ISessionAwareTokenStorage`](#isessionawaretokenstorage) (the storage it points
  at); externals `WeakReference<T>` and `Environment.TickCount64` (the clock `TrackedAt` is stamped
  from).
- **Concept reinforced, a weak back-reference keyed by token.** The map routes a 401 to the storage
  instance that attached the refused bearer, but it is static, so a strong reference would keep every
  ended circuit or scope alive. Holding the storage weakly means the map never extends a session's
  lifetime (doc at `AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:61-64`).
  - `[Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity]` assesses whether a long-lived process degrades:
    the entry carries its own timestamp, so a sweep can drop it on age as well as on a dead owner.
- **Walkthrough**: no members beyond the two positional properties. Entries are created by
  `TrackTokenOwnerAt` (`AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:84-88`) and stored in the static
  `Owners` dictionary (line 56). They are read three ways: `HasLiveOwner` (lines 102-103) and the two
  report paths resolve `Storage.TryGetTarget` to find a live owner (lines 237, 318), and `IsStale`
  (lines 178-179) treats an entry as droppable when `TrackedAt` is older than `RetentionMs` or the
  target is gone.
- **Why it's built this way**: a private nested record keeps the map's shape out of the public
  surface; only the handler and its `internal` test hooks touch it.
- **Where it's used**: only inside [`AuthDelegatingHandler`](#authdelegatinghandler); no usage outside
  the defining file.

### AuthDelegatingHandler
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:36` · Level 3 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the `DelegatingHandler` that attaches the stored JWT as a `Bearer` header on every
  outgoing API request, so no UI service ever sets an `Authorization` header by hand, and that reports
  a refused bearer back to the storage that holds it: a 401 triggers one renewal attempt, and a coded
  403 raises the "second factor required" signal. One request can opt out through the `SkipBearer`
  request option.
- **Depends on**: [`ITokenStorageService`](#itokenstorageservice) (its only constructor parameter),
  [`ISessionAwareTokenStorage`](#isessionawaretokenstorage) (the renewal capability a 401 is reported
  to), [`TokenOwner`](#tokenowner) (its owner-map entry),
  [`MultiFactorRequiredSignal`](#multifactorrequiredsignal) and
  [`AuthErrorCodes`](group-08-auth.md#autherrorcodes) (the coded 403 path), and
  [`AuthenticatedServiceBase`](#authenticatedservicebase) (replay-safety marking); externals
  `System.Net.Http.Headers.AuthenticationHeaderValue`, `DelegatingHandler`,
  `ConcurrentDictionary` and `System.Text.Json.JsonDocument`.
- **Concept introduced, the HTTP message-handler pipeline.** `HttpClient` composes handlers into a
  chain, each free to inspect or mutate a request before passing it to the next. Registering this one
  on the named `"APIClient"` client means auth is applied once, at the transport, for every typed
  service built on top of it.
  - `[Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven Design]` assesses whether concerns like auth are centralized rather
    than repeated per call. This is the client-side twin of the server's middleware pipeline: one
    registration covers every request, and the same place sees every refusal.
  - `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses session handling: a 401 to a bearer makes one refresh attempt,
    and a refused refresh ends the session so a protected page lands on the sign-in page. A token
    acquired that way is remembered and a 401 to it is not reported again, so an API that keeps
    refusing a freshly issued token cannot drive a refresh per request (class doc at
    `AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:19-26`).
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `SkipBearer` (`AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:44`) is a public static
    `HttpRequestOptionsKey<bool>` named `"MMCA.Common.UI.Auth.SkipBearer"`. The token refresh POST
    sets it: that endpoint is anonymous, and reading token storage from inside a refresh would
    re-enter the very acquisition that is waiting for the request to complete (doc at lines 39-43).
  - Three private constants: `SweepThreshold = 1024` (line 47), `RetentionMs = 24L * 60 * 60 * 1000`,
    24 hours, longer than any access token lives (line 50), and
    `ProblemJsonMediaType = "application/problem+json"` (line 53). Two static ordinal
    `ConcurrentDictionary` maps hold the cross-request state: `Owners` (token to
    [`TokenOwner`](#tokenowner), line 56) and `RenewedTokens` (token to the tick it was renewed at,
    line 59).
  - `TrackTokenOwner(accessToken, owner)` (line 68, `internal static`) records which storage attached a
    bearer. It ignores a blank token or a storage that is not an `ISessionAwareTokenStorage`
    (lines 70-73) and otherwise stores a weak reference stamped with `Environment.TickCount64`
    (line 75). The reason is in the class doc: the handler resolves its own storage in the
    `IHttpClientFactory` handler scope, which in a browser host is not the instance the component
    holds, so without this a service's 401 would go to the wrong storage (lines 27-34).
    `TrackTokenOwnerAt` (line 84) and `MarkRenewedAt` (line 93) write the maps directly and are the
    hooks tests use to age entries; `HasLiveOwner` (line 102), `IsTrackedOwner` (line 108) and
    `IsMarkedRenewed` (line 113) read them.
  - `SweepIfLarge()` (line 119) runs after every write. `SweepOwners` (line 151) and `SweepRenewed`
    (line 165) do nothing until a map holds more than `SweepThreshold` entries, then drop the owner
    entries that are stale (older than `RetentionMs` or whose storage is gone, `IsStale`, lines
    178-179) and the renewal entries older than `RetentionMs` (`IsExpired`, line 181).
  - `SendAsync(request, cancellationToken)` (line 127) is a thin wrapper: it awaits the private
    `SendWithBearerAsync` inside a `try`, and on an `HttpRequestException` calls
    `AuthenticatedServiceBase.MarkReplaySafety(ex, request)` before rethrowing (lines 131-141). The
    shared retry policy sees only the exception, not the request, so this is where it is told whether
    the request may be resent: a keyless POST or PATCH may not, once sent (comment at lines 137-138).
  - `SendWithBearerAsync` (line 183) holds the bearer logic. When `SkipBearer` is set to `true` the
    request passes straight to `base.SendAsync` without touching token storage at all (lines
    187-190). A request that already carries an `Authorization` header also gets no stored token (the
    `Authorization is null` check at line 192): the forced-refresh replay sets the token it just
    acquired, and replacing it with the stored one would resend the token the server just rejected.
    Otherwise it awaits `GetAccessTokenAsync()` (line 194), and only when the result is non-blank sets
    `request.Headers.Authorization = new AuthenticationHeaderValue("Bearer", token)` (lines 195-198).
    It then reads the bearer it is about to send with `BearerOf` (line 202; the helper at lines
    144-149 accepts only a non-blank `Bearer` scheme), before the call, because the same-origin proxy
    handler further in strips the header (comment at line 201). After `base.SendAsync` (line 203) a
    401 to a request that carried a bearer goes to `ReportRejectedAsync` (lines 205-208) and a 403
    goes to `ReportMultiFactorRequiredAsync` (lines 209-212). The response is returned unchanged
    either way (line 214): it is never replayed.
  - `ReportMultiFactorRequiredAsync` (line 231) resolves the live owner of the token, falling back to
    the handler's own storage (lines 237-239), and returns early unless that owner has a
    [`MultiFactorRequiredSignal`](#multifactorrequiredsignal) subscriber and the body is
    `application/problem+json` (lines 240-244), so a host that never called `AddTwoFactorUI()` never
    has its 403 bodies read (doc at lines 217-224). It buffers the content first so the caller still
    reads the same response (line 246), and raises the signal when `CarriesMultiFactorRequired`
    (line 257) finds `AuthErrorCodes.MultiFactorRequired` under `errors[*].code`; a body that is not
    valid JSON is ignored (lines 274-277). `PropertyOf` (line 284) matches property names ignoring case.
  - `ReportRejectedAsync(rejectedToken, fallbackOwner)` (line 310, `internal static`) is the 401 path.
    A token already in `RenewedTokens` is skipped, since refreshing again would loop (lines 312-316).
    Otherwise it resolves the live owner or the fallback as an `ISessionAwareTokenStorage` (lines
    318-324) and awaits `RenewRejectedAccessTokenAsync(rejectedToken)` (line 328). A renewed token that
    differs from the refused one is tracked to the same owner and marked renewed (lines 329-333). Any
    exception other than cancellation is swallowed under an annotated `CA1031` suppression
    (lines 335-340): the caller still receives the server's 401, which is the answer that matters.
    The doc records it is also the 401 handling for a bearer attached outside this pipeline, the
    notification hub's WebSocket handshake (lines 297-302).
  Note the freshness work happens inside the token service: by the time this handler sees a token,
  a stale one has already been re-acquired. The 401 path is the backstop for a token the server
  refuses anyway.
- **Why it's built this way**: a handler rather than a base-class helper, because the pipeline applies
  to everything the named client sends, including calls made by code that never inherits from a
  framework base. The owner and renewal maps are static because a handler instance is per handler
  scope, not per component, and the map has to bridge the two; holding owners weakly and sweeping on
  age keeps that static state bounded. It is registered `AddTransient`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:142`), the lifetime
  `AddHttpMessageHandler` expects.
- **Where it's used**: added to the `"APIClient"` pipeline alongside the culture handler
  (`DependencyInjection.cs:174-175`). Services that attach their own bearer register its owner:
  [`AuthenticatedServiceBase`](#authenticatedservicebase)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Api/AuthenticatedServiceBase.cs:84`),
  [`AuthUIService`](#authuiservice)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthUIService.cs:567`), and the
  preference reader and writer
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Preferences/ApiUserPreferenceReader.cs:52`,
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Preferences/ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:117`).
  [`NotificationHubService`](#notificationhubservice) calls `ReportRejectedAsync` for a refused hub
  handshake
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Notifications/NotificationHubService.cs:671`).
  The `SkipBearer` option is set by [`DirectApiTokenRefresher`](#directapitokenrefresher) on its
  refresh request
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/DirectApiTokenRefresher.cs:66`).
  On a WebAssembly client of a host running the same-origin proxy,
  [`SameOriginProxyRequestHandler`](#sameoriginproxyrequesthandler) sits inside this handler and
  strips whatever header it attached (`DependencyInjection.cs:181-182`). Covered
  by `AuthDelegatingHandlerTests`
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/AuthDelegatingHandlerTests.cs:18`),
  by `SessionBearerRenewalTests`
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Api/SessionBearerRenewalTests.cs:32`)
  and by a DI resolution test that exists because the pipeline must be able to construct it
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/ApiClientRegistrationTests.cs:33`).

### IPasskeyUIService
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/IPasskeyUIService.cs:14` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the client of the API's passkey endpoints under `auth/passkeys`: register a passkey
  for the signed-in user, list, rename and delete them, and sign in with one
  (`IPasskeyUIService.cs:7-13`).
- **Depends on**: [`Result`](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result) and the passkey contracts
  [`PasskeyOptionsResponse`](group-08-auth.md#passkeyoptionsresponse),
  [`PasskeyResponse`](group-08-auth.md#passkeyresponse),
  [`PasskeyRegisterRequest`](group-08-auth.md#passkeyregisterrequest) and
  [`PasskeySignInRequest`](group-08-auth.md#passkeysigninrequest), plus
  [`AuthenticationResponse`](group-08-auth.md#authenticationresponse). Implemented by
  [`AuthUIService`](#authuiservice).
- **Concept reinforced, the bespoke UI service contract (introduced at [`IAuthUIService`](#iauthuiservice)).**
  `[Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]` assesses extension without breakage: the doc states this is a
  separate interface rather than new `IAuthUIService` members, so a consumer's own `IAuthUIService`
  implementation keeps compiling, following the [`ISignInLinkUIService`](#isigninlinkuiservice)
  precedent (lines 8-11). `[Rubric §26, Front-End Security]` shows in the split between the
  authenticated management members and the anonymous sign-in pair.
- **Walkthrough**: seven members, every one returning a `Result`, in two halves.
  - Registration is a two-step WebAuthn ceremony: `BeginRegistrationAsync` (line 19,
    `POST auth/passkeys/register/options`) returns the flow and creation options, and
