    `CompleteRegistrationAsync(PasskeyRegisterRequest, ct)` (line 25, `POST auth/passkeys/register`)
    sends the browser's attestation and a name back and returns the stored passkey.
  - Management: `ListAsync` (line 30, `GET auth/passkeys`), `RenameAsync(id, name, ct)` (line 37,
    `PATCH auth/passkeys/{id}`) and `DeleteAsync(id, ct)` (line 43, `DELETE auth/passkeys/{id}`),
    whose doc names the refusal a page must expect: the last passkey of a password-less account
    (line 42).
  - Sign-in is the same two steps, anonymous: `BeginSignInAsync` (line 48,
    `POST auth/passkeys/signin/options`) and `SignInAsync(PasskeySignInRequest, ct)` (line 57,
    `POST auth/passkeys/signin`), which stores the token pair and notifies the auth state like a
    password sign-in (lines 50-53).
- **Why it's built this way**: implementing it on `AuthUIService` means a passkey sign-in stores its
  tokens through the password sign-in's path (lines 11-12, and the registration comment at
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:200-202`). The registration is
  inert until a host offers passkeys (`SignIn:OfferPasskeys`) or renders the passkeys panel. The design
  is [ADR-139](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/139-passkeys-webauthn-opt-in-sign-in.html).
- **Where it's used**: registered `TryAddScoped<IPasskeyUIService, AuthUIService>()` in `AddUIShared()`
  (`DependencyInjection.cs:203`); injected by [`PasskeySignInButton`](#passkeysigninbutton)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/PasskeySignInButton.razor.cs:40`)
  and [`PasskeysPanel`](#passkeyspanel)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/PasskeysPanel.razor.cs:39`), and
  probed by [`Login`](#login) to decide whether to offer passkeys
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor.cs:203`).

### ISignInLinkUIService
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/ISignInLinkUIService.cs:16` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the client behind the sign-in-link flow: ask for a link from the sign-in page, and
  redeem one on the `/auth/sign-in-link` landing page (`ISignInLinkUIService.cs:6-9`).
- **Depends on**: [`Result`](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result) and
  [`AuthenticationResponse`](group-08-auth.md#authenticationresponse). Implemented by
  [`AuthUIService`](#authuiservice).
- **Concept reinforced, the bespoke UI service contract (introduced at [`IAuthUIService`](#iauthuiservice)).**
  `[Rubric §11, Security]` shows twice in two members: the request side is anti-enumeration and the
  redeem side is single-use. `[Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]`: a separate interface rather than new
  `IAuthUIService` members, so a consumer's own `IAuthUIService` implementation keeps compiling, the
  [`IEmailConfirmationUIService`](#iemailconfirmationuiservice) precedent (remarks at lines 10-15).
- **Walkthrough**: two members.
  - `RequestSignInLinkAsync(email, ct)` (line 25) asks the API to email a link. The endpoint answers
    202 for every well-formed address, so a success says nothing about whether the address holds an
    account; a failure is a malformed request or an outage (lines 18-24).
  - `RedeemSignInLinkAsync(email, token, acceptedTerms, ct)` (line 36) redeems a link and, on success,
    stores the token pair and signals the signed-in state. It posts exactly once, because the token is
    single-use and a retry could only spend it twice (lines 28-29). `acceptedTerms` carries whether the
    visitor accepted the Terms of Service on the page (line 33).
- **Why it's built this way**: implementing it on `AuthUIService` means a redeemed link stores its tokens
  and signals the auth state exactly as a password sign-in does (lines 13-14, and the registration
  comment at `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:196-197`, which
  ties the flow to ADR-116).
- **Where it's used**: registered `TryAddScoped<ISignInLinkUIService, AuthUIService>()` in `AddUIShared()`
  (`DependencyInjection.cs:198`); injected by the landing page [`SignInLink`](#signinlink)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/SignInLinks/SignInLink.razor.cs:64`) and
  resolved optionally by [`Login`](#login) for the "email me a link" request
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor.cs:231`).

### IEmailConfirmationUIService
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/IEmailConfirmationUIService.cs:21` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the client-side contract for the email-confirmation flow: redeeming a confirmation
  link's token, and asking for a fresh one when the first has expired or was never received.
- **Depends on**: [`Result`](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result); externals: BCL (`Task`,
  `CancellationToken`, `string`).
- **Concept reinforced, the bespoke UI service contract (introduced at [`IAuthUIService`](#iauthuiservice)).**
  `[Rubric §18, UI Architecture & Component Design]` and `[Rubric §26, Front-End Security]` (assesses that
  a resend cannot be used to enumerate registered addresses). Two members, both returning `Result` so a
  page branches on the outcome instead of catching. `ResendEmailConfirmationAsync`'s own doc comment
  states the anti-enumeration rule directly, that the endpoint answers 202 whether or not the address
  holds an account, so a success means "accepted", never "this address exists"
  (`IEmailConfirmationUIService.cs:31-33`). The class-level remarks also record why there is no retry:
  the token is single-use and the resend spends a per-address request budget, so a repeat is a second
  request rather than a replayed response (`IEmailConfirmationUIService.cs:16-19`).
- **Walkthrough**: two methods.
  - `ConfirmEmailAsync(string email, string token, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)`
    (`IEmailConfirmationUIService.cs:28`) redeems a single-use token via `POST auth/confirm-email`; the
    doc comment records that the endpoint returns the same generic rejection for every bad token
    (`IEmailConfirmationUIService.cs:23-27`).
  - `ResendEmailConfirmationAsync(string email, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)`
    (`IEmailConfirmationUIService.cs:38`) requests a fresh link via `POST auth/send-email-confirmation`,
    always reported as success at this layer regardless of whether the address is known.
- **Why it's built this way**: a narrow interface here, rather than the generic
  [`IEntityService<,>`](#ientityservicetentitydto-tidentifiertype), matches the same reasoning
  [`IAuthUIService`](#iauthuiservice) documents: confirming an email is not a CRUD operation on a
  resource with an identity, so it gets its own contract instead of being bent to fit one
  (`[Rubric §14, Testability]`).
- **Where it's used**: implemented by [`EmailConfirmationUIService`](#emailconfirmationuiservice);
  injected by `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/ConfirmEmail.razor.cs` and by
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.UI/Pages/ConfirmEmailPageTestsBase.cs`; registered in
  `AddUIShared()` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs`).

### EmailConfirmationUIService
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/EmailConfirmationUIService.cs:22` · Level 4 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the [`IEmailConfirmationUIService`](#iemailconfirmationuiservice) implementation. It
  posts to the two confirmation endpoints and translates the response through the shared
  [`HttpResultExecutor`](#httpresultexecutor) / `ProblemDetailsResultReader` path used across the auth
  services.
- **Depends on**: [`IEmailConfirmationUIService`](#iemailconfirmationuiservice) (the contract it
  implements); `IHttpClientFactory` (its only constructor parameter, `EmailConfirmationUIService.cs:22`);
  [`HttpResultExecutor`](#httpresultexecutor) and `ProblemDetailsResultReader`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Http/ProblemDetailsResultReader.cs`) for the transport and
  response-translation work.
- **Concept reinforced, one shared execution path for every anonymous auth POST.** Both members funnel
  through the private `PostOnceAsync<TRequest>` helper, so the retry policy and response translation are
  written once rather than duplicated per endpoint.
  - `[Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality]` assesses duplication; the two public methods are each a
    single expression forwarding to the shared helper, without its own `async` state machine
    (`EmailConfirmationUIService.cs:27-32`).
  - `[Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity]` is answered by what the helper deliberately does
    not do: no retry, because a repeat here is a second request (a spent token, a second email), never a
    replayed response (`EmailConfirmationUIService.cs:40-41`).
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `ApiClientName = "APIClient"` (`EmailConfirmationUIService.cs:24`) names the shared named client.
  - `ConfirmEmailAsync` (line 28) posts a `ConfirmEmailRequest` to `auth/confirm-email`.
  - `ResendEmailConfirmationAsync` (line 32) posts a `SendEmailConfirmationRequest` to
    `auth/send-email-confirmation`.
  - `PostOnceAsync<TRequest>(relativeUrl, body, cancellationToken)` (line 35) creates a fresh
    `HttpClient` from the factory (line 39), posts the body with `PostAsJsonAsync` (lines 43-44) and
    reads the result with `ProblemDetailsResultReader.ReadAsync` (line 46), all wrapped in
    `HttpResultExecutor.ExecuteAsync` for the shared transport-fault translation.
- **Why it's built this way**: a fresh `HttpClient` per call (rather than a stored field) matches how the
  other anonymous auth services in this package are built, since the client is cheap to create from the
  factory and this service holds no other per-call state.
- **Where it's used**: covered by `EmailConfirmationUIServiceTests`
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/EmailConfirmationUIServiceTests.cs`);
  registered against [`IEmailConfirmationUIService`](#iemailconfirmationuiservice) in
  `AddUIShared()` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs`).

### IAuthUIService
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/IAuthUIService.cs:18` · Level 5 · interface

- **What it is**: the single client-side authentication contract: login, register, OAuth code
  exchange, sign-out of this device, refresh, the three password flows, the signed-in-devices list
  with revoke, the sign-in history, and sign-out of every device. The password-based auth pages in the
  framework talk to this; the sign-in-link, passkey and email-confirmation flows have their own
  narrow contracts beside it ([`ISignInLinkUIService`](#isigninlinkuiservice),
  [`IPasskeyUIService`](#ipasskeyuiservice), [`IEmailConfirmationUIService`](#iemailconfirmationuiservice)).
- **Depends on**: [`Result`](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result) and its generic form from
  `MMCA.Common.Shared.Abstractions`; the `MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth` contracts
  [`LoginRequest`](group-08-auth.md#loginrequest),
  [`RegisterRequest`](group-08-auth.md#registerrequest),
  [`AuthenticationResponse`](group-08-auth.md#authenticationresponse),
  [`RefreshSessionSummaryResponse`](group-08-auth.md#refreshsessionsummaryresponse) and
  [`SignInSummaryResponse`](group-08-auth.md#signinsummaryresponse); and
  [`ErrorType`](group-01-result-error-handling.md#errortype) for the failure kinds it documents.
  Implemented by [`AuthUIService`](#authuiservice).
- **Concept introduced, the failure travels with the call.** The interface doc states the rule
  (`IAuthUIService.cs:11-16`): every call that talks to the API returns a
  [`Result`](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result) carrying the server's own errors, so the
  failure arrives with the call rather than on a `LastError` property that the next call would
  overwrite. Pages render it through `MMCA.Common.UI.Common.ResultUiExtensions`
  ([`ResultUiExtensions`](#resultuiextensions)).
  - `[Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]` assesses whether return types carry meaning. Three different
    shapes appear here on purpose, and each deviation is argued in source rather than assumed.
  - `[Rubric §24, Forms, Validation & UX Safety]` assesses whether a form can show the server's real
    message. Because the failure is the return value, a login page can bind the error next to the
    field without a second lookup.
  - `[Rubric §11, Security]` shows in two documented behaviors: the anti-enumeration contract on
    password reset, and the OAuth exchange keeping tokens out of the address bar.
- **Walkthrough**: twelve members, in the order they appear.
  - `LoginAsync(LoginRequest, ct)` and `RegisterAsync(RegisterRequest, ct)` both return
    `Result<AuthenticationResponse>` and both store tokens on success
    (`IAuthUIService.cs:21,24`).
  - `ExchangeOAuthCodeAsync(code, ct)` (line 31) trades a single-use completion code carried in the
    redirect URL for the token pair through `auth/oauth/exchange`, stores the tokens and notifies auth
    state; the doc's closing sentence names the reason for the indirection, keeping tokens out of the
    address bar (lines 26-30).
  - `LogoutAsync()` (line 40) is the deliberate no-`Result` member: it signs out this device only,
    revoking this device's server-side refresh session through `auth/revoke/current` and clearing
    local storage, so the account stays signed in on its other devices. It returns nothing because
    the local sign-out happens whatever the server answered: a user who asked to leave must never be
    kept signed in by a failed network call (lines 33-39).
  - `TryRefreshTokenAsync(ct)` (line 51) is the deliberate `bool` member: it makes no API call of its
    own, since the host's [`ITokenRefresher`](#itokenrefresher) owns the exchange, and its two states
    ("session still live", "session gone") are not errors to render. A `false` is not always a
    sign-out: when an `ISessionAwareTokenRefresher` reports the attempt as transient
    (`TokenAcquisition.IsUnavailable`), the stored credential is kept and a later call tries again
    (lines 42-50).
  - `ChangePasswordAsync(currentPassword, newPassword, ct)` (line 54) hits `auth/password`.
  - `RequestPasswordResetAsync(email, ct)` (line 61) hits the anonymous `auth/forgot-password`. The
    doc pins the semantics: the endpoint answers 202 for every well-formed address as an
    anti-enumeration measure, so a success means "accepted", never "an account exists"
    (lines 56-60).
  - `ResetPasswordAsync(email, token, newPassword, ct)` (line 68) completes the reset via the
    anonymous `auth/reset-password`; an invalid, expired or already-consumed token comes back as a
    failure carrying the server's generic message (lines 63-67).
  - `GetSessionsAsync(ct)` (line 76) returns
    `Result<IReadOnlyList<RefreshSessionSummaryResponse>>` from `auth/my-sessions`, newest first, and
    documents that exactly one row can carry `IsCurrent`, resolved server-side from the access token's
    `sid` claim (lines 70-75).
  - `GetSignInsAsync(ct)` (line 85) returns `Result<IReadOnlyList<SignInSummaryResponse>>` from
    `auth/my-sign-ins`: one row per sign-in however often it refreshed, ended ones included with how
    they ended, newest first, at most 50, the caller's own carrying `IsCurrent` (lines 78-84).
  - `RevokeSessionAsync(sessionId, ct)` (line 94) signs one device out via `auth/revoke/{sessionId}`;
    another account's session id (or a nonexistent one) answers 404 and arrives as an
    [`ErrorType`](group-01-result-error-handling.md#errortype)`.NotFound` failure, and revoking an
    already-revoked session answers the same 404 (lines 87-90).
  - `RevokeAllSessionsAsync(ct)` (line 104) signs out of every device via `auth/revoke` and, unlike
    `LogoutAsync`, returns the server's answer as a `Result`. A failed revoke is reported rather than
    hidden, and the local session is left in place so the caller can say so and let the user retry;
    on success it also performs the same local sign-out `LogoutAsync` does (lines 96-103). The pair
    is the clearest statement of the return-shape rule: two sign-outs with opposite failure policies,
    because "leave this device" must never fail while "end every session" must never claim success it
    did not get.
- **Why it's built this way**: the interface is where the three return shapes are justified, and each
  justification is a behavior rule rather than a style preference. The twelve operations stay on one
  contract because they share one consumer set (the shipped auth and devices pages are framework
  types); newer flows were added as separate interfaces instead, so a consumer's own implementation
  of this one keeps compiling (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:192-193`).
  The device-list and revoke members are the UI surface of
  [ADR-097](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/097-multi-device-refresh-sessions.html); the OAuth
  exchange is the client end of
  [ADR-036](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/036-external-oauth-login.html) and
  [ADR-043](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/043-mobile-deep-links-and-native-oauth-callback.html).
- **Where it's used**: registered `TryAddScoped` against [`AuthUIService`](#authuiservice) by
  `AddUIShared()` (`DependencyInjection.cs:190`, the comment at line 189 noting `TryAdd` prevents
  duplicate registration when several hosts call in); injected by the shipped auth pages, including
  `Login` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor`) and
  [`Sessions`](#sessions), which lists devices and sign-ins and whose sign-out-everywhere action calls
  `RevokeAllSessionsAsync`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Sessions.razor.cs:99,131,241`).

### AuthUIService
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthUIService.cs:48` · Level 6 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the one client-side service that owns a user's session on a Blazor or MAUI head. It
  calls the WebAPI `auth/*` endpoints (sign in, register, OAuth code exchange, sign-in links, passkeys,
  change password, forgot and reset password, list and revoke devices, sign-in history, sign out),
  persists the returned token pair, and tells Blazor's authentication state that something changed, so
  `AuthorizeView` and `[Authorize]` routes react without a page reload. It implements three contracts,
  [IAuthUIService](#iauthuiservice), [ISignInLinkUIService](#isigninlinkuiservice) and
  [IPasskeyUIService](#ipasskeyuiservice) (`AuthUIService.cs:56`), so every way of signing in stores
  its tokens through one path. Every method that talks to the API hands back a
  [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result) carrying the server's own error text, so no page
  has to interpret an `HttpResponseMessage`.
- **Depends on**: first-party
  [ITokenStorageService](#itokenstorageservice) (token persistence, `AuthUIService.cs:50`),
  [ITokenRefresher](#itokenrefresher) (the host-specific renewal path, `AuthUIService.cs:51`),
  [JwtAuthenticationStateProvider](#jwtauthenticationstateprovider) (injected as the framework
  `AuthenticationStateProvider` base type at `AuthUIService.cs:52` and pattern-matched back down),
  [IPushRegistrationService](group-26-device-capability-layer.md#ipushregistrationservice) (native push
  cleanup, `AuthUIService.cs:53`),
  [ILocalCacheStore](group-26-device-capability-layer.md#ilocalcachestore) (optional device-local
  document cache, defaulted to `null`, `AuthUIService.cs:54`, wiped on sign-out),
  [IDeviceMetadataReporter](#idevicemetadatareporter) (optional per-session device reporter,
  `AuthUIService.cs:55`) run through [DeviceMetadataReporting](#devicemetadatareporting), an optional
  `ILogger<AuthUIService>` (`AuthUIService.cs:56`),
  [AuthDelegatingHandler](#authdelegatinghandler) (owner tracking for the bearers it attaches),
  [HttpResultExecutor](#httpresultexecutor) (transport-fault translation),
  [ProblemDetailsResultReader](group-08-auth.md#problemdetailsresultreader) (response translation), and
  the shared auth contracts
  [LoginRequest](group-08-auth.md#loginrequest),
  [RegisterRequest](group-08-auth.md#registerrequest),
  [OAuthCodeExchangeRequest](group-08-auth.md#oauthcodeexchangerequest),
  [ChangePasswordRequest](group-08-auth.md#changepasswordrequest),
  [ForgotPasswordRequest](group-08-auth.md#forgotpasswordrequest),
  [ResetPasswordRequest](group-08-auth.md#resetpasswordrequest),
  [SendSignInLinkRequest](group-08-auth.md#sendsigninlinkrequest),
  [RedeemSignInLinkRequest](group-08-auth.md#redeemsigninlinkrequest),
  [PasskeyRegisterRequest](group-08-auth.md#passkeyregisterrequest),
  [PasskeySignInRequest](group-08-auth.md#passkeysigninrequest),
  [PasskeyOptionsResponse](group-08-auth.md#passkeyoptionsresponse),
  [PasskeyResponse](group-08-auth.md#passkeyresponse),
  [AuthenticationResponse](group-08-auth.md#authenticationresponse),
  [RegistrationOutcome](group-08-auth.md#registrationoutcome),
  [RefreshSessionSummaryResponse](group-08-auth.md#refreshsessionsummaryresponse) and
  [SignInSummaryResponse](group-08-auth.md#signinsummaryresponse).
  Externals: `IHttpClientFactory`, `System.Net.Http.Json` (`PostAsJsonAsync`, `PutAsJsonAsync`),
  `System.Net.Http.Headers.AuthenticationHeaderValue`, and
  `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Authorization.AuthenticationStateProvider`.
- **Concept introduced, the client-side session lifecycle as one service, with a sign-out that cannot
  fail.** Everything a session needs on the client (acquire a token pair, hold it, renew it, publish the
  identity to the component tree, and tear all of that down) lives behind injectable interfaces with a
  single implementation, so no component ever touches `localStorage`, a Bearer header, or a token
  string.
  `[Rubric §26, Front-End Security]` assesses whether credentials are confined to a narrow, auditable
  surface in the browser: here the only code that reads or writes tokens is this service plus
  [AuthDelegatingHandler](#authdelegatinghandler), both of them going through
  [ITokenStorageService](#itokenstorageservice) rather than doing JS interop of their own.
  `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses the end-to-end auth design. There are two sign-outs with opposite
  failure policies. `LogoutAsync` is deliberately **local-first** and ends this device only: the remote
  revoke of `auth/revoke/current` is best effort and bounded, and both the server call and the local
  clear are wrapped so a dropped connection can never strand a user inside a session they asked to
  leave (`AuthUIService.cs:101-117`, `125-140`, `531-548`). `RevokeAllSessionsAsync` is
  **server-first**: it reports a failed revoke and only signs out locally once the server confirmed,
  so "signed out everywhere" is never claimed when it did not happen (`AuthUIService.cs:143-164`).
  `[Rubric §19, State Management]` assesses who owns mutable client state and when it is invalidated:
  this service is the single writer of auth state, and every sign-out it performs also wipes the
  device-local document cache, whose plaintext snapshots survive restarts and are keyed by surface
  rather than by user (`AuthUIService.cs:35-40`), and, through the provider, the per-tab list-page
  state.
  `[Rubric §18, UI Architecture]` sees the same shape the entity services use, a typed service over the
  named `"APIClient"` returning `Result`, so pages render failures with
  [ResultUiExtensions](#resultuiextensions) instead of catching exceptions.
  `[Rubric §14, Testability]` is served by taking every collaborator through the primary constructor
  with no statics of its own: [AuthUIServiceTests](group-29-testing-infrastructure.md#per-project-test-rollup)
  drives the whole class through a stub `HttpMessageHandler`.
- **Walkthrough**
  - Two public error codes head the class. `TokenStorageUnavailableCode = "Auth.TokenStorageUnavailable"`
    (`AuthUIService.cs:62`) is reported when authentication succeeded but the tokens could not be written
    because JS interop was unavailable (SSR prerender, or a render-mode transition), and
    `MissingAccessTokenCode = "Auth.MissingAccessToken"` (`AuthUIService.cs:68`) covers a 2xx whose body
    carried no access token, which means the response shape drifted. Both are `const string`, so tests
    and pages branch on them without duplicating literals. The private `ApiClientName = "APIClient"`
    (`AuthUIService.cs:70`) names the shared client, and `LogoutRevokeTimeout` (line 73) is 10 seconds.
  - `LoginAsync` (line 76) and `RegisterAsync` (lines 85-86) are one-liners over the private
    `AuthenticateAsync`, differing in the relative URL (`auth/login`, `auth/register`) and in
    `RegisterAsync` passing `allowConfirmationPending: true`: behind the email gate the API answers
    `202 Accepted` (account created, confirmation pending, no session), which comes back as a success
    carrying `RegistrationOutcome.ConfirmationPending` with nothing stored and no sign-in (remarks at
    lines 80-84).
  - `ExchangeOAuthCodeAsync` (`AuthUIService.cs:89`) guards the code client-side first: a blank code
    returns `Error.Validation("Auth.OAuth.MissingCode", ...)` without a round trip
    (`AuthUIService.cs:91-95`), then it posts an
    [OAuthCodeExchangeRequest](group-08-auth.md#oauthcodeexchangerequest) to `auth/oauth/exchange`
    (`AuthUIService.cs:97`). The single-use code arrives in the redirect URL, which is what keeps the
    tokens themselves out of the address bar (ADR-036,
    `Website/docs-src/adr/036-external-oauth-login.md`).
  - `AuthenticateAsync` (`AuthUIService.cs:419`) is the shared body of every sign-in: login, register,
    OAuth exchange, sign-in-link redemption and passkey sign-in. It posts the credential on the plain
    factory client through [HttpResultExecutor](#httpresultexecutor) (lines 426-439); when a 202 is
    allowed it short-circuits to the confirmation-pending success (lines 431-435), otherwise it reads
    `ProblemDetailsResultReader.ReadAsync<AuthenticationResponse>` (line 437). It returns early on
    failure or confirmation-pending (lines 441-444), then checks the access token is actually present
    and fails with `MissingAccessTokenCode` if it is not (lines 447-451). Only then does it call
    `tokenStorageService.SetTokensAsync` (line 455) inside a `try` that converts an
    `InvalidOperationException` into a `TokenStorageUnavailableCode` failure carrying the exception
    message as detail (lines 457-479). The point of that branch is that valid credentials nothing can
    hold are a failure, not a silent no-op; on browser hosts it also fires when the HttpOnly cookie
    write reports failure, because the token storage services throw on a `false` from
    [ISessionCookieSync](#isessioncookiesync). Before returning that failure it cleans up after itself:
    the server already minted a session and the storage took the access token in memory before the
    cookie write failed, so it revokes the session through
    `TryRevokeAsync(authentication.AccessToken, ...)` (line 464) and then clears the stored tokens
    (line 467, swallowing a second `InvalidOperationException`, lines 469-472), or the API client would
    behave signed in behind a page that reported failure (comment at lines 459-463).
    On success it pattern-matches the injected `AuthenticationStateProvider` down to
    [JwtAuthenticationStateProvider](#jwtauthenticationstateprovider) and awaits its `SignInAsync`
    (lines 483-486), which forgets the previous account's list-page state before publishing the new
    identity (comment at lines 481-482). The `is` test rather than a cast is what lets a host register
    a different provider without breaking sign-in. Last it runs `ReportDeviceAsync` (line 489), after
    the tokens are stored so the report's bearer names the new session.
  - `ReportDeviceAsync` (lines 499-505) calls `DeviceMetadataReporting.ReportAsync` (line 503) only
    when a reporter was injected. The constructor doc records that the registered default is a no-op,
    the MAUI package replaces it, and its wait is bounded with failures logged and swallowed, so it can
    never fail or hold up a sign-in (lines 41-46).
  - `LogoutAsync` (`AuthUIService.cs:101`) runs three steps, each isolated so a failure cannot stop the
    next. First the private `UnregisterPushAsync()` (line 103). Second, if a token can be read
    (lines 105-106), it calls the private `TryRevokeAsync` under a `CancellationTokenSource` of
    `LogoutRevokeTimeout` (lines 112-113): the comment at lines 108-111 records that the revoke is
    awaited but never fails, and is bounded by 10 seconds rather than the client's 90 s
    `HttpClient.Timeout`, so a hung backend cannot hold the sign-out. `TryRevokeAsync` (line 125) is the
    shared best-effort revoke: it creates an APIClient, sets the Bearer header by hand (line 128) and
    posts `auth/revoke/current` (line 132) inside a bare `catch` that ignores every failure
    (lines 134-139). It ends only the session that token belongs to, so the account stays signed in on
    its other devices (doc at lines 119-124). The helper is shared with the login path that cannot
    store the session it was just issued, so the two revokes cannot drift. Third, the private
    `SignOutLocallyAsync()` (line 116).
  - `RevokeAllSessionsAsync` (`AuthUIService.cs:143`) posts `auth/revoke` through
    [HttpResultExecutor](#httpresultexecutor) on an authenticated client, reading it with the
    non-generic reader (lines 145-153). Only when the result is a success does it run
    `UnregisterPushAsync()` then `SignOutLocallyAsync()`, in the same order as `LogoutAsync` so the push
    unregister still holds a valid access token (lines 155-161); either way it returns the server's
    `Result` (line 163). A failure leaves the local session intact for the caller to report and retry.
  - `TryRefreshTokenAsync` (`AuthUIService.cs:167`) makes no HTTP call of its own. It asks the injected
    `tokenRefresher` for a token, through one of two paths. When the refresher is an
    `ISessionAwareTokenRefresher` (pattern-matched at line 178) it calls `TryAcquireAccessTokenAsync`
    and, if the answer `IsUnavailable` (a transient outcome that says nothing about the session, for
    the direct refresher a 409 refresh-superseded), returns `false` immediately (lines 180-184) without
    clearing anything: the stored credential is kept for the next attempt, because clearing it would
    stop this client from ever presenting a token someone else rotated, which is what lets the server's
    reuse detection (BR-206) revoke the other holder's session (comment at lines 172-176). Any other
    refresher falls back to `AcquireAccessTokenAsync` (line 190). Browser hosts renew through the
    same-origin cookie proxy so the refresh token never reaches JS
    ([SameOriginProxyTokenRefresher](#sameoriginproxytokenrefresher)) and MAUI renews straight from
    secure storage ([DirectApiTokenRefresher](#directapitokenrefresher)). A null or blank answer means
    the session is gone, which this method treats exactly like a sign-out: it calls
    `SignOutLocallyAsync()` and returns `false` (lines 193-199). A token that comes back is published
    with `NotifyUserAuthentication`, not the provider's `SignInAsync`, because a refresh is not a
    sign-in and keeps the list-page state, and is answered with `true` (lines 201-206). The `bool`
    return is the honest type here, because neither outcome is an error a page would render
    (`IAuthUIService.cs:42-51`).
  - The password trio all wrap [HttpResultExecutor](#httpresultexecutor).
    `ChangePasswordAsync` (line 210) is the only one that authenticates: it builds a
    [ChangePasswordRequest](group-08-auth.md#changepasswordrequest) and `PUT`s it to `auth/password`
    (line 220). `RequestPasswordResetAsync` (line 226) and `ResetPasswordAsync` (line 268) deliberately
    use the plain factory client with no Bearer header (line 232 for the first), because a reset must
    not be bound to whatever session happens to be open (comment at lines 230-231). The comment at
    lines 236-237 records the contract that matters: `auth/forgot-password` answers 202 for every
    well-formed address, so a success never means "this account exists".
  - The sign-in-link pair implements [ISignInLinkUIService](#isigninlinkuiservice).
    `RequestSignInLinkAsync` (line 243) posts a
    [SendSignInLinkRequest](group-08-auth.md#sendsigninlinkrequest) to the anonymous `auth/sign-in-link`
    (line 250) and reads it with the non-generic reader (line 252). `RedeemSignInLinkAsync` (line 257)
    hands a [RedeemSignInLinkRequest](group-08-auth.md#redeemsigninlinkrequest) to `AuthenticateAsync`
    against `auth/sign-in-link/redeem`, so a redeemed link is stored and signalled exactly like a
    password sign-in.
  - The session methods back the devices page. `GetSessionsAsync` (line 286) `GET`s `auth/my-sessions`
    and reads it with the **generic** reader into `IReadOnlyList<RefreshSessionSummaryResponse>`
    (lines 293-294); `GetSignInsAsync` (line 300) does the same for `auth/my-sign-ins` into
    `IReadOnlyList<SignInSummaryResponse>` (lines 307-308). `RevokeSessionAsync` (line 314) posts
    `auth/revoke/{sessionId}` and reads it with the **non-generic** reader (lines 319-324), because that
    endpoint answers 204 and
    [ProblemDetailsResultReader](group-08-auth.md#problemdetailsresultreader)'s generic overload would
    turn an empty 2xx body into an "empty response" failure (comment at lines 321-322). Picking the
    wrong overload there would turn every successful revoke into an error.
  - The passkey members implement [IPasskeyUIService](#ipasskeyuiservice), each on an authenticated
    client except the sign-in pair: `BeginRegistrationAsync` (line 329, `auth/passkeys/register/options`),
    `CompleteRegistrationAsync` (line 341, `auth/passkeys/register`), `ListAsync` (line 353),
    `RenameAsync` (line 364), `DeleteAsync` (line 376, the non-generic reader again because the
    endpoint answers 204, comment at line 382), `BeginSignInAsync` (line 389,
    `auth/passkeys/signin/options`) and `SignInAsync` (lines 402-403), which goes through
    `AuthenticateAsync` against `auth/passkeys/signin`.
  - Private helpers close the class. `UnregisterPushAsync` (line 512) calls
    `pushRegistration.UnregisterAsync()` (line 516) inside a bare `catch` (lines 518-523): the Devices
    DELETE is authenticated, so it has to happen while the access token is still valid, and it is a
    no-op on web heads (ADR-044, `Website/docs-src/adr/044-native-push-delivery.md`).
    `SignOutLocallyAsync` (line 531) is the local half of every sign-out, shared by Logout, Sign out
    everywhere and an unrefreshable session (doc at lines 526-530):
    `tokenStorageService.ClearTokensAsync()` under `catch (InvalidOperationException)` for the
    interop-unavailable case (lines 533-540), then `ClearLocalCacheAsync()` (line 542), then the
    provider's `SignOutAsync()` behind the type test (lines 544-547), which forgets the list-page state
    and notifies logout. The two `#pragma warning disable CA1031` blocks (lines 134-136 in
    `TryRevokeAsync`, 518-520 in `UnregisterPushAsync`) are deliberate and annotated in place:
    catching everything is the correct policy for a best-effort cleanup step.
    `CreateAuthenticatedClientAsync` (line 556) creates the APIClient, sets
    `DefaultRequestHeaders.Authorization` from the stored token (line 563) and registers that token's
    owner with `AuthDelegatingHandler.TrackTokenOwner` (line 567), so a 401 to it renews or ends the
    session this page holds rather than the handler's own storage (comment at lines 565-566); its doc
    comment states that it mirrors [AuthenticatedServiceBase](#authenticatedservicebase) and cannot
    inherit it, because this is not an entity service and takes a different dependency set
    (lines 550-555). `ReadAccessTokenAsync` (line 573) swallows `InvalidOperationException` from the
    store and returns `null`, so an SSR prerender proceeds tokenless and lets the API answer 401 like
    any other failure (lines 579-584). `ClearLocalCacheAsync` (line 590) no-ops when `localCache` is
    `null` (lines 592-595), otherwise calls `localCache.ClearAsync()` (line 599) inside a
    `catch (InvalidOperationException)` for the same JS-interop-gone case the token clear guards
    against (lines 601-604), so a device-local offline snapshot never survives to be read by the next
    account on the same device.
- **Why it's built this way**: ADR-051 (`Website/docs-src/adr/051-client-auth-token-lifecycle.md`) is the
  record behind the split visible in the constructor: storage, renewal and orchestration are three
  different abstractions because each render mode (SSR prerender, Blazor Server, WebAssembly, MAUI) can
  hold and renew a credential differently, while the orchestration above them stays identical. The
  refresh path itself is server-side rotation with reuse detection (ADR-050,
  `Website/docs-src/adr/050-jwt-refresh-token-rotation.md`), generalized to one row per device by ADR-097
  (`Website/docs-src/adr/097-multi-device-refresh-sessions.md`), which is what gives `GetSessionsAsync`,
  `RevokeSessionAsync` and the this-device-only `auth/revoke/current` something to list and revoke.
  Browser hosts keep the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie rather than in reachable storage (ADR-022,
  `Website/docs-src/adr/022-browser-session-cookie-auth.md`), which is exactly why `TryRefreshTokenAsync`
  delegates instead of calling a refresh endpoint itself. Implementing the sign-in-link and passkey
  contracts on this class rather than in their own services means every sign-in shares
  `AuthenticateAsync`, so token storage, the storage-failure revoke, the provider sign-in and the
  device report cannot drift between flows (registration comments at
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:196-202`). Returning `Result`
  instead of throwing keeps every auth failure renderable: the API's Problem Details payload already
  carries the server's own wording and [ErrorType](group-01-result-error-handling.md#errortype), so the
  page shows that rather than a client-invented message.
- **Where it's used**: registered three times in `AddUIShared()`, as
  `TryAddScoped<IAuthUIService, AuthUIService>()`, `TryAddScoped<ISignInLinkUIService, AuthUIService>()`
  and `TryAddScoped<IPasskeyUIService, AuthUIService>()`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:190,198,203`), so every host
  that adds the shared UI gets it. Consumers inside the shared UI are the auth pages
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor:361`,
  `Pages/Auth/Register.razor:250`, `Pages/Auth/OAuthComplete.razor:86`,
  `Pages/Auth/ForgotPassword.razor:95`, `Pages/Auth/ResetPassword.razor:157`), the devices page
  [Sessions](#sessions) (`Pages/Auth/Sessions.razor.cs:99`, `131`, `175`, `241`), the sign-in-link and
  passkey surfaces through their own interfaces, and the components that sign out
  (`Layout/MainLayout.razor:219`, `Layout/NavMenu.razor.cs:70`,
  `Components/Capabilities/BiometricGate.razor.cs:266`, `Components/Legal/TermsAcceptanceGate.razor.cs:235`,
  `Pages/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorAccount.razor.cs:311`, all calling `LogoutAsync`). Downstream, the
  shared [ChangePasswordCard](#changepasswordcard) calls `ChangePasswordAsync`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/ChangePasswordCard.razor.cs:149`),
  and the consumer profile pages ([Profile](group-24-identity-module.md#profile)) host that card
  rather than calling the service themselves. `ForgotPassword.razor` discards the `Result` of its call
  (line 95), because the page must look identical whether or not the address exists. The component
  gallery substitutes
  [NoOpAuthUIService](group-29-testing-infrastructure.md#noopauthuiservice), and
  [AuthUIServiceTests](group-29-testing-infrastructure.md#per-project-test-rollup)
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/AuthUIServiceTests.cs:39`) pins the
  behavior end to end.
- **Caveats**: `TryRefreshTokenAsync` has no call site in `MMCA.Common.UI` outside its own declaration;
  renewal in a running app happens further down, inside the storage service, the refreshers and the
  [AuthDelegatingHandler](#authdelegatinghandler) 401 path, so this method is a public entry point for
  hosts and tests. `CreateAuthenticatedClientAsync` sets a `DefaultRequestHeaders` Bearer while
  [AuthDelegatingHandler](#authdelegatinghandler) would otherwise attach one to every APIClient request
  from storage (`DependencyInjection.cs:174`); the handler skips its own lookup when the request already
  carries an `Authorization` header (`Services/Auth/AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:192`), so the stored token
  is read once here and the handler leaves that header alone. Behind the same-origin proxy both are
  then stripped by [SameOriginProxyRequestHandler](#sameoriginproxyrequesthandler).

### AppUserAgent
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Devices` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Devices/AppUserAgent.cs:10` · Level 0 · class (public, static)

- **What it is**: builds the `User-Agent` header value a native MMCA app sends, in the shape
  `Name/Version (Platform OsVersion; MmcaApp)`, so the server can tell an app session from a browser
  session and the signed-in-devices page can label it.
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party; BCL only (`string.Normalize`, `CharUnicodeInfo`, `StringBuilder`).
- **Concept introduced, a header value built from untrusted text must be made header-safe.** App name,
  version and OS version come from the device, and an HTTP header token cannot hold spaces,
  parentheses, slashes or non-ASCII. `Build` therefore sanitizes every part instead of trusting it.
  - `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether externally sourced text is neutralized before it reaches
    a protocol boundary. Comment text drops the delimiters `(`, `)`, the escape `\` and the separator
    `;` (`AppUserAgent.cs:112`), so a hostile or odd OS string cannot close the comment early or
    forge the `MmcaApp` marker.
  - `[Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality]` shows in the single `Sanitize` routine shared by both
    character classes (`AppUserAgent.cs:79`), parameterized by predicate and replacement character.
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `Marker = "MmcaApp"` (`AppUserAgent.cs:13`) is the public token the reader side looks for;
    `FallbackName = "App"` (line 16) stands in when nothing of the app name survives sanitizing, and
    `TokenSymbols` (line 19) lists the punctuation an RFC 9110 token may hold.
  - `Build(appName, appVersion, platform, osVersion)` (line 29) rejects a blank `appName` with
    `ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace` (line 31), tokenizes the name (falling back to `App`,
    lines 33-37) and the version, joins them as `name/version` or just `name` (lines 39-40), then
    builds the comment from the normalized platform and OS version (lines 42-44). The result is
    `product (system; MmcaApp)`, or `product (MmcaApp)` when both system parts are empty (lines 46-48).
  - `NormalizePlatform` (line 55) renames MAUI's UI-stack names to OS names: `WinUI` becomes
    `Windows` and `MacCatalyst` becomes `macOS` (lines 59-64).
  - `ToToken` (line 71) and `ToCommentText` (line 77) call `Sanitize` (line 79): it folds accents with
    `FormD` and drops non-spacing marks, then collapses each run of disallowed characters into one
    replacement (a hyphen for tokens, a space for comment text), never leading with one.
    `IsTokenChar` (line 110) is ASCII letters, digits and `TokenSymbols`; `IsCommentChar` (line 112)
    is visible ASCII minus the four reserved characters.
- **Why it's built this way**: the writer and the reader are separate classes with one shared constant,
  so the marker cannot drift: [`UserAgentSummary`](#useragentsummary) matches on `AppUserAgent.Marker`
  rather than a literal. Sanitizing at the writer keeps the reader's parse trivially simple.
- **Where it's used**: called once by
  [`MauiAppUserAgentHandler`](group-26-device-capability-layer.md#mauiappuseragenthandler) to build its
  cached header (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Maui/Services/MauiAppUserAgentHandler.cs:21`);
  read back by `UserAgentSummary.ParseApp` (`UserAgentSummary.cs:185`, `161`). Pinned by
  `AppUserAgentTests`
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/Devices/AppUserAgentTests.cs`).

### BackfillGate
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Devices` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Devices/DeviceMetadataReporting.cs:95` · Level 0 · class (private, sealed, nested)

- **What it is**: the two-flag state [`DeviceMetadataReporting`](#devicemetadatareporting) keeps per
  reporter instance, answering "is the refresh backfill done?" and "is one running right now?" so the
  backfill reports until one report succeeds and never runs twice at once.
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party; BCL `Volatile` and `Interlocked` only.
- **Walkthrough**: two `int` fields, `_reported` and `_running` (`DeviceMetadataReporting.cs:97-98`).
  `TryBegin` (lines 100-101) returns `true` only when `_reported` still reads 0 and a
  `CompareExchange` flips `_running` from 0 to 1, so a concurrent refresh that loses the race skips
  rather than waits. `End` (line 103) releases `_running`; `MarkReported` (line 105) sets `_reported`
  for good, after which `TryBegin` always refuses.
- **Why it's built this way**: an `int` pair with `Volatile`/`Interlocked` is the lock-free form of a
  one-shot gate: nothing blocks, and a joiner simply skips the backfill because another call is already
  doing it. The class doc states the two questions it answers (line 94).
- **Where it's used**: only inside [`DeviceMetadataReporting`](#devicemetadatareporting), created on
  demand by `Gates.GetValue` (`DeviceMetadataReporting.cs:47`, `75`), opened by `TryBegin` (line 76),
  released in a `finally` (line 87) and closed by `MarkReported` after any recorded report (line 47).

### IDeviceMetadataReporter
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Devices` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Devices/IDeviceMetadataReporter.cs:22` · Level 0 · interface

- **What it is**: the client-side contract that reports the device this app runs on to the server,
  which records it on the caller's current refresh session (`PUT auth/sessions/current/device`), so
  the signed-in devices list and the sign-in history name the device instead of describing its
  user-agent (`IDeviceMetadataReporter.cs:3-6`).
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party in its signature. Implemented by
  [`NullDeviceMetadataReporter`](#nulldevicemetadatareporter) (the default on every head) and by
  [`MauiDeviceMetadataReporter`](group-26-device-capability-layer.md#mauidevicemetadatareporter) on
  native heads; the metadata it sends is the server-side
  [`DeviceMetadata`](group-08-auth.md#devicemetadata) record.
- **Concept introduced, a best-effort side call with a boolean contract.** The device report rides
  behind a sign-in or a refresh that already succeeded, so it must never be able to fail or delay
  either. The interface encodes that in two ways: the class doc makes "should not throw" part of the
  contract and says the callers bound the wait and swallow whatever escapes
  (`IDeviceMetadataReporter.cs:14-20`), and the single method returns `bool` instead of throwing, so
  "not recorded, try again later" is an ordinary answer.
  - `[Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]` assesses whether a contract states its failure semantics.
    `ReportAsync` documents both answers (`IDeviceMetadataReporter.cs:28-32`): `true` when the server
    recorded the report or there is nothing to report, `false` when it was not recorded, so the
    refresh backfill tries again on the next refresh.
- **Walkthrough**: one member, `Task<bool> ReportAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)`
  (`IDeviceMetadataReporter.cs:33`). The caller cancels the token after a short bound (line 27; the
  bound is [`DeviceMetadataReporting.Timeout`](#devicemetadatareporting)).
- **Why it's built this way**: the class doc (`IDeviceMetadataReporter.cs:7-13`) explains the two
  callers. The sign-in path reports every time; the native token storage also reports after a
  successful refresh until one report in the process has succeeded, so a session that began before
  the server stored device metadata gets described within one access-token lifetime without a new
  sign-in. Rotation then carries the metadata to every successor session. It must be registered as a
  singleton because the once-per-process state is tracked per reporter instance (lines 17-19). The
  device capability abstraction this sits in is
  [ADR-042](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/042-device-capability-abstraction.html); the refresh
  lifecycle it piggybacks on is
  [ADR-051](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/051-client-auth-token-lifecycle.html).
- **Where it's used**: registered as the no-op default with `TryAddSingleton`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Capabilities/DependencyInjection.cs:71`)
  and replaced on MAUI with `AddSingleton`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Maui/DependencyInjection.cs:80`). Called through
  [`DeviceMetadataReporting`](#devicemetadatareporting) by
  [`AuthUIService`](#authuiservice) after each sign-in
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthUIService.cs:503`) and by
  [`SecureStoreTokenStorageService`](#securestoretokenstorageservice) after a refresh
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/SecureStoreTokenStorageService.cs:143`).
  Pinned by `AuthUIServiceDeviceReportTests` and `SecureStoreDeviceBackfillTests`
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/Devices/`).

- **What it is**: one configured generic OIDC sign-in provider as the sign-in page sees it: `Name`

  per entry (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor:260`) and offers
  the organization step when any entry has `UsesDomains` (line 304). Pinned by `LoginOidcTests` and

### DeviceMetadataReporting
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Devices` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Devices/DeviceMetadataReporting.cs:14` · Level 1 · class (internal, static, partial)

- **What it is**: the one place that runs an [`IDeviceMetadataReporter`](#idevicemetadatareporter) for
  its two callers, the sign-in path and the refresh backfill, under the same rules: the wait is capped,
  and any failure (cancellation included) is logged and swallowed, so a report never fails or holds up
  the call it follows (`DeviceMetadataReporting.cs:6-13`).
- **Depends on**: [`IDeviceMetadataReporter`](#idevicemetadatareporter) and its own nested
  [`BackfillGate`](#backfillgate); externals `ConditionalWeakTable`, `CancellationTokenSource`,
  `Task.WaitAsync` and the `[LoggerMessage]` source generator.
- **Concept introduced, bounding a call you do not control.** A cancellation token only works if the
  callee honors it. `ReportAsync` therefore applies the bound twice: it links the caller's token to a
  `CancelAfter(Timeout)` source and passes that to the reporter, and it also wraps the returned task in
  `WaitAsync(Timeout, cancellationToken)`, so a reporter that ignores cancellation still cannot hold the
  caller past the bound (comment and call at `DeviceMetadataReporting.cs:41-43`).
  - `[Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]` assesses whether swallowed failures stay visible.
    The broad `catch` is deliberate (the `CA1031` suppression at lines 52-54 names the reason,
    best-effort) and still logs through a generated `LogReportFailed` at `Warning` level
    (lines 58, 91-92).
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `Timeout = 3` seconds (`DeviceMetadataReporting.cs:20`): the report follows a request that just
    succeeded, so it normally takes a fraction of that; the bound only caps a hung connection
    (lines 16-19).
  - `Gates` (line 27) is a `ConditionalWeakTable<IDeviceMetadataReporter, BackfillGate>`: backfill state
    keyed by reporter instance rather than a static flag, so it lives and dies with the reporter it
    describes (lines 22-26).
  - `ReportAsync(reporter, logger, cancellationToken)` (line 34) runs one bounded report
    (lines 38-43). When the report was recorded it marks the reporter's gate reported, whoever the
    caller was, because a recorded device needs no backfill: rotation carries it forward (lines 44-48).
    Any exception is logged when a logger was supplied and turned into `false` (lines 53-62).
  - `ReportOncePerProcessAsync(reporter, logger)` (line 73) is the refresh backfill. It gets the gate,
    returns immediately when `TryBegin` refuses (lines 75-79: already reported, or a report is already
    running), otherwise runs `ReportAsync` with `CancellationToken.None` and releases the gate in a
    `finally` (lines 81-88). A failed report leaves the gate open, so the next successful refresh (one
    per access-token lifetime) tries again; nothing retries in between (doc at lines 65-69).
- **Why it's built this way**: two callers with one rule set is a duplication risk; centralizing the
  bound, the swallow and the gate here keeps [`AuthUIService`](#authuiservice) and
  [`SecureStoreTokenStorageService`](#securestoretokenstorageservice) to a one-line call each. Keying
  the gate by instance is what makes the "register as a singleton" requirement on
  [`IDeviceMetadataReporter`](#idevicemetadatareporter) load-bearing.
- **Where it's used**: `ReportAsync` from `AuthUIService.ReportDeviceAsync`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthUIService.cs:503`);
  `ReportOncePerProcessAsync` from the native token storage after a refresh, deliberately after the
  hydrate slot is cleared because the report authenticates through the `APIClient` pipeline whose
  bearer read comes back to that storage
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/SecureStoreTokenStorageService.cs:139-144`).

### IOAuthUISettings
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.OAuth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/OAuth/IOAuthUISettings.cs:9` · Level 1 · interface

- **What it is**: tells the shared login page which external identity providers this host can actually
  use: three booleans for the built-in providers plus the list of configured generic OIDC providers, so
  a sign-in button renders only where the provider is really wired up.
- **Depends on**: [`OidcProviderOption`](#oidcprovideroption) (the element type of `OidcProviders`).
  Implemented in the framework by [`DefaultOAuthUISettings`](#defaultoauthuisettings) and
  [`ConfigurationOAuthUISettings`](#configurationoauthuisettings); consumed by the shared
  [`Login`](#login) page.
- **Concept introduced, default interface members as a safe-off baseline.** All four members carry a
  body: the three flags return `false` and the provider list returns `[]`
  (`IOAuthUISettings.cs:12,15,18,21`), so an implementation can be an empty class and still compile
  with every provider hidden. That is what makes the framework's default a seven-line file rather than
  a stub with four properties.
  - `[Rubric §18, UI Architecture & Component Design]` assesses whether a component asks a typed
    contract rather than reaching into configuration. The login page injects this interface and never
    touches `IConfiguration`, so the same markup works on a host that has no OAuth at all.
  - `[Rubric §26, Front-End Security]` assesses what the client is told. The contract carries
    availability only: no client id, no secret, no redirect URI, and the OIDC entries carry a name,
    a display name and a domains flag. The class docs state the intent directly, that implementations
    declare availability so the login page can conditionally render social buttons
    (`IOAuthUISettings.cs:3-8`).
- **Walkthrough**: three get-only flags, `GoogleEnabled` (`IOAuthUISettings.cs:12`), `GitHubEnabled`
  (line 15) and `AppleEnabled` (line 18), each declared as `bool X => false`, and
  `IReadOnlyList<OidcProviderOption> OidcProviders => []` (line 21), documented as the providers
  configured under `OAuth:Oidc:<Name>`, one sign-in button each (line 20).
- **Why it's built this way**: external login is optional per host, and the decision has to be readable
  from the render tree. Making the interface the question (rather than a settings object) lets the
  framework register a no-op default and lets a host swap in a real answer without any page change.
  Adding OIDC as a defaulted member kept every existing implementation compiling. The federated login
  flow the flags gate is recorded in
  [ADR-036](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/036-external-oauth-login.html), and the mobile callback
  variant in [ADR-043](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/043-mobile-deep-links-and-native-oauth-callback.html).
- **Where it's used**: `AddUIShared()` registers the no-op default with `TryAddSingleton`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:245`, with the override
  instructions in the comment at lines 243-244). The shared login page injects it
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor:16`), guards the Apple,
  Google and GitHub buttons on it (lines 192, 214, 236), renders one button per OIDC provider
  (line 260), and in `OnInitialized` folds everything into one `_hasExternalProviders` value
  (lines 305-306) that decides whether the whole external-login block renders (line 180). MMCA.ADC
  registers [`ConfigurationOAuthUISettings`](#configurationoauthuisettings) on all three heads
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web/Program.cs:86`,
  `MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web.Client/Program.cs:38`,
  `MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI/MauiProgram.cs:96`).

### IOidcDiscoveryUIService
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.OAuth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/OAuth/IOidcDiscoveryUIService.cs:9` · Level 1 · interface

- **What it is**: the client behind the sign-in page's "Sign in with your organization" step. It asks
  the API which configured OIDC provider owns an email address's domain, which is home-realm discovery
  (`IOidcDiscoveryUIService.cs:5-8`).
- **Depends on**: [`OidcDiscoveryResponse`](group-08-auth.md#oidcdiscoveryresponse) (the shared
  answer: provider name and display name).
- **Concept introduced, home-realm discovery.** With many organization providers configured, a button
  per provider stops scaling and leaks which organizations use the app. The email-first step instead
  takes the address, and the server maps its domain to a provider; the client only learns the one
  match. The server side is [`OidcProviderRegistry`](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#oidcproviderregistry).
- **Walkthrough**: one member, `DiscoverAsync(string email, CancellationToken)`
  (`IOidcDiscoveryUIService.cs:15`), returning the provider or `null` when no provider claims the domain
  (line 14).
- **Where it's used**: registered with `TryAddScoped` to
  [`OidcDiscoveryUIService`](#oidcdiscoveryuiservice)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:207`, comment at 205-206:
  inert until the host configures an OIDC provider that declares email domains). The [`Login`](#login)
  page resolves it at the click with `GetService` rather than injecting it, so a host or a component
  test that never offers the step does not have to register it
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor.cs:283-289`). Pinned by
  `LoginOidcTests`.

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Devices` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Devices/NullDeviceMetadataReporter.cs:8` · Level 1 · class (sealed)

  whether a pattern removes branching. The detail that matters is the answer: `ReportAsync` returns

### OAuthFlowStateStore
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.OAuth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/OAuth/OAuthFlowStateStore.cs:20` · Level 1 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: binds an OAuth authorize-redirect to the client that started it, by minting a random
  `state` value, persisting it with a start time, and later checking that the value the provider's
  callback returns matches. It is the anti-CSRF half of the flow described by ADR-036.
- **Depends on**: [`ILocalCacheStore`](group-26-device-capability-layer.md#ilocalcachestore)
  (device-local storage, injected, `OAuthFlowStateStore.cs:20`) for persistence, `TimeProvider`
  (injected, defaulted to `TimeProvider.System`, `OAuthFlowStateStore.cs:20`, `31`) for the expiry
  check, `System.Security.Cryptography.RandomNumberGenerator` to mint the state value, and its own
  private record [PendingAttempt](#pendingattempt) as the stored shape.
- **Concept introduced, device-local state binding for a redirect-based flow.** A browser or MAUI OAuth
  challenge leaves the app entirely and comes back on a different navigation, so nothing in memory
  survives the round trip; the only thing that can prove the callback belongs to the request this
  client made is a value written to durable storage before the redirect and checked after it.
  `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses this exact class of defense: `BeginAsync` mints the value with
  `RandomNumberGenerator.GetHexString(32, lowercase: true)` (`OAuthFlowStateStore.cs:57`), a
  cryptographically strong source, not `Guid.NewGuid()` or a counter. It also fails closed: with no
  storage to bind against, a completion is refused rather than waved through.
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `StorageKey = "auth.oauth-flow"` (`OAuthFlowStateStore.cs:23`) and `AttemptLifetime = 10` minutes
    (`OAuthFlowStateStore.cs:29`, "comfortably longer than a provider round trip and far shorter than a
    session, so an abandoned attempt cannot be revived days later").
  - `IsEnforced` (`OAuthFlowStateStore.cs:38`) reports `store.IsAvailable`: `false` only on a host that
    registered neither the browser nor the native local-storage capability. There nothing durable can
    be written across the redirect, so every completion is refused (doc at `33-37`).
  - `BeginAsync` (`OAuthFlowStateStore.cs:50`) returns `null` immediately when storage is unavailable
    (`52-55`), otherwise mints the state, stores a `PendingAttempt` under `StorageKey` (`57-60`), then
    reads the attempt back and compares its state ordinally (`64-65`). The read-back exists because the
    browser store swallows a failed write (comment at `62-63`); if the attempt was not kept (storage
    full, site data blocked, private mode) it throws `InvalidOperationException` (`67-68`, documented
    at `45-49`), so the failure surfaces before the redirect for the page to explain rather than one
    redirect later as an unexplained refusal. On success it returns the state for the caller to append
    to the challenge URL (`71`).
  - `TryCompleteAsync` (`OAuthFlowStateStore.cs:85`) returns `false` when storage is unavailable
    (`87-92`, "fail closed: with nowhere to keep the attempt, no completion can be shown to belong to
    this client"), otherwise reads and unconditionally removes the pending attempt (`94-95`, "removed
    either way, so a value is good for exactly one completion"), and fails if there was none or it
    expired (`97-100`). When a pending attempt exists, it accepts only a non-empty `returnedState` that
    matches exactly, ordinal comparison (`105-106`). An absent or empty value is refused: every
    legitimate flow round-trips the state, and accepting an omitted parameter would let a pasted link
    bypass the binding (comment at `102-104`, doc at `74-81`).
- **Why it's built this way**: ADR-036 (`Website/docs-src/adr/036-external-oauth-login.md`) is the OAuth
  design this binds into; the single-use, time-boxed local record, together with refusing a completion
  that omits the state or cannot be bound at all, is what keeps a replayed, stale, or forged callback
  from being accepted.
- **Where it's used**: registered in
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:215` (`TryAddScoped`). The
  web flow begins on the [`Login`](#login) page
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor.cs:378`) and completes on
  the `OAuthComplete` page
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/OAuthComplete.razor:75`); the native
  callback path takes it in the constructor of
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Maui/Capabilities/Auth/MauiExternalAuthBroker.cs:40`.
  Pinned by `OAuthFlowStateStoreTests`
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/OAuthFlowStateStoreTests.cs`),
  with the page wiring covered by `LoginOAuthAttemptTests` and `OAuthCompleteTests`.

### UserAgentSummary
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.Devices` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Devices/UserAgentSummary.cs:21` · Level 1 · class (internal, static)

- **What it is**: a deliberately tiny `User-Agent` reader that turns a session's header into the device
  label a person recognizes their own device by: the browser and the platform for a web session, or the
  app name and platform for a native MMCA app. When a native client reported device metadata, the label
  uses that instead. Shared by the signed-in-devices page, the administrator's sessions table and the
  sign-in history table.
- **Depends on**: [`AppUserAgent`](#appuseragent) (its `Marker` constant, `UserAgentSummary.cs:185`),
  [`DeviceMetadata`](group-08-auth.md#devicemetadata) (the reported name, model and platform);
  externals `IStringLocalizer` (for `Describe`) and `string.Contains` with
  `StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase`.
- **Concept introduced, scoping a parser to the question actually asked.** The class doc argues the
  design rather than describing it (`UserAgentSummary.cs:6-15`): a device list only has to let someone
  answer "is that me?", so a full UA database buys precision nobody reads, while the
  browser-and-platform pair separates a phone from a work laptop. Anything unrecognized reports
  `null` from `Parse`, and `Describe` supplies its own "unknown device" wording rather than dumping the
  raw header, which is neither readable nor localizable.
  - `[Rubric §27, Internationalization & Localization]` assesses whether user-visible text survives
    translation. This is the sharpest example in the package: the parts are returned separately
    and never joined in code, because composing "Chrome on Windows" would hard-code English word
    order. `Describe` formats them through localizer resources (`Auth.Sessions.Device.Format`,
    `Auth.Sessions.Device.AppFormat`, `Auth.Sessions.Device.Unknown`, `UserAgentSummary.cs:114-124`,
    and `Auth.Sessions.Device.NamedFormat`, line 146; ADR-027 is named in the class doc, lines 16-19).
  - `[Rubric §32, Dependency & Supply-Chain]` applies to what is absent: no UA-parsing library and no
    data file to keep current, which is a real dependency avoided for a cosmetic feature.
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `Browsers`, eleven `(Token, Name)` pairs in most-specific-first order
    (`UserAgentSummary.cs:28-41`). Order is load-bearing and the comment says why (lines 23-26): every
    Chromium browser also says "Chrome", and Chrome and Edge both say "Safari", so `Edg/`, `EdgiOS/`
    and `EdgA/` come before `OPR/`, which comes before `CriOS/` and `Chrome/`, which come before
    `Safari/`.
  - `Platforms`, ten pairs with the same rule (`UserAgentSummary.cs:47-59`): `Windows Phone` before
    `Windows`, `Mac OS X` and `Macintosh` before `Linux`, because an iPad reports "Macintosh" in
    desktop mode and Android reports "Linux".
  - `AppPlatforms`, nine `(Word, Name)` pairs (`UserAgentSummary.cs:65-76`) for the one-word platform a
    native app header carries, including MAUI's desktop names (`WinUI` to `Windows`, `MacCatalyst` to
    `macOS`).
  - `Parse(string? userAgent)` (line 86) returns `(null, null)` for a missing or blank header
    (lines 88-91), otherwise runs the shared matcher over each table and returns the pair (line 93).
  - `Describe(userAgent, localizer)` (line 103) is the header-only label. It reads the native-app
    marker BEFORE the browser tokens, because an app header that also carries a WebView's `Chrome/`
    token is still the app (lines 107-115). Otherwise a `switch` over the `Parse` pair covers all four
    null combinations: both present uses the `Format` resource, one present returns it bare, neither
    returns the localized unknown string (lines 117-125).
  - `Describe(device, userAgent, localizer)` (line 137) is the overload every view calls. It treats
    blank metadata values as absent through `Blank` (line 163), takes the device name, and builds a
    detail from the model and platform with `DescribeHardware` (line 154), which reuses the same
    `Format` resource so the word order stays a resource (comment at line 153). Name and detail
    together use `NamedFormat` (line 146), either one alone is returned bare, and with neither it falls
    back to the header-only `Describe` (line 149), which is every browser session.
  - `ParseApp` (line 169) finds the first `(` and the `)` after it (searching only from the `(` on,
    through `AsSpan(commentStart).IndexOf(')')`, lines 182-183), splits the comment on `;`, and returns
    `(null, null)` unless the parts contain `AppUserAgent.Marker` (lines 184-188). The app name is the
    product token before any `/` (lines 190-196); the platform is the first word of the first comment
    part, mapped by `MatchAppPlatform` (lines 198-201).
  - `MatchAppPlatform` (line 208) checks `AppPlatforms` case-insensitively, then falls back to the
    browser `Platforms` table, then to the raw word (lines 210-218).
  - `Match(userAgent, candidates)` (line 221) walks a table in order and returns the first name whose
    token appears case-insensitively, or `null`.
- **Why it's built this way**: ordered tables plus one loop keep the whole implementation small, so
  adding a browser is one line and the ordering rule is visible at the point it matters. It is
  `internal` because nothing outside the package should treat it as a UA parser, and `Describe` lives
  here (rather than in each view) so the views cannot label the same session differently. Reported
  metadata wins over the header because a native app's header names only the app and the platform,
  while the metadata names the device itself.
- **Where it's used**: three call sites of the metadata-aware `Describe`:
  [`Sessions.DescribeDevice`](#sessions)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Sessions.razor.cs:266`), the admin
  [`UserSessionsTable.DescribeDevice`](#usersessionstable)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/UserSessionsTable.razor.cs:69`) and
  [`SignInHistoryTable`](#signinhistorytable)
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/SignInHistoryTable.razor.cs:74`).
  Pinned by `UserAgentSummaryTests`
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Auth/Devices/UserAgentSummaryTests.cs`).
  The devices page is the UI half of
  [ADR-097](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/097-multi-device-refresh-sessions.html).

### ConfigurationOAuthUISettings
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.OAuth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/OAuth/ConfigurationOAuthUISettings.cs:19` · Level 2 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the real [`IOAuthUISettings`](#ioauthuisettings): it computes provider availability
  and the generic OIDC provider list once at construction from the `OAuth` configuration section, and
  covers both a server host and a WASM client with a single class.
- **Depends on**: [`IOAuthUISettings`](#ioauthuisettings) (the contract it implements) and
  [`OidcProviderOption`](#oidcprovideroption) (the list element); externally
  `Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration` (`IConfiguration`, `IConfigurationSection`).
- **Concept introduced, one class over two configuration shapes.** A server host holds the actual
  OAuth client ids, so "is Google available" is answered by whether `OAuth:Google:ClientId` is
  populated. A WASM client must never receive a client id, so it is handed pre-computed
  `OAuth:GoogleEnabled` flags through its runtime configuration endpoint instead
  (`ConfigurationOAuthUISettings.cs:5-18`). The class accepts either signal. Generic OIDC providers
  follow the same two shapes under `OAuth:Oidc:<Name>`: a server lists a section whose `ClientId` is
  set, a WASM client lists a section flagged `Enabled` (class doc, lines 12-17).
  - `[Rubric §26, Front-End Security]` assesses what configuration reaches the browser. The WASM path
    carries availability flags only, never the client id, and the class shape is what makes that
    possible without a second implementation.
  - `[Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality]` assesses duplication. One class, one rule per shape,
    every provider.
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `ReservedOidcNames` (`ConfigurationOAuthUISettings.cs:21-23`) is a case-insensitive set of
    `google`, `github`, `apple`, `complete`, `exchange` and `discover`: the built-in provider names and
    the OAuth route segments, which a configured OIDC section may never shadow.
  - Four get-only auto-properties, `GoogleEnabled`, `GitHubEnabled`, `AppleEnabled` (lines 26, 29, 32)
    and `OidcProviders` (line 35, "in configuration order"), set in the constructor (line 37), which
    null-guards the configuration (line 39), takes the `OAuth` section (line 41), evaluates each
    built-in provider through the shared helper (lines 42-44) and reads the `Oidc` child section
    (line 45).
  - `IsProviderEnabled(oauth, provider)` (line 48) is the built-in rule: parse `{provider}Enabled` as a
    bool (line 50), and return true when that flag is set **or** when `{provider}:ClientId` is
    non-empty (line 51).
  - `ReadOidcProviders(oidc)` (line 54) keeps each child section whose key is not reserved and that is
    enabled (line 56), and projects it to an `OidcProviderOption` with the section key as `Name`, a
    trimmed `DisplayName` falling back to the key (line 59), and `UsesDomains` (lines 54-61).
    `IsOidcProviderEnabled` (line 63) is the same flag-or-client-id disjunction on `Enabled` and
    `ClientId`; `UsesDomains` (line 66) is true for a `UsesDomains` flag or any non-blank `Domains`
    entry.
  - Because the values are read once into properties, a render pass never re-walks configuration.
- **Why it's built this way**: the flag-or-client-id disjunction is what lets the same type serve both
  hosts. The server side of the pairing is documented from the API package, which notes that the same
  `OAuth:{Provider}:ClientId` keys the API reads are what this class reads for its `GoogleEnabled` /
  `GitHubEnabled` answers
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authentication/ExternalAuthExtensions.cs:18`). The
  federated-login design behind the flags is
  [ADR-036](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/036-external-oauth-login.html).
- **Where it's used**: MMCA.ADC registers it with `AddSingleton` (which replaces the framework's
  `TryAddSingleton` default regardless of ordering) on the Blazor Server head
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web/Program.cs:86`), the WASM client
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web.Client/Program.cs:38`) and MAUI
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI/MauiProgram.cs:96`, whose comment at lines 77-79 explains that
  the MAUI registration goes before `AddUIShared` because that call `TryAdd`s the default). The
  server head also projects the resolved flags to the WASM client through its `/client-config`
  endpoint (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI.Web/Program.cs:172-174`); that projection carries the
  three built-in flags only, not an `Oidc` section.

### DefaultOAuthUISettings
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.OAuth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/OAuth/DefaultOAuthUISettings.cs:7` · Level 1 · class (internal, sealed)

- **What it is**: the framework's no-op [`IOAuthUISettings`](#ioauthuisettings), which reports every
  provider as unavailable so an app that has not configured external login shows no social buttons.
- **Depends on**: [`IOAuthUISettings`](#ioauthuisettings) only.
- **Concept reinforced, the Null Object as a registration default** (the same move
  [`NullNotificationScopeProvider`](#nullnotificationscopeprovider) makes for notification scoping).
  `[Rubric §2, Design Patterns]` assesses whether a pattern removes branching: because a default is
  always registered, the login page injects the interface unconditionally and never tests whether one
  exists.
- **Walkthrough**: the entire type is one line,
  `internal sealed class DefaultOAuthUISettings : IOAuthUISettings;`
  (`DefaultOAuthUISettings.cs:7`). It has no members because
  [`IOAuthUISettings`](#ioauthuisettings) gives all three properties `false`-returning default
  implementations; the class doc records the contract, that downstream apps override this registration
  to enable specific providers (lines 3-6).
- **Why it's built this way**: `internal` because nothing outside the package should name it, and a
  semicolon body because the default interface members already say everything. It is registered with
  `TryAddSingleton` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:245`), so
  a host that registers first keeps its own, and a host that registers afterwards with `AddSingleton`
  wins the resolution.
- **Where it's used**: resolved as [`IOAuthUISettings`](#ioauthuisettings) in every host that has not
  registered its own, which today is all of MMCA.Store's UI heads and MMCA.Helpdesk.

### OidcDiscoveryUIService
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Auth.OAuth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/OAuth/OidcDiscoveryUIService.cs:11` · Level 2 · class (internal, sealed)

- **What it is**: the framework's [`IOidcDiscoveryUIService`](#ioidcdiscoveryuiservice) over the API's
  anonymous `GET auth/oauth/discover` endpoint, through the named `"APIClient"` HttpClient
  (`OidcDiscoveryUIService.cs:6-10`).
- **Depends on**: [`IOidcDiscoveryUIService`](#ioidcdiscoveryuiservice),
  [`OidcDiscoveryResponse`](group-08-auth.md#oidcdiscoveryresponse); externals `IHttpClientFactory`
  and `System.Net.Http.Json`.
- **Concept reinforced, a status code that is an answer versus one that is a failure.** A 404 here
  means "no provider claims this domain", a normal outcome the page turns into a message, while a
  throttle or an outage must not be mistaken for that answer.
  `[Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]` assesses whether a client maps the server's contract faithfully:
  this one maps exactly one status to `null` and lets every other failure throw (the
  `HttpRequestException` is documented at `OidcDiscoveryUIService.cs:16`).
