### IUserPreferenceReader

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Preferences` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Preferences/IUserPreferenceReader.cs:9` · Level 1 · interface

- **What it is**: the read half of cross-device preferences. It fetches the signed-in user's stored
  culture and theme, used at login to reapply a returning user's choices on a new device.
- **Depends on**: [UserPreferences](#userpreferences) (its return type); implemented by
  [ApiUserPreferenceReader](#apiuserpreferencereader). The write half is
  [IUserPreferenceWriter](#iuserpreferencewriter).
- **Concept introduced**: nothing new; it mirrors the best-effort contract the writer introduced. The
  doc comment (`IUserPreferenceReader.cs:3-8`) pins the failure mode: implementations return an empty
  `UserPreferences` (both fields null) for anonymous users or on any error, so a failed read never
  blocks login. `[Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow]` applies, since this is the moment the
  roaming copy is reconciled against the local one.
- **Walkthrough**
  - `GetAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)` returning `Task<UserPreferences>`
    (`IUserPreferenceReader.cs:13`). There is no failure channel in the signature at all, which is the
    contract making itself unmistakable.
- **Why it's built this way**:
  [ADR-027](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/027-multi-locale-i18n.html) and
  [ADR-028](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/028-dark-theme-mode.html). A `Result<T>` here would
  invite a caller to surface an error the user cannot act on during a login they just completed
  successfully.
- **Where it's used**: injected by the login page (`Login.razor:14`) and read once in
  `ApplyStoredPreferencesAndNavigateAsync` (`Login.razor:228-230`), which applies the theme through
  [ThemeService](#themeservice) (`Login.razor:232-235`) and the culture through
  [ICultureApplier](#icultureapplier) (`Login.razor:243`), skipping the culture round-trip when the
  stored value already matches the current one (`Login.razor:237-238`).

### PendingWrite

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Offline` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/PendingWrite.cs:12` · Level 1 · record (sealed)

- **What it is**: one entry of the offline write queue, exactly as it is persisted to the device's local
  store: what to replay, with which payload, for which user, and how often it has failed.
- **Depends on**: [ConcurrencyETag](group-08-auth.md#concurrencyetag) (formats `IfMatch`, line 47);
  `System.Text.Json` (`JsonSerializerOptions.Web`, `[JsonIgnore]`).
- **Concept introduced**: nothing new beyond the queue taught under
  [OfflineWriteQueue](#offlinewritequeue). `[Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow]` applies: the
  record is the durable state, so everything a later replay needs (including the user it belongs to)
  travels inside it rather than in memory.
- **Walkthrough**
  - Identity and routing: `Id` (`PendingWrite.cs:15`) and `Kind` (line 18), the handler key, for example
    `Engagement.Bookmark.Create.v1`.
  - Replay safety: `IdempotencyKey` (line 21) so a write the server already ran is not run twice, and
    `BasedOnRowVersion` (line 25), a `byte[]?` with a `CA1819` suppression justified by the record being
    persisted locally, not a domain type (line 24).
  - Payload: `PayloadJson` (line 28), serialized with `JsonSerializerOptions.Web`, and the generic
    `ReadPayload<TPayload>()` (line 52) that deserializes it with the same options.
  - Scoping and bookkeeping: `CoalesceKey` (line 31), `UserScope` (line 34, the signed-in user's id or
    `null` for an anonymous user), `EnqueuedOn` (line 37) and `Attempts` (line 40), the count of transient
    replay failures so far.
  - `IfMatch` (line 47) is computed, not stored (`[JsonIgnore]`, line 46): the weak ETag of
    `BasedOnRowVersion` via `ConcurrencyETag.Format`, or `null` when no row version was given.
- **Why it's built this way**: `required` + `init` members keep an entry immutable; the queue changes
  `Attempts` with a `with` expression
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/OfflineWriteQueue.cs:430-442`).
  Storing the payload as JSON text keeps the list one homogeneous type in the local store whatever the
  payload type. See ADR-144.
- **Where it's used**: built by `OfflineWriteQueue.EnqueueAsync` (`OfflineWriteQueue.cs:136`), handed to
  every [IOfflineWriteHandler](#iofflinewritehandler), and carried by
  [OfflineWriteSettledEventArgs](#offlinewritesettledeventargs). ADC's
  [BookmarkCreateReplayHandler](group-22-engagement-module.md#bookmarkcreatereplayhandler) and
  [BookmarkDeleteReplayHandler](group-22-engagement-module.md#bookmarkdeletereplayhandler) read it.

### IOfflineWriteHandler

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Offline` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/IOfflineWriteHandler.cs:9` · Level 3 · interface

- **What it is**: the per-kind replay strategy. A module registers one handler per write kind; the queue
  hands it a [PendingWrite](#pendingwrite) and gets back the server's answer.
- **Depends on**: [PendingWrite](#pendingwrite), [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result).
- **Concept introduced**: nothing new; the queue that drives it is taught under
  [OfflineWriteQueue](#offlinewritequeue). `[Rubric §1, SOLID]` applies: the framework queue knows no
  endpoint, and each module adds a write kind by adding a handler, not by editing the queue.
- **Walkthrough**
  - `Kind` (`IOfflineWriteHandler.cs:12`): the key the handler answers to, for example
    `Engagement.Bookmark.Create.v1`.
  - `ReplayAsync(PendingWrite, CancellationToken)` returning `Task<Result>` (line 23). The doc comment
    (lines 14-19) fixes the contract: send the write with its `IdempotencyKey` (and `IfMatch` when set),
    and report the answer as a `Result`. A transport failure, a timeout, or an unexpected,
    too-many-requests or unauthorized error keeps the write for a later replay; a conflict or any other
    failure discards it.
- **Why it's built this way**: returning a `Result` rather than an outcome lets a handler reuse the
  normal HTTP-to-`Result` path, and the queue alone decides what counts as transient
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/OfflineWriteQueue.cs:263-283`).
- **Where it's used**: registered with `AddOfflineWriteHandler<THandler>()` as a scoped
  `TryAddEnumerable` entry
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:437-440`); implemented in ADC by
  [BookmarkCreateReplayHandler](group-22-engagement-module.md#bookmarkcreatereplayhandler)
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Bookmarks/BookmarkCreateReplayHandler.cs:24`)
  and [BookmarkDeleteReplayHandler](group-22-engagement-module.md#bookmarkdeletereplayhandler)
  (`BookmarkDeleteReplayHandler.cs:19`).
- **Caveats**: when two handlers share a `Kind`, the first one registered wins (`OfflineWriteQueue.cs:100`
  uses `TryAdd`).

### OfflineWriteSettledEventArgs

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Offline` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/OfflineWriteSettledEventArgs.cs:9` · Level 3 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the payload of `IOfflineWriteQueue.WriteSettled`: which write left the queue, how, and
  with what handler result.
- **Depends on**: [PendingWrite](#pendingwrite), [OfflineWriteOutcome](#offlinewriteoutcome),
  [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result); derives from `EventArgs`.
- **Concept introduced**: nothing new.
- **Walkthrough**: a primary-constructor class (`OfflineWriteSettledEventArgs.cs:9`) exposing `Write`
  (line 12), `Outcome` (line 15) and `Result` (line 18), which is `null` for
  [OfflineWriteOutcome](#offlinewriteoutcome)`.Expired` because an expired write is never sent.
- **Why it's built this way**: the standard `EventHandler<TEventArgs>` shape, raised by
  `OfflineWriteQueue.SettleAsync` only after the store no longer holds the write
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/OfflineWriteQueue.cs:424-428`).
- **Where it's used**: Common's `OfflineWriteNotifier`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Capabilities/OfflineWriteNotifier.razor:46`)
  and ADC's `SessionBookmarkReplayTests`.

### ApiUserPreferenceWriter

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Preferences` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Preferences/ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:30` · Level 4 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the default [IUserPreferenceWriter](#iuserpreferencewriter). It PUTs the
  culture/theme choice to `auth/preferences` through the shared `"APIClient"`, and it declines to make
  the call at all when the request is already known to be doomed.
- **Depends on**: [IUserPreferenceWriter](#iuserpreferencewriter) (implemented),
  [ITokenStorageService](#itokenstorageservice), [JwtTokenInfo](#jwttokeninfo) and the nested
  [UserPreferencesRequest](#userpreferencesrequest). Externals: `IHttpClientFactory` and
  `System.Net.Http.Json`.
- **Concept introduced, best-effort writes still have a cost.**
  `[Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]` assesses whether the system's own traffic keeps its
  signals meaningful; the class comment (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:21-26`) makes the argument
  explicitly. Because the caller never learns the write failed, a doomed request cannot help the user
  and still lands in failed-request telemetry, and at low traffic one 401 per theme or culture toggle
  is enough on its own to trip a failed-request alert rule. Both guards below therefore exist for the
  alerting story, not the user's story. `[Rubric §11, Security]` also touches this: the writer never
  inspects the token's claims itself: it asks `JwtTokenInfo` whether one is usable, then attaches it as the `Authorization: Bearer` header of the request message (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:113`), the same explicit per-request bearer the reader attaches.
- **Walkthrough**
  - The primary constructor takes `IHttpClientFactory` and `ITokenStorageService`
    (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:30-32`). `ExpirySkew` is 30 seconds and is documented as matching the
    token-storage skew so this class agrees with the layer that does the refreshing
    (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:34-35`). `_rejectedToken` (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:47`) holds the
    token the API last refused, for the lifetime of this scoped writer.
  - Saves are serialized in call order. `SaveAsync` (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:66`) is not `async`:
    under a `System.Threading.Lock` gate (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:37,68`) it chains the new save
    onto `_lastSave` (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:50`), stores the new task as the latest, and returns it
    (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:70-72`). The remarks (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:59-65`) give the
    reason: a theme toggle followed quickly by a language switch used to send two concurrent PUTs, and the
    switcher force-reloads as soon as its own save returns, so the reload either cut off the theme PUT
    (WASM) or the two raced on the user row's concurrency token and the server kept the old theme.
    Serializing means the switcher's existing await also drains the earlier save.
  - `SaveAfterAsync` (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:76`) waits for the previous save with
    `WaitAsync(PreviousSaveWait, cancellationToken)` under
    `ConfigureAwaitOptions.SuppressThrowing` (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:80-81`), so a fault, timeout or
    cancellation of the earlier save only ends the wait (comment, `ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:78-79`).
    `PreviousSaveWait` is an `internal` init property defaulting to 5 seconds
    (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:56`), bounded so a hung earlier request delays the next save, and the
    culture reload behind it, by a few seconds at most (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:52-55`). It then
    calls `PutAsync` (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:83`).
  - `PutAsync` (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:86`) reads the access token
    (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:88`), then applies guard one:
    `JwtTokenInfo.IsFresh(token, ExpirySkew)` (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:93`, the helper at
    `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/JwtTokenInfo.cs:16`). The comment
    (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:90-92`) notes that `IsFresh` also covers null and unreadable tokens,
    which makes this the anonymous-user guard as well.
  - Guard two compares the current token against `_rejectedToken` with `StringComparison.Ordinal`
    (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:101`); the comment (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:98-100`) explains why
    expiry alone is not enough, since a token can be unexpired and still rejected (revoked session,
    rotated signing key, a user the API now treats as gone).
  - The call itself is a hand-built PUT `HttpRequestMessage` with a JSON body, sent through `SendAsync`, to the relative `auth/preferences`
    (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:108-118`), and a `401 Unauthorized` latches `_rejectedToken`
    (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:120-123`). Just before `SendAsync` it calls
    `AuthDelegatingHandler.TrackTokenOwner(token!, tokenStorageService)` (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:117`,
    the helper at `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:68`).
    The comment (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:115-116`) gives the reason: the handler's own token storage is
    a different instance, so it is told which storage this bearer came from, and a 401 then renews (or ends)
    this session rather than the handler's. The helper records the owner weakly and only when it is an
    [ISessionAwareTokenStorage](#isessionawaretokenstorage) (`AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:70`), so
    [AuthDelegatingHandler](#authdelegatinghandler) can route the 401; the comment names
    `CreateAuthenticatedClientAsync` as the path that already does the same.
  - Both `HttpRequestException` (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:125`) and `TaskCanceledException`
    (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:129`) are swallowed, each with a comment noting that the cookie already
    holds the choice for this device.
- **Why it's built this way**:
  [ADR-027](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/027-multi-locale-i18n.html) and
  [ADR-028](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/028-dark-theme-mode.html) make the local cookie the
  runtime channel and this write a roaming extra. Storing the rejected token rather than setting a
  boolean latch is the deliberate detail (`ApiUserPreferenceWriter.cs:41-46`): a fresh sign-in produces
  a different token, so writing resumes with no reset step and no staleness of its own.
- **Where it's used**: registered with `TryAddScoped` in [DependencyInjection](#dependencyinjection-2)
  (`MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:240`); resolved optionally by the theme toggle
  (`ThemeToggle.razor:23-27`) and the culture switcher (`CultureSwitcher.razor:38-42`). Pinned by
  `ApiUserPreferenceWriterTests`, including the ordering and the bounded wait
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Preferences/ApiUserPreferenceWriterTests.cs:146,173`).

### ApiUserPreferenceReader
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Preferences` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Preferences/ApiUserPreferenceReader.cs:22` · Level 4 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the default [IUserPreferenceReader](#iuserpreferencereader). It GETs
  `auth/preferences` with the signed-in user's bearer token and hands back the culture and theme the
  user chose on some other device, or empty preferences when there is nothing to read.
- **Depends on**: [IUserPreferenceReader](#iuserpreferencereader) (the contract,
  `ApiUserPreferenceReader.cs:24`), [UserPreferences](#userpreferences) (the two-nullable-field record
  it returns, constructed at line 26), [ITokenStorageService](#itokenstorageservice) (primary-constructor parameter,
  line 24), [JwtTokenInfo](#jwttokeninfo) (the freshness check, line 39); `IHttpClientFactory` and
  `System.Net.Http.Json` (BCL) for the named `"APIClient"`.
- **Concept introduced, a best-effort read that cannot fail its caller.**
  `[Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven Design]` assesses whether a secondary concern is prevented from
  changing the outcome of the primary operation. Applying a stored preference is a nicety attached to
  login; a network hiccup while reading it must not turn a successful sign-in into an error page. This
  class encodes that as a type-level promise: `GetAsync` returns `UserPreferences` rather than a
  [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result), and there is no path out of it that reports a
  failure. That is the posture ADR-096 records for side effects generally
  (`Website/docs-src/adr/096-best-effort-side-effects.md`), applied on the read side.
  `[Rubric §26, Front-End Security]` also applies, in a small but real way: the class refuses to spend
  a round trip on a token it can already see is stale.
- **Walkthrough**
  - Two statics carry the whole configuration. `Empty` is a single shared
    `new UserPreferences(null, null)` (line 26), so the failure paths allocate nothing, and
    `ExpirySkew` is `TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30)` (line 29) with a comment stating why the value is
    duplicated here: it must agree with the token-storage layer that does the refreshing, or the two
    would disagree about when a token is still usable.
  - `GetAsync(CancellationToken)` (line 32) reads the access token (line 34) and gates on
    `JwtTokenInfo.IsFresh(token, ExpirySkew)` (line 39). The comment (lines 36-38) spells out the two
    cases this covers: an expired or unreadable token buys a guaranteed 401, and `IsFresh` also covers
    the anonymous (null) case. Both return `Empty` (line 41).
  - The request is built by hand: resolve the named `"APIClient"` (line 46), which already carries
    the culture and auth handlers
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:174-175`), then
    an `HttpRequestMessage` GET to the relative URI `auth/preferences` with the token it already read set as the `Authorization: Bearer` header on that request (lines 47-48). The reader sets it itself because in Blazor Server `AuthDelegatingHandler` resolves in a separate DI scope whose token store is empty, which would send the read anonymous; the handler leaves an existing header alone, so WASM and MAUI see no change (class doc comment). Before sending it calls `AuthDelegatingHandler.TrackTokenOwner(token!, tokenStorageService)` (line 52, the helper at `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:68`); the comment (lines 50-51) explains that the handler's own storage is another instance, so it is told which storage this bearer came from and a 401 renews (or ends) this session. `SendAsync` (line 53) is followed by a non-success short-circuit to `Empty` (lines 54-57), and only then `ReadFromJsonAsync<UserPreferences>` (line 59).
  - Null-coalescing on the deserialized value (line 60) means a body of literal `null` is the same as
    no preference.
  - Two catch blocks, `HttpRequestException` (line 62) and `TaskCanceledException` (line 66), both
    return `Empty`. Note what is not caught: anything else, including a `JsonException` from a
    malformed body, still escapes, so a contract break is loud while a transport failure is quiet.
- **Why it's built this way**: ADR-027 (`Website/docs-src/adr/027-multi-locale-i18n.md`) and ADR-028
  make the stored culture and theme a per-user server-side value so the choice follows a user between
  devices, and login is the one moment where reading it is worth a round trip. Catching narrowly and
  returning a shared empty record is what makes the reconciliation safe to await unconditionally in the
  login flow. It is the read half of a pair: [ApiUserPreferenceWriter](#apiuserpreferencewriter) is the
  write half, and the two are registered together
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:240-241`).
- **Where it's used**: registered by `AddUIShared` with `TryAddScoped`
  (`DependencyInjection.cs:241`) and injected by exactly one page, the framework's login page
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor:14`). Its
  `ApplyStoredPreferencesAndNavigateAsync` calls `GetAsync`, applies a stored theme through
  [ThemeService](#themeservice), and, when the stored culture differs from the current one, hands the
  rest of the navigation to [ICultureApplier](#icultureapplier), which owns the head-specific switch
  (`Login.razor:228-248`).
- **Caveats**: the reader is pinned by `ApiUserPreferenceReaderTests` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Preferences/ApiUserPreferenceReaderTests.cs`) and `ServerSignInPreferenceReadTests` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web.Tests/Services/ServerSignInPreferenceReadTests.cs`), alongside its sibling writer's
  [ApiUserPreferenceWriterTests](group-29-testing-infrastructure.md#per-project-test-rollup).
  Because `TaskCanceledException` is caught
  unconditionally, a caller that cancels its own token receives `Empty` rather than an
  `OperationCanceledException`, which is the opposite of the convention
  [HttpResultExecutor](#httpresultexecutor) enforces elsewhere in this package; the single caller
  passes no token (`Login.razor:230`), so the difference is invisible in current use.

### IOfflineWriteQueue

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Offline` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/IOfflineWriteQueue.cs:11` · Level 4 · interface

- **What it is**: the contract of the opt-in durable offline write queue: queue a write now, replay it
  when the device is back online, and tell subscribers how each write settled.
- **Depends on**: [PendingWrite](#pendingwrite), [OfflineWriteOptions](#offlinewriteoptions),
  [OfflineWriteSettledEventArgs](#offlinewritesettledeventargs),
  [Result](group-01-result-error-handling.md#result).
- **Concept introduced**: the queue itself is taught under [OfflineWriteQueue](#offlinewritequeue); this
  is its surface. `[Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity]` applies: the interface lets a UI
  service accept a write while offline instead of failing it.
- **Walkthrough**
  - `IsAvailable` (`IOfflineWriteQueue.cs:18`): false only with the default `NullLocalCacheStore`; a host
    that calls `AddBrowserDeviceCapabilities` (Blazor Server and WebAssembly) or the MAUI capabilities
    has a store (doc comment, lines 13-17). See
    [NullLocalCacheStore](group-26-device-capability-layer.md#nulllocalcachestore).
  - Two events: `WriteSettled` (line 21), raised once per write that left by a replay after the store no
    longer holds it, and `PendingChanged` (line 24), raised after every persisted change.
  - `EnqueueAsync<TPayload>(kind, payload, options, cancellationToken)` (line 33) returns
    `Result<PendingWrite>`: the queued write, or the `OfflineWrites.Unavailable` / `OfflineWrites.QueueFull`
    failure (doc, line 32).
  - `GetPendingAsync` (line 38) lists the current user's writes oldest first; `CancelPendingAsync(coalesceKey)`
    (line 44) removes every write of the current user with that key (ordinal) without raising
    `WriteSettled`.
  - `ReplayAsync` (line 52) returns the number of writes that settled, and does nothing (returns 0) when
    the store is unavailable, the device is offline, or another replay is running (lines 46-49).
- **Why it's built this way**: ADR-144 (`Website/docs-src/adr/144-offline-writes-and-delta-reads.md`).
  Failures a caller can act on (no store, queue full) come back as a `Result`; replay outcomes, which
  arrive later, come back as events.
- **Where it's used**: registered scoped by `AddOfflineWriteQueue`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:419`), which no framework code
  calls (doc comment, line 413); injected into ADC's
  [SessionBookmarkUIService](group-22-engagement-module.md#sessionbookmarkuiservice)
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Engagement/MMCA.ADC.Engagement.UI/Services/Bookmarks/SessionBookmarkUIService.cs:40`)
  and drained by Common's `OfflineWriteNotifier`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Capabilities/OfflineWriteNotifier.razor:54`).

### OfflineWriteQueue

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Services.Offline` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Offline/OfflineWriteQueue.cs:47` · Level 5 · class (sealed, partial)

- **What it is**: the default [IOfflineWriteQueue](#iofflinewritequeue). It keeps the whole queue as one
  `List<PendingWrite>` under one key of the device's
  [ILocalCacheStore](group-26-device-capability-layer.md#ilocalcachestore), scoped per signed-in user,
  and replays it through per-kind [IOfflineWriteHandler](#iofflinewritehandler)s on reconnect, on
  demand, and on its own backoff timer.
- **Depends on**: [ILocalCacheStore](group-26-device-capability-layer.md#ilocalcachestore),
  [IConnectivityStatusService](group-26-device-capability-layer.md#iconnectivitystatusservice),
  [IOfflineWriteHandler](#iofflinewritehandler), [OfflineWriteQueueOptions](#offlinewritequeueoptions),
  [PendingWrite](#pendingwrite), [OfflineWriteOutcome](#offlinewriteoutcome),
  [HttpResultExecutor](#httpresultexecutor) (its transport and timeout error codes),
  [Error](group-01-result-error-handling.md#error) and [ErrorType](group-01-result-error-handling.md#errortype).
  Externals: `AuthenticationStateProvider`, `TimeProvider`, `IOptions<T>`, `ILogger<T>`, `System.Text.Json`.
- **Concept introduced, a durable client-side outbox for writes.** A write the user makes while offline
  is persisted on the device with an idempotency key, then replayed in order once the device is online.
  It is the client-side counterpart of the server outbox idea (ADR-003): durability first, delivery later,
  and idempotency so a delivery that happens twice is harmless. `[Rubric §29, Resilience & Business
  Continuity]` assesses whether the system degrades gracefully when a dependency is down; here a lost
  network becomes a delayed write rather than a failed one. `[Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow]`
  applies because the queue's state is the device store, re-read on every change rather than cached.
  `[Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]` applies through the three `[LoggerMessage]` warnings
  (`OfflineWriteQueue.cs:549-556`).
- **Walkthrough**
  - Retry timing constants: `InitialRetryDelay` 5 seconds (`OfflineWriteQueue.cs:50`) and `MaxRetryDelay`
    5 minutes (line 53). Fields include an ordinal handler dictionary (line 57), a `SemaphoreSlim(1, 1)`
    `_gate` (line 62) for store edits, and a `Lock` `_scheduleSync` for the timer.
  - The constructor (line 79) indexes handlers by `Kind` with `TryAdd`, so the first registered wins
    (line 100), and subscribes to `ConnectivityChanged` (line 103). `IsAvailable` is the store's own
    flag (line 113).
  - `EnqueueAsync` (line 122) fails with `OfflineWrites.Unavailable` when there is no store (line 133),
    builds the [PendingWrite](#pendingwrite) (line 136, a new `"N"` GUID when no idempotency key was
    given, line 140, and the current user as `UserScope`), and adds it through `MutateAsync` unless
    `MaxPendingWrites` is reached (line 152), else `OfflineWrites.QueueFull` (line 176). When the kind has
    a handler it bumps `_replayableEnqueues` and schedules a retry (lines 162-171).
  - `GetPendingAsync` (line 180) and `CancelPendingAsync` (line 193) filter by the current user's scope;
    `InScope` (line 254) orders oldest first.
  - `ReplayAsync` (line 211) returns 0 unless the store is available, the device is online and no other
    replay holds the `Interlocked.CompareExchange` flag (line 213). Its `finally` always calls
    `CompletePass` (line 231), so a pass that threw still schedules the next attempt.
  - `ReplayPassAsync` (line 293) walks a snapshot: it skips an entry that left the store since the
    snapshot (line 307, so a write cancelled meanwhile is not sent), expires one older than `MaxAge`
    unsent (line 312), keeps an entry whose kind has no handler in this app (line 319), and otherwise
    calls the handler. A thrown handler exception is logged, counts an attempt and stops the pass
    (lines 335-341); a `Result` goes through `Classify` (line 343).
  - `Classify` (line 263) maps success to `Completed`, any transient error to `null` (keep and stop),
    any `ErrorType.Conflict` to `Conflict`, and everything else to `Rejected`. `IsTransient` (line 280)
    is the transport or timeout code of `HttpResultExecutor`, or `ErrorType.Unexpected`,
    `TooManyRequests` or `Unauthorized`; the transient check runs first.
  - Backoff: `CompletePass` (line 361) resets the delay to the initial value after a pass that settled
    something and otherwise doubles it via `NextDelay` (line 285) up to the 5-minute cap, reschedules when
    a replayable write was queued during the pass, and cancels the timer otherwise. `ScheduleRetryLocked`
    (line 383) keeps at most one one-shot timer on the injected `TimeProvider`, and never while offline
    or disposed; a per-schedule token object lets `OnRetryTimer` (line 405) ignore a stale callback.
  - Persistence: `MutateAsync` (line 449) re-reads the list, applies the edit and writes it back under the
    semaphore, then raises `PendingChanged`; `SettleAsync` (line 424) removes the entry and then raises
    `WriteSettled`; `CountAttemptAsync` (line 430) bumps `Attempts`.
  - `OnConnectivityChanged` (line 501) cancels the timer when the device goes offline and starts a
    background replay, not awaited, when it comes back; `ReplayInBackgroundAsync` (line 522) catches and
    logs every fault so no unobserved task escapes. `Dispose` (line 237) removes the timer and unsubscribes.
- **Why it's built this way**: ADR-144 (`Website/docs-src/adr/144-offline-writes-and-delta-reads.md`).
  One list under one key with a read-edit-write under one semaphore means concurrent callers of the same
  instance never lose a write; the class remarks say plainly that two instances over one store (two tabs,
  two circuits) are not coordinated (`OfflineWriteQueue.cs:14-20`). User scoping means one device can
  hold writes for several accounts, and signing out clears the local store and the queue with it
  (remarks, line 44).
- **Where it's used**: registered scoped, together with `TimeProvider.System` and the options, by
  `AddOfflineWriteQueue`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:417-429`); exercised by
  `OfflineWriteQueueTests` and `OfflineWriteQueueRetryTests`
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services/Offline/`) and by ADC's bookmark tests.
  ADC's [SessionBookmarkUIService](group-22-engagement-module.md#sessionbookmarkuiservice) is the one
  consumer.
- **Caveats**: the scope is "scoped" because the browser connectivity service and store it reads are
  scoped (`DependencyInjection.cs:407-408`), so each Blazor Server circuit has its own queue instance over
  the same browser store, which is exactly the uncoordinated two-instances case the remarks name.

### BrandColors

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Theme` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/BrandColors.cs:10` · Level 0 · class (static)

- **What it is**: the single C# source of truth for every hex value in the theme. It holds the two brand triads (primary and secondary), the app-chrome colors shared by both modes, and the full light and dark palettes, so every hex value [MMCATheme](#mmcatheme) assigns in either MudBlazor variant is one of these constants (doc comment, `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/BrandColors.cs:4-5`).
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party. Part of it is mirrored by CSS custom properties in `wwwroot/app.css`; the doc comments name `--mmca-primary`, `--mmca-primary-dark`, `--mmca-primary-light`, `--mmca-secondary`, `--mmca-secondary-dark` (`BrandColors.cs:12,15,18,22,28`), plus `--mmca-sidebar-bg` on `ChromeBackground` (line 36) and `--mmca-divider` on `LightDivider` (line 80).
- **Concept introduced, a fitness-tested duplication.** `[Rubric §20, Design System & Theming]` assesses whether visual tokens are centralized rather than scattered as literals; here the whole palette lives in exactly one C# class, and the theme carries no hex literal of its own. `[Rubric §34, Architecture Governance & Documentation]` assesses whether *necessary* duplication is monitored: C# cannot read CSS at build time, so the brand colors must exist in both `BrandColors` and `app.css`, and `BrandColorTokenTests` in MMCA.Common.UI.Tests asserts the two stay in sync so the copy cannot silently drift (`BrandColors.cs:6-8`). The test pins the five brand tokens, one `InlineData` row each (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Theme/BrandColorTokenTests.cs:35-39`); the `--mmca-sidebar-bg` and `--mmca-divider` mirrors are named in the doc comments but have no row there.
  - `[Rubric §21, Accessibility]` lands here rather than only in the theme: the `Secondary` constant carries its own contrast math in source, Teal 700 `#00796B` holding about 5.3:1 on light surfaces, replacing the Teal 600 `#00897B` that measured about 4.0:1 and sat under the WCAG 2.1 AA 4.5:1 floor for normal text (`BrandColors.cs:21-26`). The contrast reasoning for `LightWarning` and `DarkError` is deliberately not here: their summaries point at [MMCATheme](#mmcatheme), where the math sits beside the assignment (lines 56, 116, 122).
- **Walkthrough**: `public const string` fields in four commented groups.
  - The primary triad: `Primary = "#1565C0"` (line 13), `PrimaryDark = "#0D47A1"` (line 16), `PrimaryLight = "#42A5F5"` used for accents and dark-mode contrast (line 19). The secondary triad: `Secondary = "#00796B"` (line 26, with the contrast rationale immediately above it at lines 21-25), `SecondaryDark = "#00695C"` (line 29), and `SecondaryLight = "#4DB6AC"` (line 32).
  - Shared chrome, identical in both palettes (line 34): `ChromeBackground = "#1A2035"` for the app bar and sidebar (line 37), `ChromeText = "#FFFFFF"` (line 40), and `ChromeTextMuted = "#FFFFFFB3"`, white at 70% alpha for sidebar text and icons (line 43).
  - The light palette (lines 45-84): `LightTertiary` Purple 700, `LightInfo` Blue 700, `LightSuccess` Green 800, `LightWarning = "#A85D00"` with `LightWarningContrastText = "#FFFFFF"`, `LightError` Red 800, then `LightBackground = "#FAFBFC"`, `LightSurface`, the two text tones, `LightActionDefault`, and the two dividers.
  - The dark palette (lines 86-154): `DarkPrimaryLighten` Blue 200, `DarkPrimaryDarken = "#1E88E5"` (Blue 600, the hover, focus and active fill of a filled primary control, whose dark label still reaches 5.14:1 on it, line 96), `DarkSecondaryDarken = "#00897B"` (Teal 600, the same value the light `Secondary` was moved off for contrast, line 99), `DarkSecondaryLighten`, `DarkTertiary`, `DarkInfo`, `DarkSuccess`, `DarkWarning` Orange 400, `DarkError = "#FF8A80"` (line 117), then the four state fills `DarkInfoDarken = "#64B5F6"` (Blue 300, line 124), `DarkSuccessDarken = "#81C784"` (line 127), `DarkWarningDarken = "#FFB74D"` (line 130) and `DarkErrorDarken = "#EF9A9A"` (line 133), each the text colour of a text or outlined alert and the hover, focus and active fill of the matching filled control, then `DarkBackground = "#1A2027"`, `DarkSurface = "#27303A"`, text, action and divider tones. Note `DarkInfo` and `PrimaryLight` share `#42A5F5`, and `DarkTextSecondary` and `DarkActionDefault` share `#B0BEC5`: each keeps its own name so a role can change without dragging the other.
- **Why it's built this way**: `const` rather than `static readonly` means the values can appear in contexts that require compile-time constants; the governance is the fitness test, not the language keyword. Keeping every palette value in one class means a rebrand or a contrast fix touches one file plus the mirrored CSS, and the theme reads as a mapping of roles to names rather than a wall of hex.
- **Where it's used**: every palette entry of [MMCATheme](#mmcatheme) that is not an `rgba(...)` literal (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/MMCATheme.cs:18-54,60-139`); `BrandColorTokenTests`; the doc comment of `BrandColorTokenTestsBase`, the per-host stylesheet check that consumer repos subclass (`MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Bases/Ui/BrandColorTokenTestsBase.cs:6-13`); any component that references a brand color programmatically.

### IInitialThemeModeSource
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Theme` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/IInitialThemeModeSource.cs:16` · Level 0 · interface

- **What it is**: an optional hook that lets a head tell the theme providers the stored Day/Dark mode without JavaScript, so the first render already has the right palette instead of light-then-dark (ADR-028). Its one member, `bool? IsDarkMode` (line 21), is `true` for dark, `false` for light, and `null` when nothing is stored yet, which leaves the first render unchanged.
- **Depends on**: nothing.
- **Concept introduced, an optional capability probed with `GetService`.** `[Rubric §20, Design System, Theming & UI Consistency]` covers theming that works from the first paint. The provider asks the container for the interface and treats absence and `null` identically (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/MmcaThemeProviders.razor:43-50`), so web heads register nothing and still behave as before, while the JS path in `OnAfterRenderAsync` stays the source of truth for them.
- **Why it's built this way**: the MAUI head can read its stored mode synchronously from device preferences, which a Blazor circuit cannot do with a cookie before the first render. A nullable bool keeps "unknown" distinct from "light".
- **Where it's used**: implemented by `MauiInitialThemeModeSource` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Maui/Theme/MauiInitialThemeModeSource.cs:12`) and registered as a singleton (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Maui/DependencyInjection.cs:69`); consumed by `MmcaThemeProviders.razor:47`; pinned by `MmcaThemeProvidersInitialModeTests`.

### ThemeInterop
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Theme` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/ThemeInterop.cs:9` · Level 0 · class (internal static)

- **What it is**: a one-method guard, `TryAsync(Func<Task>)` (`ThemeInterop.cs:18`), that runs a best-effort JS interop call and returns `false` instead of throwing when it fails.
- **Depends on**: `Microsoft.JSInterop` exception types (`JSException`, `JSDisconnectedException`) and `InvalidOperationException` (BCL).
- **Concept introduced, theme interop failure must not escape the component lifecycle.** `[Rubric §18, UI Architecture & Component Design]` covers resilient component lifecycles. The filter catches exactly three cases: the asset is missing or the browser call failed (`JSException`), the circuit was torn down mid-call (`JSDisconnectedException`), and interop is unavailable on this renderer (`InvalidOperationException`, a prerender race or disposed dispatcher). Any other exception still propagates.
- **Why it's built this way**: theming is cosmetic, so a failed cookie read or write degrades to "the page keeps its current mode" rather than killing the circuit from the root layout.
- **Where it's used**: `MmcaThemeProviders.razor:62,90` and `ThemeToggle.razor:22` (all under `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/`). No dedicated test file; it is exercised through the provider and toggle component tests.

### TwoFactorPageRequirement
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.TwoFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/TwoFactor/TwoFactorPageRequirement.cs:14` · Level 0 · class (internal sealed)

- **What it is**: the authorization requirement behind the policy the two-factor account page declares
  instead of a bare `[Authorize]`. Its one member is the policy name,
  `PolicyName = "mmca:two-factor-pages"` (`TwoFactorPageRequirement.cs:17`).
- **Depends on**: `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization.IAuthorizationRequirement` (ASP.NET Core). The
  doc comment names [TwoFactorPageGate](#twofactorpagegate) and
  [TwoFactorPageAuthorizationHandler](#twofactorpageauthorizationhandler) (`TwoFactorPageRequirement.cs:5-13`).
- **Concept introduced**: none new. This is the two-factor copy of the "signed in, unless the page is
  hidden for this host" policy first taught at [NotificationPageRequirement](#notificationpagerequirement);
  the doc comment says the notification pages' policy follows the same rule (`TwoFactorPageRequirement.cs:10-11`).
  `[Rubric §25, Navigation & IA]` assesses whether a route answers consistently with what the host
  actually offers: a host that never registered the two-factor UI answers the page with a 404 rather
  than a sign-in challenge for a page that does not exist for it (`TwoFactorPageRequirement.cs:6-10`).
- **Walkthrough**: a marker class with no state; the requirement means "an authenticated caller, exactly
  as `[Authorize]` asks, except when the host never called `AddTwoFactorUI()`, in which case every
  caller passes" (`TwoFactorPageRequirement.cs:6-9`). The decision itself lives in
  [TwoFactorPageAuthorizationHandler](#twofactorpageauthorizationhandler).
- **Why it's built this way**: authorization runs before the router, so a plain `[Authorize]` would send
  an anonymous visitor of a host without the feature to sign-in for a page that will then 404. Letting
  the request through to the router hands the answer to [TwoFactorPageGate](#twofactorpagegate).
- **Where it's used**: `AddUIShared` registers the policy unconditionally, so the page's attribute
  resolves in every host (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:94-100`);
  the [TwoFactorAccount](#twofactoraccount) page references it with
  `[Authorize(Policy = TwoFactorPageRequirement.PolicyName)]`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorAccount.razor:4`).
  Pinned by `TwoFactorRoutesTests` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/TwoFactor/TwoFactorRoutesTests.cs:26`).

### ThemeService
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Theme` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/ThemeService.cs:23` · Level 1 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the single owner of the Day/Dark preference (ADR-028). It holds the current mode for
  the circuit, persists a change through a small JS module to a cookie plus `localStorage`, and raises
  an event so every subscriber re-renders together.
- **Depends on**: [LazyJsModule](#lazyjsmodule) (single-flight importer for its JS module,
  `ThemeService.cs:26`); `Microsoft.JSInterop.IJSRuntime` (ASP.NET Core, primary-constructor parameter
  at line 23); an optional [IInitialThemeModeSource](#iinitialthememodesource), the second
  primary-constructor parameter, defaulting to `null` (line 23); the asset it imports,
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/wwwroot/theme.js`, which owns the cookie and
  `localStorage` access (`theme.js:5,23,33`). `IAsyncDisposable` (BCL) is implemented so the module
  reference is released with the circuit.
- **Concept introduced, one scoped service as the theme's single source of truth.**
  `[Rubric §20, Design System, Theming & UI Consistency]` assesses whether theming is a first-class,
  centrally owned concern rather than per-page CSS toggling. Here exactly one scoped service holds
  `IsDarkMode` (line 32); the toggle button, the `MudThemeProvider` wrapper and, on MAUI, the native
  chrome all read from it and all subscribe to `OnChange` (line 38). Nothing else stores a copy.
  `[Rubric §19, State Management & Data Flow]` is the same fact viewed as state: an event-plus-property
  service is the framework's pattern for cross-component UI state that is not routed, and the cost of
  that pattern is unsubscription discipline in every consumer.
- **Concept introduced, JS interop is not available during prerender.**
  `[Rubric §18, UI Architecture & Component Design]` covers the render-mode contract a Blazor component
  must respect (ADR-056, `Website/docs-src/adr/056-blazor-render-mode-strategy.md`). Reading a cookie
  or `localStorage` requires a live browser, so `InitializeAsync` can only run after the first
  interactive render; the class documents that requirement on itself (`ThemeService.cs:11-14`) rather
  than guarding it internally, and the component that owns the lifecycle calls it from
  `OnAfterRenderAsync(firstRender)`
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/MmcaThemeProviders.razor:59-69`).
- **Walkthrough**
  - `ModulePath` is the `_content/MMCA.Common.UI/theme.js` static-web-asset path (line 25), wrapped in
    a [LazyJsModule](#lazyjsmodule) field (line 26). Two components resolving the same scoped service
    therefore share one import rather than racing two.
  - `IsDarkMode` (line 32) and `IsInitialized` (line 35) are public with a private setter: subscribers
    read the state, only this class writes it. `OnChange` (line 38) is a plain `EventHandler?`.
    `IsDarkMode` is seeded from the constructor's `initialModeSource?.IsDarkMode ?? false` (line 32),
    so on a head with a native store (MAUI registers one) every reader, the app-bar toggle's icon and
    label among them, starts in the mode the page is painted in rather than light until initialization
    runs (doc comment, lines 17-22); a web head passes no source and starts at `false`.
  - `InitializeAsync()` (line 44) is idempotent by an early return on `IsInitialized` (lines 46-49).
    It imports the module (line 51), asks `get` for the stored value (line 53), and resolves the mode:
    a stored value wins by an ordinal case-insensitive compare against `"dark"` (lines 54-55),
    otherwise it falls back to the OS setting through `systemPrefersDark` (line 56), which reads
    `prefers-color-scheme` (`theme.js:33-35`). Only then does it set `IsInitialized` and raise
    `OnChange` (lines 59-60), so the first notification carries the resolved answer, not the default.
  - `InitializeAtStartupAsync(bool?)` (line 72, `internal`) is the entry point `MmcaThemeProviders` calls on first render, passing the mode of an optional [IInitialThemeModeSource](#iinitialthememodesource) it resolved in `OnInitialized` (`MmcaThemeProviders.razor:50,69`). A `null` falls through to `InitializeAsync`; a known native value takes `InitializeFromNativeAsync` (lines 75-92), which is also idempotent on `IsInitialized` (lines 77-80), adopts the value, sets `IsInitialized` and raises `OnChange` (lines 82-84), and only then reseeds the cookie and `localStorage` through `set` (lines 88-90), so a stale WebView value can neither win now nor be mirrored back over the native one. The reseed is last on purpose: a failure leaves the native value in force and surfaces to the caller's best-effort guard (comment, lines 86-87).
  - Each of the three JS calls that can fail sits inside a `#pragma warning disable BL0016` block whose
    justification names why the failure must propagate rather than be caught here: the caller observes
    it through [ThemeInterop](#themeinterop) (lines 52-57, 89-91, 101-103).
  - `SetDarkModeAsync(bool)` (line 96) persists first, through `set` (line 102), then writes the field
    (line 104) and notifies (line 105): a failed import or JS call leaves `IsDarkMode` and every subscriber
    on the mode that is actually stored (comment, `ThemeService.cs:98-99`). The JS side writes a non-HttpOnly cookie with a one-year `max-age` and
    `samesite=lax` and mirrors it to `localStorage`, guarding the mirror in a `try` because private
    browsing can refuse storage (`theme.js:23-31`). The cookie is deliberately readable by the server,
    which is how SSR can paint the right theme on the first response (`theme.js:1-2`).
  - `ToggleAsync()` (line 109) is `SetDarkModeAsync(!IsDarkMode)`, the entire body of the app-bar
    toggle's click handler.
  - `DisposeAsync()` (line 114) forwards to the module wrapper, which is where the guarded release of a
    torn-down circuit's `IJSObjectReference` lives.
- **Why it's built this way**: ADR-028 (`Website/docs-src/adr/028-dark-theme-mode.md`) requires the
  preference to survive a reload and to be visible to the server for a no-flash first paint, which is
  why the value goes to a cookie and `localStorage` rather than to component state, and why the service
  holds no `MudTheme` of its own: it publishes a boolean and lets the theme providers decide what that
  means visually. Not gating `InitializeAsync` on `RendererInfo` is also deliberate and pinned: the
  prerender test uses the `get` invocation as proof that the first render ran at all
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Theme/MmcaThemeProvidersPrerenderTests.cs:29-33`).
- **Where it's used**: registered by `AddUIShared` as scoped
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:221`) and consumed by
  `MmcaThemeProviders`, which subscribes in `OnInitialized`, initializes on first render and
  unsubscribes on dispose
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/MmcaThemeProviders.razor:56,69,147`), by
  `ThemeToggle` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/ThemeToggle.razor:2,7`), by
  the MAUI head's `NativeThemeSync`, which mirrors the in-app choice onto the native chrome
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Maui/Components/NativeThemeSync.razor:17,41,52`),
  and by the login flow, which applies a returning user's stored theme
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Login.razor:393`). Hosts that compose
  their own DI register it directly, for example MMCA.Helpdesk
  (`MMCA.Helpdesk/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.Helpdesk.UI.Web/Program.cs:23`). Behavior is pinned through the
  two components that drive it,
  [MmcaThemeProvidersTests](group-29-testing-infrastructure.md#per-project-test-rollup) and
  [ThemeToggleTests](group-29-testing-infrastructure.md#per-project-test-rollup), and end to end by
  `DarkModeE2ETests`
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.E2E.Tests/Layout/DarkModeE2ETests.cs:54`).
- **Caveats**: no test file in `MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Services` is named
  for this type; its behavior is covered only through those components, so a change to
  `InitializeAsync` surfaces as a component-test failure rather than a direct one. `OnChange` is a
  plain event with no weak-reference handling, so a subscriber that fails to unsubscribe outlives its
  component for the life of the circuit; both in-framework subscribers unsubscribe on dispose and both
  have a test asserting it. `SetDarkModeAsync` sets `IsDarkMode` only after the JS write succeeds, so a
  failed `set` throws out of the call with the in-memory mode, the persisted mode and the subscribers
  still in agreement and no `OnChange` raised. The native-first path orders it the other way on purpose: `InitializeFromNativeAsync` adopts the native value and raises `OnChange` before the `set` reseed, so a failed reseed throws with the in-memory mode already the native one. The exception is not swallowed here: the callers that
  must not take down the circuit wrap the call in [ThemeInterop](#themeinterop) (`ThemeToggle.razor:22`).

### ColorModeStamp
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Theme` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/ColorModeStamp.cs:14` · Level 1 · class (internal static)

- **What it is**: the opt-in colour-mode hook of `MmcaThemeProviders`. When the host sets
  `Layout:StampColorModeOnDocument`, it mirrors the Day/Dark mode onto
  `<html data-mmca-color-mode="light|dark">` so an app's own stylesheet can follow it; with the setting
  off (the default) it does nothing (doc comment, `ColorModeStamp.cs:8-13`).
- **Depends on**: [LayoutSettings](#layoutsettings) (its `StampColorModeOnDocument` flag,
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Common/Settings/LayoutSettings.cs:51`),
  and the `stampColorMode` export of
  `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/wwwroot/theme.js:103`. Externals:
  `Microsoft.JSInterop.IJSRuntime` (with its `JSException` and `JSDisconnectedException`) and
  `Microsoft.Extensions.Options.IOptions<T>`.
- **Concept introduced, an opt-in styling hook that cannot break theming.**
  `[Rubric §20, Design System, Theming & UI Consistency]` covers whether app CSS can follow the theme:
  `MudThemeProvider` only swaps its palette variables, which gives CSS nothing to select on
  (`LayoutSettings.cs:41-50`), so this hook gives a host an attribute to key its own rules on. The
  attribute is deliberately not `data-mmca-theme`, which belongs to the MAUI head's pre-paint script
  and its rules in `app.css` (`theme.js:83-84`). `[Rubric §18, UI Architecture & Component Design]`
  applies too: the stamp is best-effort because, like the interactivity marker, an app's styling hook
  must never break theme initialisation (comment, `ColorModeStamp.cs:29`). It tolerates exactly the
  failures [ThemeInterop](#themeinterop) tolerates, but catches them inline so the guard is visible at
  the call (comment, `ColorModeStamp.cs:30`).
- **Walkthrough**
  - One method, `ApplyAsync(IJSRuntime js, IServiceProvider services, bool isInteractive, bool isDarkMode)`
    (`ColorModeStamp.cs:22`). It returns early unless the render is interactive (JS interop is
    unavailable otherwise) and the scope resolves `IOptions<LayoutSettings>` with the flag set to `true`
    (`ColorModeStamp.cs:24-27`); a head with no layout settings registered therefore never stamps.
  - Otherwise it imports `./_content/MMCA.Common.UI/theme.js` and calls `stampColorMode` with `"dark"` or
    `"light"`, disposing the module reference with `await using` (`ColorModeStamp.cs:31-36`). The
    `try` is filtered with `catch (Exception ex) when (ex is JSException or JSDisconnectedException or
    InvalidOperationException)` (`ColorModeStamp.cs:37`), the same three cases [ThemeInterop](#themeinterop)
    catches; on any of them the stamp is skipped and the theme stays as it is (comment,
    `ColorModeStamp.cs:39`). Any other exception propagates.
  - On the JS side `stampColorMode` records the last mode, sets the attribute, and attaches one
    `enhancedload` listener that re-stamps it, because enhanced navigation resynchronises `<html>`'s
    attributes from the new document (`theme.js:85-86,103`).
- **Why it's built this way**:
  [ADR-028](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/028-dark-theme-mode.html) makes [ThemeService](#themeservice)
  the single owner of the mode; this class only reflects it outward and owns no state. Keeping it
  opt-in and off by default means a host adopting nothing sees no change to its document. Being
  interactive-only, a prerendered page carries no attribute until the page is interactive
  (`LayoutSettings.cs:44-45`).
- **Where it's used**: called only by `MmcaThemeProviders`, after its first interactive render
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/MmcaThemeProviders.razor:76`) and after every
  theme change (`MmcaThemeProviders.razor:127`). Pinned by `MmcaThemeProvidersColorModeTests`
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Theme/MmcaThemeProvidersColorModeTests.cs:21,29,49`).

### MMCATheme

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Theme` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Theme/MMCATheme.cs:9` · Level 2 · class (static)

- **What it is**: the single application-wide MudBlazor `MudTheme` instance, defining the brand palette (light and dark), typography, and layout radius, applied once via `MudThemeProvider` in the root layout.
- **Depends on**: [BrandColors](#brandcolors) (the palette source of truth); MudBlazor (NuGet: `MudTheme`, `PaletteLight`, `PaletteDark`, `Typography`, `LayoutProperties`).
- **Concept introduced, one theme, accessibility-justified, with contrast math for both text and non-text UI.** `[Rubric §20, Design System & Theming]` assesses whether an app has a single coherent theme rather than per-page overrides; `MMCATheme.Instance` is that one object (line 11). `[Rubric §21, Accessibility]` is unusually visible here, because most non-default color choices carry inline WCAG 2.1 AA/1.4.11 contrast math in a comment immediately above the value:
  - light `Warning = BrandColors.LightWarning` (`#A85D00`) / `WarningContrastText = BrandColors.LightWarningContrastText` (`#FFFFFF`) (lines 35-36): the palette color is used as text and as a border as often as it is a fill (`Color.Warning` on `MudText`/`MudLink`/`MudIcon` and on outlined chips/buttons), and MudBlazor's default `#F57F17` is only about 2.65:1 on Surface, failing the 4.5:1 floor everywhere it is text; `#A85D00` is 4.96:1 on Surface and 4.79:1 on Background, and is dark enough that white becomes the correct on-color label (comment, lines 29-34);
  - light `LinesInputs = "rgba(0,0,0,0.45)"` (line 42): outlined-field borders answer to the 3:1 non-text floor (WCAG 1.4.11); MudBlazor's default is only 3.03:1/3.01:1, passing with no margin, so any host that darkens Background drops it below (comment, lines 38-41);
  - dark `PrimaryDarken = BrandColors.DarkPrimaryDarken` (`#1E88E5`, line 66): MudBlazor repaints a filled primary control with `PrimaryDarken` on hover, focus-visible and active while the label keeps `PrimaryContrastText`, so the darken has to carry the dark label too; the brand `#1565C0` left it at about 3.4:1, under the 4.5:1 floor, while Blue 600 holds 5.14:1 and still reads as a darker state than `#42A5F5`, and `PrimaryFillContrastTests` pins both fills (comment, lines 61-65);
  - dark `PrimaryContrastText = "rgba(0,0,0,0.87)"` (line 71), because white on the lightened dark-mode primary `#42A5F5` is about 2.65:1 fill-on-fill while dark text is about 6.6:1 (comment, lines 68-70);
  - dark `SecondaryContrastText`/`TertiaryContrastText`/`InfoContrastText`/`SuccessContrastText` (lines 81, 83, 85, 87): every lightened dark-mode accent takes the same Material treatment, white is 2.36-2.65:1 as a fill across the four colors while `rgba(0,0,0,0.87)` lands at 6.96-7.70:1, and each accent stays legible as text on Surface too (comment, lines 75-80);
  - dark `WarningContrastText` (line 90), white on `#FFA726` being about 2.0:1 against about 10.8:1 (line 89);
  - dark `Error = BrandColors.DarkError` (`#FF8A80`) / `ErrorContrastText = "rgba(0,0,0,0.87)"` (lines 95, 98): the previous `#EF5350` was only 3.84:1 as text on Surface, below the 4.5:1 floor wherever `Color.Error` is a label rather than a fill (inline validation copy, outlined error chips); `#FF8A80` reads 5.86:1 on Surface, with the white-vs-dark label question resolved the same way as Primary (comments, lines 91-94, 96-97);
  - dark `InfoDarken`/`SuccessDarken`/`WarningDarken`/`ErrorDarken` from `BrandColors.DarkInfoDarken` and its three siblings (lines 109-112): a text (default-variant) or outlined alert paints its message in the `*Darken` colour over the base colour at `HoverOpacity` (0.06) composited on Surface, and left unset MudBlazor darkens each accent, which on a dark surface moves the text towards the background (Info `#2094F3` is 3.82:1 on its tint, Success `#4DAC52` 4.23:1, Error `#FF695C` 4.31:1, all under the 4.5:1 floor); the Material 300-level tints clear it (tint / Surface: Info 5.49 / 6.04, Success 6.01 / 6.65, Warning 6.93 / 7.73, Error 5.66 / 6.22, with Red 200 for Error because its base is already lighter than Red 300), the same values are the hover, focus and active fill of filled Info/Success/Warning/Error buttons, chips and FABs whose dark label reads 8.2:1 or better, and `AlertTextContrastTests` pins all eight ratios (comment, lines 99-108);
  - dark `LinesInputs = "rgba(255,255,255,0.5)"` (line 117): the dark default `rgba(255,255,255,0.3)` is only 2.6:1 on Surface, effectively invisible to a low-vision user, while `0.5` is 4.59:1/5.10:1 (comment, lines 113-116);
  - dark `TableStriped = "rgba(0,0,0,0.2)"` / `TableHover = "rgba(0,0,0,0.32)"` (lines 126-127): the row overlays darken rather than lighten, because a link sits on the composited row and MudBlazor's default white striping turns Surface `#27303A` into about `rgb(82,89,97)`, where the link colour `#42A5F5` is only about 2.66:1 (any white overlay above roughly 3% already drops under 4.5:1); the black overlays read 5.77:1 (striped) and 6.15:1 (hover) on Surface and 6.61:1 / 6.87:1 on Background while staying visibly distinct from the plain row and from each other, and `LinkContrastTests` pins both (comment, lines 118-125).

  The `Secondary` (light) contrast rationale is deliberately *not* repeated here: line 21 points at [BrandColors](#brandcolors), where the value and its justification live together. The reverse holds for `Warning` and `Error`: their constants live in [BrandColors](#brandcolors), whose summaries point back here for the math.
- **Walkthrough**: a single `static MudTheme Instance { get; }` (line 11) initialized with four blocks. Every hex value in both palettes is a [BrandColors](#brandcolors) constant (comment, lines 15-17); the only literals left are the `rgba(...)` on-color labels and input lines, each justified by the contrast comment above it.
  - `PaletteLight` (lines 13-55) reads its primary and secondary triads from [BrandColors](#brandcolors) (lines 18-24), sets the semantic colors from the `Light*` constants (`Tertiary`, `Info`, `Success`, `Warning`, `Error`, lines 25-37, including the WCAG-driven `Warning` and `LinesInputs` values above), and then fixes app chrome: `AppbarBackground` and `DrawerBackground` from `BrandColors.ChromeBackground`, `DrawerText`/`DrawerIcon` from `ChromeTextMuted`, and background, surface, text, action and divider values from the matching `Light*` constants (lines 43-54).
  - `PaletteDark` (lines 56-140) lightens the primary for contrast on dark surfaces (`Primary = BrandColors.PrimaryLight`, line 60), pairs it with a Blue 600 `PrimaryDarken` (line 66) and `*Darken` state colours for Info, Success, Warning and Error (lines 109-112, above), darkens the table row overlays (lines 126-127, above), takes the same `Chrome*` constants for app bar and drawer so the shell reads identically in both modes (lines 128-134), and darkens the surface stack (`Background = BrandColors.DarkBackground`, `Surface = BrandColors.DarkSurface`, lines 130-131) with the `Dark*` text and divider tones.
  - `Typography` (lines 141-219). `Default` sets the font stack `Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica Neue, Arial, sans-serif`; the comment above it records that Inter is self-hosted by this RCL (`wwwroot/fonts` plus an `@font-face` block in `wwwroot/app.css`) and that before those faces existed the stack silently fell through to Segoe UI, so the two must stay in step. `H1` through `H4` use display weights 800/800/700/700 with slight negative letter spacing, which the comment explains is how Inter is meant to be set at large sizes; `H5` and `H6` stay at weight 600 with no negative tracking. `Subtitle1`/`Subtitle2` sit at weight 500, `Body1`/`Body2` set line heights 1.6 and 1.5, and `Button` sets `TextTransform = "none"`, because MudBlazor's default uppercasing wrecks localized strings (German compounds, accented capitals) and reads dated; weight 600 keeps the label as prominent as the shouting did.
  - `LayoutProperties` sets `DefaultBorderRadius = "6px"` (lines 220-223).
- **Why it's built this way**: a static get-only property means the theme is constructed once and shared by every `MudThemeProvider`. Sourcing every hex value from [BrandColors](#brandcolors) rather than re-typing it is what lets `BrandColorTokenTests` police C# versus CSS drift and keeps this class a mapping of roles to named colors, and the per-color contrast comments turn accessibility decisions into reviewable source rather than tribal knowledge, now covering both text-on-fill (4.5:1) and non-text UI like input borders (3:1, WCAG 1.4.11) rather than text alone. The button-casing override is a small but instructive case of `[Rubric §27, Internationalization & Localization]` reaching into theming: a purely visual default became a localization problem.
- **Where it's used**: applied in the root layout of the Blazor Web and MAUI hosts via `MudThemeProvider Theme="MMCATheme.Instance"`.

### TwoFactorUIModule
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.TwoFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/TwoFactor/TwoFactorUIModule.cs:16` · Level 3 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the two-factor authentication module descriptor. Registering it is what gives a host
  the account page's navigation item and the layout listener that sends a session refused for want of a
  second factor to that page; a host that never registers it has no page (the router answers 404), no
  nav item and no listener (doc comment, `TwoFactorUIModule.cs:10-15`).
- **Depends on**: [IUIModule](#iuimodule) (the contract it implements), [NavItem](#navitem),
  [NavSection](#navsection), [SharedResource](#sharedresource) (the localization resource for the nav
  label), [MultiFactorRequiredListener](#multifactorrequiredlistener) (its layout component), and
  MudBlazor's `Icons.Material.Filled.Security`.
- **Concept introduced**: none new; it is a framework-owned instance of the UI module descriptor taught
  at [IUIModule](#iuimodule) ([ADR-067](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/067-ui-module-shell-composition.html)),
  shaped like [NotificationUIModule](#notificationuimodule). `[Rubric §25, Navigation & IA]` assesses
  whether navigation reflects the features a host actually has: the nav item exists only when the
  module is registered.
- **Walkthrough**
  - `AccountPath = "/profile/two-factor"` (`TwoFactorUIModule.cs:19`), the single route constant the
    listener uses to build its redirect and to recognise that it is already on the page
    (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/MultiFactorRequiredListener.cs:47,83`).
  - `NavItems` (`TwoFactorUIModule.cs:22-25`): one item, key `"Nav.TwoFactor"`, the security icon,
    resolved against `SharedResource`, placed in `NavSection.User`.
  - `LayoutComponentTypes` (`TwoFactorUIModule.cs:28`): `[typeof(MultiFactorRequiredListener)]`, so the
    shell renders the listener only in a host that registered the module.
  - `Assembly` (`TwoFactorUIModule.cs:31`) returns this class's own assembly, `MMCA.Common.UI`.
- **Why it's built this way**: a module descriptor is the existing switch the shell already reads for
  nav, layout components and router presence, so making two-factor a module gives the feature an
  all-or-nothing opt-in without new shell code. [TwoFactorPageGate](#twofactorpagegate) keys on the
  presence of this type.
- **Where it's used**: registered by `AddTwoFactorUI()` in this namespace's
  [DependencyInjection](#dependencyinjection-3) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/TwoFactor/DependencyInjection.cs:30`);
  probed by [TwoFactorPageGate](#twofactorpagegate) (`TwoFactorPageGate.cs:25`); pinned by
  `TwoFactorUIModuleTests` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/TwoFactor/TwoFactorUIModuleTests.cs:21`).

### DependencyInjection
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.TwoFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/TwoFactor/DependencyInjection.cs:13` · Level 5 · class (static, with one `extension(IServiceCollection)` block)

- **What it is**: the two-factor UI opt-in ([ADR-116](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/116-identity-completions-opt-in.html)).
  One method, `AddTwoFactorUI()`, registers the account page at `TwoFactorUIModule.AccountPath`, its
  navigation item and the listener; a host that does not call it gets none of them (doc comment,
  `DependencyInjection.cs:8-12`). This is the `MMCA.Common.UI.TwoFactor` class of that name, not the
  shared-UI composition root `AddUIShared` lives in.
- **Depends on**: [ITwoFactorUIService](#itwofactoruiservice) / [TwoFactorUIService](#twofactoruiservice),
  [IUIModule](#iuimodule) / [TwoFactorUIModule](#twofactoruimodule); externals
  `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection` and its `Extensions` namespace (`TryAddScoped`,
  `TryAddEnumerable`).
- **Concept introduced**: none new; it uses the `extension(IServiceCollection services)` block
  (`DependencyInjection.cs:15`) taught in the [primer](00-primer.md#c-extensiont-types-read-this-once).
  `[Rubric §33, Developer Experience]` assesses how few calls a host needs to adopt a feature: here one
  call, placed next to `AddUIShared` in every UI head (web server, WebAssembly client, MAUI) whose API
  hosts the `auth/two-factor` endpoints (doc comment, `DependencyInjection.cs:17-20`).
- **Walkthrough**: `AddTwoFactorUI()` (`DependencyInjection.cs:23`) does two things and returns the
  collection for chaining (line 32).
  - `TryAddScoped<ITwoFactorUIService, TwoFactorUIService>()` (line 26): `TryAdd`, so an app (or the
    gallery) that registered its own client keeps it (comment, line 25).
  - `TryAddEnumerable(ServiceDescriptor.Singleton<IUIModule, TwoFactorUIModule>())` (line 30):
    calling the method from two places still registers the module once, because a second module would
    render the nav item and the listener twice (comment, lines 28-29).
- **Why it's built this way**: the authorization pieces (the policy and
  [TwoFactorPageAuthorizationHandler](#twofactorpageauthorizationhandler)) are registered by `AddUIShared`
  unconditionally (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:94-105`), so the
  page attribute resolves in every host; this method only adds what makes the page reachable. The
  module's presence is then the single fact the router gate and the handler both read.
- **Where it's used**: the three Store UI heads
  (`MMCA.Store/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.Store.UI.Web/Program.cs:71`,
  `MMCA.Store/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.Store.UI.Web.Client/Program.cs:43`,
  `MMCA.Store/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.Store.UI/MauiProgram.cs:65`); no ADC host calls it. In Common the
  component gallery calls it over a canned client
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Gallery/GalleryHost.cs:116`), and the opt-in is pinned
  by `TwoFactorOptInRenderTests` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/TwoFactor/TwoFactorOptInRenderTests.cs:39,61`).
- **Caveats**: the group already has a `### DependencyInjection` section for the shared-UI root
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs`), so the two headings share
  one anchor in the assembled chapter and `#dependencyinjection` resolves to whichever comes first.

### TwoFactorPageGate
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.TwoFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/TwoFactor/TwoFactorPageGate.cs:12` · Level 7 · class (internal static)

- **What it is**: the router-side check that answers the two-factor account page with the not-found
  page when the host never registered the two-factor UI, because that page needs a client such a host
  does not have and an API with no two-factor endpoints (doc comment, `TwoFactorPageGate.cs:6-11`).
- **Depends on**: [IUIModule](#iuimodule), [TwoFactorUIModule](#twofactoruimodule) and the
  [TwoFactorAccount](#twofactoraccount) page type.
- **Concept introduced**: none new; it is the two-factor sibling of [NotificationPageGate](#notificationpagegate),
  and the two sit in the same router condition. `[Rubric §25, Navigation & IA]` applies as at
  [TwoFactorPageRequirement](#twofactorpagerequirement).
- **Walkthrough**
  - `Hides(Type pageType, IEnumerable<IUIModule> modules)` (`TwoFactorPageGate.cs:18-19`): true only
    when the matched page is `TwoFactorAccount` and the host hides two-factor pages.

### TwoFactorPageAuthorizationHandler
> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.TwoFactor` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/TwoFactor/TwoFactorPageAuthorizationHandler.cs:12` · Level 8 · class (internal sealed)

- **What it is**: the handler that evaluates [TwoFactorPageRequirement](#twofactorpagerequirement): an
  authenticated caller passes, and every caller passes while the host hides the two-factor page (doc
  comment, `TwoFactorPageAuthorizationHandler.cs:6-10`).

- **Concept introduced**: none new; it mirrors
  [NotificationPageAuthorizationHandler](#notificationpageauthorizationhandler). `[Rubric §11, Security]`
  assesses that relaxing a check is narrow and deliberate: the bypass applies only when the page cannot
