### ApiEndpointUrl

> MMCA.Common.UI.Web · `MMCA.Common.UI.Web.Security` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Security/ApiEndpointUrl.cs:12` · Level 0 · class (internal, static)

- **What it is**: the one shared test for whether a configured API endpoint value is usable, applied by the Content-Security-Policy provider, the `/client-config` endpoint and the Blazor Web host registration, so a deployment placeholder such as `SET-VIA-ENVIRONMENT-VARIABLE` is refused the same way everywhere instead of booting a client against a non-URL (class doc, `ApiEndpointUrl.cs:5-11`).
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party. Externals: BCL `Uri` (`Uri.TryCreate`, `Uri.UriSchemeHttp`, `Uri.UriSchemeHttps`), `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis` (`NotNullWhenAttribute`).
- **Concept introduced, one definition of "a usable endpoint" for every consumer of the same keys.** The fail-fast configuration contract of [ADR-070](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/070-fail-fast-configuration-contract.html) asks that a misconfigured setting be caught at startup or at its first use, with one meaning. Three call sites read `Api:ApiEndpoint` and `Api:WasmApiEndpoint`; when each wrote its own check they could disagree about what a placeholder is. This class is the single answer, and it is strict about scheme: a value only qualifies when `Uri.TryCreate(..., UriKind.Absolute, ...)` succeeds AND the scheme is http or https (`ApiEndpointUrl.cs:37-39`), because on Linux a rooted path such as `/relative/path` parses as an absolute `file://` URI (doc, lines 27-30).
  - `[Rubric §26, Front-End Security]` assesses browser-side hardening: the CSP's `connect-src` origin is derived from a value this class has already accepted, so a non-http(s) string never becomes a policy source.
- **Walkthrough**
  - `TryParseAbsoluteHttp(string? value, out Uri? uri)` (lines 35-47) rejects null or whitespace, then requires an absolute parse with an http(s) scheme; on success it hands back the parsed `Uri` (`[NotNullWhen(true)]`, line 35), otherwise `uri` is null.
  - `IsAbsoluteHttp(string? value)` (line 52) is the boolean form of the same test.
  - `IsAbsoluteHttpOrServiceDiscovery(string? value)` (lines 63-74) accepts everything `IsAbsoluteHttp` does, plus an Aspire service-discovery URL whose scheme is a `+`-joined list made only of http and https, such as `https+http://gateway` (lines 70-73). The doc (lines 54-60) scopes it: that form is valid only for the server head's `Api:ApiEndpoint`, which `IHttpClientFactory` clients resolve through the service-discovery handler `AddServiceDefaults()` adds; a browser cannot, so `Api:WasmApiEndpoint` uses `IsAbsoluteHttp`.
  - `IsHttpScheme` (lines 76-78) compares the scheme to `Uri.UriSchemeHttp` and `Uri.UriSchemeHttps` with `StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase`.
- **Why it's built this way**: a static, internal helper keeps the rule in one place without widening the package's public API, and splitting the browser form from the server form encodes the real difference (who can resolve a service-discovery name) instead of letting the looser test leak into the browser configuration.
- **Where it's used**: [BlazorCspPolicyProvider](#blazorcsppolicyprovider) calls `TryParseAbsoluteHttp` to pin `connect-src` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Security/BlazorCspPolicyProvider.cs:55`); [ClientConfigEndpointExtensions](#clientconfigendpointextensions)`.MapClientConfigEndpoint` throws when `Api:WasmApiEndpoint` fails `IsAbsoluteHttp` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/ClientConfig/ClientConfigEndpointExtensions.cs:81-88`); [BlazorWebHostExtensions](#blazorwebhostextensions) throws at registration when `Api:ApiEndpoint` fails `IsAbsoluteHttpOrServiceDiscovery` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Hosting/BlazorWebHostExtensions.cs:114-121`). Pinned by `ApiEndpointUrlTests` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web.Tests/Security/ApiEndpointUrlTests.cs`).

### TrustedCallerHandler

> MMCA.Common.UI.Web · `MMCA.Common.UI.Web.Security` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Security/TrustedCallerHandler.cs:35` · Level 0 · class (sealed, `DelegatingHandler`)

- **What it is**: an outgoing `HttpClient` handler that stamps a shared-secret header onto a request
  only when the request targets the configured gateway origin, so the gateway can trust that the call
  came from this app rather than from an arbitrary caller.
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party. Externals: `System.Net.Http` (`DelegatingHandler`,
  `HttpRequestMessage`, `HttpResponseMessage`), BCL `Uri`.
- **Concept introduced, an edge-trust header scoped to origin match, not applied blindly.**
  `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether a trust signal is bounded to the audience it is meant for.
  The constructor takes a header name, a shared secret, and the gateway origin
  (`TrustedCallerHandler.cs:39`), and `SendAsync` only stamps the header when the outgoing request's
  scheme, host, and port match that origin (`TrustedCallerHandler.cs:57-63`); a request to any other
  destination goes out unmodified, so the secret cannot leak to a third-party origin the same
  `HttpClient` happens to call. [ADR-088](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/088-gateway-edge-responsibilities.html)
  is the policy this enforces on the client side.
- **Walkthrough**
  - The constructor (`TrustedCallerHandler.cs:39-48`) null/blank-guards `headerName` and `secret` and
    null-guards `gatewayOrigin`, storing all three as readonly fields.
  - `SendAsync` (`TrustedCallerHandler.cs:51-72`) null-guards the request, then compares
    `request.RequestUri` against `_gatewayOrigin` with `Uri.Compare` over
    `UriComponents.Scheme | UriComponents.HostAndPort`, case-insensitive
    (`TrustedCallerHandler.cs:57-63`). On a match it removes any existing value for the header and adds
    exactly one via `TryAddWithoutValidation` (`TrustedCallerHandler.cs:67-68`); the comment
    (`TrustedCallerHandler.cs:65-66`) explains the replace-not-append choice, the gateway compares one
    header value in constant time, so a second value would silently fail the comparison. It then calls
    `base.SendAsync` unconditionally.
- **Why it's built this way**: a `DelegatingHandler` composes into the existing `HttpClient` pipeline
  without every call site having to remember to add the header itself, and gating on origin means the
  same registered handler is safe to reuse on a client that also talks to other hosts.
- **Where it's used**: registered in `MMCA.Common.UI.Web`'s
  [DependencyInjection](#dependencyinjection-1) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/DependencyInjection.cs`);
  its behavior is pinned by `TrustedCallerHandlerTests`
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web.Tests/Security/TrustedCallerHandlerTests.cs`).

### BlazorCspSettings

> MMCA.Common.UI.Web · `MMCA.Common.UI.Web.Security` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Security/BlazorCspSettings.cs:18` · Level 0 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the bindable options type for an opt-in `frame-src` allowance on the Blazor host's Content-Security-Policy, one string list of origins a page may embed in an `<iframe>` (`BlazorCspSettings.cs:23-35`).
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party. It is read by [BlazorCspPolicyProvider](#blazorcsppolicyprovider) through `BuildFrameSrc` and validated at startup by [BlazorCspSettingsValidator](#blazorcspsettingsvalidator). Externals: `Microsoft.Extensions.Options` binding conventions (BCL `IList<string>`).
- **Concept introduced, an empty default that changes nothing.** `[Rubric §26, Front-End Security]` assesses whether a security-relevant default stays strict until a deployment explicitly opts out. `SectionName = "BlazorCsp"` (line 28) names the configuration section; `FrameSources` (line 42) initializes to an empty list, so an unconfigured host emits no `frame-src` directive at all and the policy stays byte-identical to the pre-existing baseline (comment, lines 30-33). Only a deployment that needs to embed a specific third-party origin (the doc comment's example is a map provider's embed endpoint, lines 30-31) adds entries.
  - The doc comment (lines 33-40) states the origin shape a configured entry must satisfy: an absolute `https` origin with no path, query, fragment, user info, wildcard, quote, semicolon, comma or whitespace, so the field carries the contract [BlazorCspSettingsValidator](#blazorcspsettingsvalidator) enforces rather than leaving it implicit.
- **Walkthrough**: two members: `SectionName` (line 28, a `public const string`) and `FrameSources` (line 42, `public IList<string>` initialized to `[]`).
- **Why it's built this way**: a settings class bound through `IOptions<BlazorCspSettings>` fits the same registration and validation pipeline every other options type in the host uses, so adding `frame-src` support did not need a new configuration mechanism, only a new section.
- **Where it's used**: bound and validated in `MMCA.Common.UI.Web`'s [DependencyInjection](#dependencyinjection-1) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/DependencyInjection.cs`), consumed by [BlazorCspPolicyProvider](#blazorcsppolicyprovider)'s constructor as `IOptions<BlazorCspSettings>`.

### BrowserOriginHandler

> MMCA.Common.UI.Web · `MMCA.Common.UI.Web.Services` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Services/BrowserOriginHandler.cs:32` · Level 0 · class (internal sealed, `DelegatingHandler`)

- **What it is**: an outgoing `HttpClient` handler that stamps the visitor's browser origin (`X-Forwarded-For` with its address, `User-Agent` with its user-agent) on the server-side `"APIClient"` calls a Blazor Server host makes for that visitor (`BrowserOriginHandler.cs:5-11`). Without it the API would see this host's own address for every visitor, and the host's HTTP client sends no user-agent at all.
- **Depends on**: nothing first-party. Externals: `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http` (`IHttpContextAccessor`, `ConnectionInfo.RemoteIpAddress`), `System.Net.Http` (`DelegatingHandler`, `HttpRequestMessage`).
- **Concept introduced, per-client policy keyed on the visitor rather than the host.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether a trust or rate-limit signal is attributed to the right principal. The API keys the registration rate limit, the session's recorded IP and the recorded device on the caller; behind a Blazor Server host every caller would collapse onto the host's address. The handler copies two values from the HTTP request that carries the work (the page request during prerender, the connection the circuit was established on afterwards, `BrowserOriginHandler.cs:14-17`). The address is `RemoteIpAddress`, which has already passed through this host's forwarded-headers middleware, so it is only as far back as the host trusts its own proxies, and a client-supplied `X-Forwarded-For` is never copied verbatim (`BrowserOriginHandler.cs:16-19`).
- **Walkthrough**
  - The primary constructor (line 32) takes `IHttpContextAccessor`, an async-local that crosses the handler's own DI scope (parameter doc, lines 30-31). Two internal constants name the headers: `ForwardedForHeaderName` (line 35) and `UserAgentHeaderName` (line 38).
  - `SendAsync` (lines 41-55) null-guards the request, reads `httpContextAccessor.HttpContext` (line 47) and, only when a request is in scope, calls `Replace` for the connection's remote address (line 50) and the request's `User-Agent` (line 51), then calls `base.SendAsync` unconditionally (line 54). With no visitor behind the call (a background job) nothing is sent.
  - `Replace` (lines 57-68) returns early on a null or blank value (lines 59-62), so a blank user-agent is not forwarded; otherwise it removes any existing header (line 66) and adds exactly one value via `TryAddWithoutValidation` (line 67). The comment (lines 64-65) gives the reason for skipping validation: a real browser user-agent does not always parse as a strict product-token list, and neither value needs parsing on this side.
- **Why it's built this way**: a `DelegatingHandler` composes into the named client's pipeline without any call site remembering to add the headers, and replace-not-append keeps each header single-valued so a caller cannot smuggle a second value in. It is the same shape as [TrustedCallerHandler](#trustedcallerhandler), but unconditional on origin because the target is always this app's own API.
- **Where it's used**: registered transient and attached to the `"APIClient"` named client by `AddCommonServerTokenStorage()` in the `MMCA.Common.UI.Web` [DependencyInjection](#dependencyinjection-1) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/DependencyInjection.cs:47-48`); only a Blazor Server host calls that, because the WebAssembly client reaches the API through the same-origin proxy, which forwards the browser's own headers (`BrowserOriginHandler.cs:23-28`). Pinned by `BrowserOriginHandlerTests` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web.Tests/Services/BrowserOriginHandlerTests.cs`).

### BlazorCspSettingsValidator

> MMCA.Common.UI.Web · `MMCA.Common.UI.Web.Security` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Security/BlazorCspSettingsValidator.cs:13` · Level 1 · class (internal, sealed)

- **What it is**: the startup `IValidateOptions<BlazorCspSettings>` that rejects a `frame-src` origin the moment it is misshapen, so a bad entry fails fast rather than silently reaching the CSP header.
- **Depends on**: first-party: [BlazorCspSettings](#blazorcspsettings) (the options type it validates). Externals: `Microsoft.Extensions.Options` (`IValidateOptions<T>`, `ValidateOptionsResult`), BCL `SearchValues<char>`, `Uri`.
- **Concept introduced, an explicit character denylist plus a shape check, not a regex.** The fail-fast configuration contract of ADR-070 (Website/docs-src/adr/070-fail-fast-configuration-contract.md) assesses whether a misconfigured setting is caught at startup instead of at request time. `Validate` (lines 21-31) runs every configured `FrameSources` entry through `IsValidOrigin` and fails the whole registration with one message per bad entry (lines 26-30) rather than starting the host on a policy it cannot honor.
  - `ForbiddenCharacters` (line 18, a `SearchValues<char>` over `*'";,@?#`) is the set that could either break out of a CSP source expression or widen it, plus the URL delimiters (user info, query, fragment) a plain origin never carries. `IsValidOrigin` (lines 21-25 of the walkthrough below) rejects on that set before it ever calls `Uri.TryCreate`, so a value crafted to look like a URL but carrying a CSP metacharacter never reaches the parser.
  - `[Rubric §26, Front-End Security]` assesses browser-side hardening; this validator is what keeps [BlazorCspSettings](#blazorcspsettings)'s contract (an absolute https origin, no path, wildcard, or delimiter) a checked invariant instead of a comment.
- **Walkthrough**
  - `Validate(string? name, BlazorCspSettings options)` (lines 21-31) null-guards `options`, projects every entry that fails `IsValidOrigin` into a message naming the section, the entry, and the shape it must satisfy (lines 26-30), and returns `ValidateOptionsResult.Success` only when that list is empty.
  - `IsValidOrigin(string? source)` (lines 34-49), `internal static`: rejects null, whitespace-only, any entry containing whitespace, anything matching `ForbiddenCharacters`, or anything `Uri.TryCreate` cannot parse as absolute (lines 36-41). What remains must be `https` (ordinal case-insensitive), have a non-empty host, and have `PathAndQuery` equal to exactly `"/"` (lines 46-48); the comment (lines 44-45) notes the forbidden set already rules out user info, a query, and a fragment, so a root-only path is the last thing separating an origin from a full URL.
  - `ToOrigin(string source)` (lines 55-56), `internal static`: `new Uri(source, UriKind.Absolute).GetLeftPart(UriPartial.Authority)`, the canonical `scheme://host[:port]` form used to splice a validated entry into the CSP header, lower-cased host, default port dropped, no trailing slash.
- **Why it's built this way**: an explicit character denylist checked before parsing is stricter than trusting `Uri` alone, because `Uri` will happily parse strings a CSP source expression cannot safely contain; failing every bad entry at once (rather than the first) gives a deployment the whole list of what to fix in one pass.
- **Where it's used**: registered alongside [BlazorCspSettings](#blazorcspsettings) in `MMCA.Common.UI.Web`'s [DependencyInjection](#dependencyinjection-1) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/DependencyInjection.cs`); `ToOrigin` is reused by [BlazorCspPolicyProvider](#blazorcsppolicyprovider)'s `BuildFrameSrc` to canonicalize an already-validated entry.

### HttpContextForbiddenReExecutionDetector

> MMCA.Common.UI.Web · `MMCA.Common.UI.Web.Services` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Services/HttpContextForbiddenReExecutionDetector.cs:18` · Level 1 · class (internal, sealed)

- **What it is**: the Blazor Web host's [IForbiddenReExecutionDetector](#iforbiddenreexecutiondetector). It reads the status code of the request being rendered, so the shared not-found page can tell a 403 that status-code-pages re-executed to `/not-found` from a genuine missing page and render the Access Denied view instead of "Page Not Found" (class doc, `HttpContextForbiddenReExecutionDetector.cs:6-10`).
- **Depends on**: first-party: [IForbiddenReExecutionDetector](#iforbiddenreexecutiondetector) (the contract, line 18, `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Navigation/IForbiddenReExecutionDetector.cs:17`). Externals: `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http` (`IHttpContextAccessor`, `StatusCodes`).
- **Concept introduced, a status only the server render can see.** Status-code-pages re-execution keeps the original status on the response, so a 403 re-executed to `/not-found` is still 403 while that page renders (lines 8-9). Only a host with a live request can read it, which is why the shared UI package registers an always-false default ([NoForbiddenReExecutionDetector](#noforbiddenreexecutiondetector), `TryAddSingleton` at `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/DependencyInjection.cs:250`) and this server-side reader replaces it. During static server rendering `IHttpContextAccessor` returns the request being rendered; with no request in scope the answer is `false`, and an interactive circuit's connection request never carries a 403 (a refused connection opens no circuit), so an interactive render keeps rendering Page Not Found (lines 11-16).
  - `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether an authorization refusal is reported honestly: a user denied a page sees that access was denied rather than being told the page does not exist.
- **Walkthrough**
  - The constructor (lines 24-28) null-guards and stores the `IHttpContextAccessor`.
  - `IsForbiddenReExecution` (lines 31-32) is `_httpContextAccessor.HttpContext?.Response.StatusCode == StatusCodes.Status403Forbidden`: a null context compares as `false`.
- **Why it's built this way**: the page lives in `MMCA.Common.UI`, which depends on Shared only and must run under WebAssembly and MAUI, so it cannot touch `HttpContext`; an interface with a false default there and an `HttpContext` reader in the server host keeps the page head-agnostic.
- **Where it's used**: registered by [BlazorWebHostExtensions](#blazorwebhostextensions) with `services.Replace(ServiceDescriptor.Singleton<IForbiddenReExecutionDetector, HttpContextForbiddenReExecutionDetector>())` right after `AddHttpContextAccessor()` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Hosting/BlazorWebHostExtensions.cs:136-139`); read by the shared not-found page (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/NotFound.razor:6`, `:55`). Pinned by `HttpContextForbiddenReExecutionDetectorTests` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web.Tests/Services/HttpContextForbiddenReExecutionDetectorTests.cs`).

### BlazorCspPolicyProvider

> MMCA.Common.UI.Web · `MMCA.Common.UI.Web.Security` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Security/BlazorCspPolicyProvider.cs:28` · Level 2 · class (internal, sealed)

- **What it is**: the Content-Security-Policy provider for a Blazor Web host. It computes one CSP string at construction, pinning `connect-src` to `'self'` plus the configured API or Gateway origin (https and its matching WebSocket origin), optionally adding an opt-in `frame-src` directive, and hands the result to the shared security-headers middleware on every request.
- **Depends on**: first-party: [ICspPolicyProvider](group-16-aspire-orchestration.md#icsppolicyprovider) (the contract it implements, line 28), [CspPolicy](group-16-aspire-orchestration.md#csppolicy) (the value it returns, a policy string plus an `Enforce` flag), [SecurityHeadersMiddleware](group-16-aspire-orchestration.md#securityheadersmiddleware) (its only consumer, named in the class doc at line 12), [ApiSettings](#apisettings) (the endpoint source, injected as `IOptions<ApiSettings>`, line 34), [ApiEndpointUrl](#apiendpointurl) (the shared endpoint test, `TryParseAbsoluteHttp`, line 55), and [BlazorCspSettings](#blazorcspsettings) (the frame-src source, injected as `IOptions<BlazorCspSettings>`, line 35) whose entries it canonicalizes with [BlazorCspSettingsValidator](#blazorcspsettingsvalidator)`.ToOrigin` (line 90). Externals: `Microsoft.Extensions.Options` (`IOptions<T>`), `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting` (`IWebHostEnvironment`), `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http` (`HttpContext`), BCL `Uri`.
- **Concept introduced, a computed CSP that fails closed.** `[Rubric §26, Front-End Security]` assesses whether the browser is told which origins may load scripts and open connections. A static CSP cannot express "this deployment's API origin", because that origin is configuration, so the policy is *built* rather than hard-coded. The two directives that matter for exfiltration are locked: `script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'` (line 102, where the WASM allowance is what lets the Blazor WebAssembly runtime instantiate) and the computed `connect-src` (line 65). The load-bearing decision is what happens when the origin cannot be determined. The provider narrows `connect-src` to `'self'`, keeps the rest of the policy unchanged, and stays **enforced** (`Enforce: true`, line 59). A misconfigured endpoint therefore surfaces immediately as blocked API calls in the browser console rather than as a permissive header that protects nothing and that nobody notices, and the class doc states the reasoning outright: a security response header that quietly stops being enforced is the worse failure mode (lines 16-20).
  - `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses the wider defense posture; this class is one control in a chain that also includes the session-cookie auth design and the security-headers middleware, and it is deliberately `internal` (line 28) so the only supported way to get it is the registration call, not a hand-wired `new`.
  - **`frame-src` is opt-in and null-safe.** [BlazorCspSettings](#blazorcspsettings)'s default is an empty `FrameSources` list, and `BuildFrameSrc` (line 82) returns `null` when it is empty (lines 84-87), which keeps the policy byte-identical to the baseline for every deployment that has not opted in (comment, lines 79-81; class doc, lines 21-24).
- **Walkthrough**
  - `_policy` (line 31) is a single `CspPolicy` field computed once. The constructor (lines 33-42) null-guards `apiOptions`, `cspOptions`, and `environment` and calls `BuildCsp(apiOptions.Value, BuildFrameSrc(cspOptions.Value), environment.IsDevelopment())` (line 41). Because the type is registered as a singleton, this runs exactly once per process.
  - `GetPolicy(HttpContext context)` (line 45) ignores the context and returns the cached policy, so the per-request cost is a field read.
  - `BuildCsp` (lines 49-77) takes the pre-computed `frameSrc` as a parameter and resolves the endpoint as `api.WasmApiEndpoint ?? api.ApiEndpoint` (line 51). The guard on line 55 delegates to [ApiEndpointUrl](#apiendpointurl)`.TryParseAbsoluteHttp`, the same test `/client-config` and `AddMmcaBlazorWebHost` apply to those keys (comment, lines 53-54): it rejects a blank value, a non-absolute URI, and any scheme that is not http or https, which matters on Linux, where a rooted path such as `/relative/path` parses as an absolute `file://` URI. A rejected endpoint returns the enforced `connect-src 'self'` policy, still carrying `frameSrc` (line 59).
  - With a valid endpoint it derives `origin` via `apiUri.GetLeftPart(UriPartial.Authority)` (line 63, `scheme://host:port`), picks `wss` or `ws` to match (line 64), and composes `connect-src 'self' {origin} {wsScheme}://{authority}` (line 65). The WebSocket origin is there for the SignalR notification hub, so the live push channel is allowed without opening `connect-src` to the world.
  - Development only (lines 71-74) appends `http://localhost:*` and `ws://localhost:*` for Visual Studio Browser Link and Hot Reload, whose ports change per run (comment, lines 67-70); the production policy is untouched.
  - `BuildFrameSrc(BlazorCspSettings settings)` (lines 82-94) returns `null` on an empty `FrameSources` (lines 84-87), so the directive is omitted entirely rather than emitted empty; otherwise it maps every entry through [BlazorCspSettingsValidator](#blazorcspsettingsvalidator)`.ToOrigin`, de-duplicates with `StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase` (lines 89-91), and joins the result into `"frame-src 'self' {origins}"` (line 93). The comment (lines 79-81) notes every entry already passed the startup validator, so canonicalization here cannot fail.
  - `BuildPolicy` (lines 100-110) takes `frameSrc` as a parameter and assembles the directive list: `default-src 'self'`, the `script-src` above plus `'unsafe-inline'` **in Development only** (line 102, for the injected Hot Reload bootstrap), `style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'`, `img-src 'self' data: https:` (line 104, deliberately open because profile pictures and content images come from arbitrary external hosts, per the comment on lines 96-99), `font-src 'self'`, the computed `connect-src`, the `frame-src` directive when non-null (line 107, spliced in with its own trailing `"; "` so a null value leaves the rest of the policy unchanged), `base-uri 'self'`, `form-action 'self'`, and `frame-ancestors 'none'` (line 110, clickjacking protection).
- **Why it's built this way**: computing once and caching keeps the hot path free, and returning a [CspPolicy](group-16-aspire-orchestration.md#csppolicy) record rather than writing a header directly keeps the provider testable and lets one middleware own header emission. Registering it with `AddSingleton` (not `TryAdd`) is what makes it *replace* the default static provider, which is why the ordering rule in the class doc (lines 25-26) matters: call `AddCommonBlazorCsp()` before `AddCommonSecurityHeaders`. `frame-src` is threaded through as a plain `string?` parameter rather than read a second time inside `BuildPolicy`, so the policy string is built from one pass over its inputs. Delegating the endpoint test to [ApiEndpointUrl](#apiendpointurl) means the CSP cannot accept a value the host registration or `/client-config` would refuse.
- **Where it's used**: registered by `AddCommonBlazorCsp()` in the `MMCA.Common.UI.Web` [DependencyInjection](#dependencyinjection-1) with `AddSingleton<ICspPolicyProvider, BlazorCspPolicyProvider>` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/DependencyInjection.cs:67-77`, whose XML doc, lines 53-58, describes the enforced `connect-src 'self'` fallback); the policy it returns is emitted by [SecurityHeadersMiddleware](group-16-aspire-orchestration.md#securityheadersmiddleware). The class doc notes it was hoisted out of the app Blazor Web hosts where it had been byte-identical (line 25). Pinned by `BlazorCspPolicyProviderTests` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web.Tests/Security/BlazorCspPolicyProviderTests.cs`).

### ServerTokenStorageService

> MMCA.Common.UI.Web · `MMCA.Common.UI.Web.Services` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Services/ServerTokenStorageService.cs:48` · Level 5 · class (sealed)

- **What it is**: the Blazor **Server** implementation of [ISessionAwareTokenStorage](#isessionawaretokenstorage), the [ITokenStorageService](#itokenstorageservice) that can also report a held session ending and renew a token the API rejected: a cookie-only token store with no `localStorage`. During SSR prerender it reads the access token from the HttpOnly session cookie; on the live interactive circuit it holds the access token in memory only and re-acquires it from those cookies through the registered refresher (the same-origin `/auth/session/token` endpoint, or the protected `/auth/session/handoff` when the same-origin API proxy is enabled, class doc lines 14-15). The refresh token is never readable from JavaScript.
- **Depends on**: first-party: [ISessionAwareTokenStorage](#isessionawaretokenstorage) (the contract, line 53; it extends [ITokenStorageService](#itokenstorageservice) with the `SessionEnded` event and the defaulted `RenewRejectedAccessTokenAsync`, `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/Tokens/ISessionAwareTokenStorage.cs:12-37`), [CookieTokenReader](group-08-auth.md#cookietokenreader) (reads the access and refresh cookies off the request), [ISessionCookieSync](#isessioncookiesync) (seeds and clears the HttpOnly cookies, and reports whether the write succeeded), [ITokenRefresher](#itokenrefresher) (acquires a fresh access token from the session cookies), [JwtTokenInfo](#jwttokeninfo) (client-side freshness check), and [ISessionAwareTokenRefresher](#isessionawaretokenrefresher) with its [TokenAcquisition](#tokenacquisition) result (`AccessToken`, `IsUnavailable`), the optional refresher capability that tells a definitive "no session" from an unavailable one (`ServerTokenStorageService.cs:279-289`). Its WASM sibling is [WasmTokenStorageService](#wasmtokenstorageservice) (named in the class doc, line 17). Externals: `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http` (`IHttpContextAccessor`, `HttpContext`), `Microsoft.AspNetCore.SignalR` (`HubMetadata`), BCL `Lock`, `TimeProvider`, `Interlocked`, `Volatile`, `Task`, `TimeSpan`, `EventHandler`, `InvalidOperationException`.
- **Concept introduced, the two-world token store (SSR request versus interactive circuit).** A Blazor Web page runs twice: first as a server-side prerender inside a live HTTP request, where an `HttpContext` exists and JS interop does not, and then as a stateful circuit whose `HttpContext` is not null but is only the request that opened the hub connection, sent before any sign-in on that circuit and never updated, so its cookie is stale by construction (class doc, lines 29-41). One store has to serve both worlds, and this class decides which source of truth applies in `TryAnswerFromCookie` (lines 325-353, called at line 109), which looks at whether an `HttpContext` exists and whether memory has yet become authoritative.
  - **Cookie-first answer** (`TryAnswerFromCookie`, lines 325-353): when an `HttpContext` exists and memory is not yet authoritative, the request's HttpOnly cookie is read via `cookieTokenReader.ReadAccessToken()` (line 334). On a page request being prerendered (not `IsHubConnection`, line 338) the cookie wins outright, because the middleware may have just refreshed it in place on this navigation. On the request that opened the Blazor Server hub connection (`IsHubConnection`, lines 360-362, recognized by SignalR `HubMetadata` or a WebSocket request) the cookie is only the session the circuit started with: a cookie token there marks the session as held (lines 347-350), and the cookie answers only when absent or still fresh (`JwtTokenInfo.IsFresh`, line 352); an expired one is never handed back, since it would 401 every call for the life of the circuit, and the refresher re-acquires instead.
  - **Interactive circuit** (lines 114-152): the token lives in the `_accessToken` field (line 63). If `JwtTokenInfo.IsFresh(_accessToken, ExpirySkew)` (line 115) says it survives the 30-second skew (line 55), it is returned as is; otherwise it is re-acquired, unless a recent definitive "no session" answer is still remembered (the anonymous grace, below).
  - `[Rubric §26, Front-End Security]` assesses how credentials are held in the browser. This is a deliberate XSS-hardening design: the long-lived refresh token stays in an HttpOnly cookie unreachable from script, the access token exists only in circuit memory and is never persisted, and the refresh token transits JS exactly once, for the same-origin POST that seeds the cookies at login, as protected handoff ciphertext when the same-origin API proxy is enabled (`SetTokensAsync`, comment lines 211-215).
  - `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses the wider auth model; this store is one edge of the browser session-cookie design ([ADR-022](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/022-browser-session-cookie-auth.html)) and of the client token lifecycle ([ADR-051](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/051-client-auth-token-lifecycle.html)), the piece that decides *where* a bearer token is read on each side of the prerender boundary.
  - **Login fails loudly, logout stays best-effort.** The two cookie writes are deliberately asymmetric. `SetTokensAsync` throws `InvalidOperationException("The session cookie could not be written.")` when `SyncAsync` returns `false` (lines 216-219), after the in-memory token is already set, so [AuthUIService](#authuiservice) reports `Auth.TokenStorageUnavailable` instead of a login that looks successful and then silently signs out at the first access-token expiry, when no cookie exists to refresh from (comment above the sync call). `ClearTokensAsync` discards the boolean (`_ = await sessionCookieSync.ClearAsync()`, line 233), because logout is best-effort by contract (`IAuthUIService.LogoutAsync` never fails); a caller that needs proof the session ended uses `IAuthUIService.RevokeAllSessionsAsync` (comment above it).
  - **Anonymous grace, so a signed-out visitor costs one token round trip, not one per API call.** `AnonymousGrace` is a 15-second `static readonly TimeSpan` (line 58). When a hydrate returns no token and the refresher did not report itself unavailable, `HydrateAsync` sets `_anonymousUntil = now + AnonymousGrace` (line 302); `GetAccessTokenAsync` then answers null from memory while `_accessToken is null` and the clock is before `_anonymousUntil` (line 120). `SetTokensAsync` resets `_anonymousUntil` (line 207) so a login right after anonymous browsing does not wait out the grace, and a session created in another tab is seen within the window (class doc, lines 19-28). Only a DEFINITIVE answer starts it: a refresher implementing `ISessionAwareTokenRefresher` reports a 429, a 5xx, a dropped connection or unavailable interop as unavailable (comment, lines 267-274), so the next read hydrates again instead of treating a signed-in user as anonymous; a refresher without that capability keeps the earlier reading, where null means "no session" (lines 286-289).
  - **Session ended on the server, so the circuit signs out (A-34).** The `volatile` `_sessionHeld` flag (line 85) records whether the circuit holds a session: it is set by a login (line 210), by a hydrate that acquired a token (lines 305-308), by a hub-connection cookie that carried one (lines 347-350) and by a rejected-token renewal (line 186), and cleared by a logout (line 229). When a hydrate gets a definitive "no session" (`definitiveNoSession`, line 284, only possible from an `ISessionAwareTokenRefresher` whose answer is null and not unavailable) while `_sessionHeld` is true, it clears the flag and raises `SessionEnded` (lines 309-315, event declared at line 88). A plain refresher's null still starts the grace but is not proof enough to sign a held session out (comment, lines 273-274), and a transient failure leaves the flag alone (field doc, lines 81-84).
  - **A 401 renews the rejected token once.** A still-fresh token can be refused by the API (a locked account, a revoked session), and without a renewal path the circuit would stay signed in behind 401s until the token expired (`ISessionAwareTokenStorage.cs:31-36`). [AuthDelegatingHandler](#authdelegatinghandler) reports the rejected token to `RenewRejectedAccessTokenAsync` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:328`); this store drops it and runs one hydrate through the same single-flight a stale token takes, so a definitive "no session" ends the session exactly as an expired token's refresh does (remarks, lines 155-162).
- **Walkthrough**
  - The primary constructor (lines 48-53) takes `IHttpContextAccessor`, [CookieTokenReader](group-08-auth.md#cookietokenreader), [ISessionCookieSync](#isessioncookiesync), and [ITokenRefresher](#itokenrefresher), and a nullable `TimeProvider`. A public four-argument constructor (from line 98) chains to it with `timeProvider: null`, kept so code compiled against the original signature keeps binding. The type is `sealed` and carries no app-specific state, which is why it could be hoisted out of the app Blazor Web hosts (class doc, lines 16-17).
  - Fields: `ExpirySkew` (line 55, a `static readonly TimeSpan` of 30 seconds), `AnonymousGrace` (line 58, 15 seconds), the `Lock _hydrateSync` (line 60, the .NET 9+ dedicated lock object), `_timeProvider` (line 61, `timeProvider ?? TimeProvider.System`), the in-memory `_accessToken` (line 63), `_hydrateInFlight` (line 64, the shared acquisition task), `_anonymousUntil` (line 65, the end of the remembered "no session" answer), `_tokenVersion` (line 72, bumped by every login and logout so a stale hydrate can be recognized), the `volatile` `_memoryIsAuthoritative` (line 78, set once this instance has stored, cleared or hydrated a token, which only happens on the circuit, so from then on memory wins over the connection request's stale cookie) and the `volatile` `_sessionHeld` (line 85). The public `SessionEnded` event (line 88) implements the [ISessionAwareTokenStorage](#isessionawaretokenstorage) member.
  - `GetAccessTokenAsync` (lines 107-152): the cookie-first branch (`TryAnswerFromCookie`, line 109), the freshness check (line 115), the anonymous-grace short-circuit (line 120), then the **single-flight** guard. `_hydrateInFlight ??= HydrateAsync()` executes *inside* `lock (_hydrateSync)` (lines 130-134) and the resulting task is copied to a local before the lock is released, because two callers could otherwise each start a hydrate and the later completion would overwrite the other's token; `HydrateAsync` reaches its first await immediately, so nothing slow runs under the lock. The `finally` (from line 140) clears `_hydrateInFlight` **only when it is still reference-equal to the task this caller awaited** (line 146), so a newer hydrate started after this one completed is not dropped, which would split the next set of callers again.
  - `RenewRejectedAccessTokenAsync(string rejectedAccessToken)` (lines 163-192): throws on a null or blank argument (line 165), then, under `_hydrateSync` (lines 168-189), works out which token the store holds: the cookie's while an `HttpContext` exists and memory is not authoritative, otherwise `_accessToken` (lines 171-172). A held token that differs from the rejected one (already replaced, or never held here) is returned unchanged (lines 173-176), and so is a rejection during the SSR prerender, where no JS interop exists to refresh with (lines 178-181). Otherwise it nulls the token, clears `_anonymousUntil`, marks memory authoritative so the stale cookie never answers again, marks the session held (lines 183-186), joins or starts the shared hydrate (lines 187-188), and awaits it through `AwaitHydrateAsync` (line 191).
  - `GetRefreshTokenAsync` (lines 194-201): returns `cookieTokenReader.ReadRefreshToken()` (line 199) whenever an `HttpContext` exists, the live request during SSR and, on the circuit, the hub-connection request whose cookie can be as stale as the class remarks describe; otherwise `null`. The refresh token is never held in memory. It wraps the value in `Task.FromResult` rather than being `async`.
  - `SetTokensAsync` (lines 203-220): bumps `_tokenVersion` (line 206), resets `_anonymousUntil` (line 207), caches the access token in memory, marks memory authoritative (line 209) and the session held (line 210), then awaits `sessionCookieSync.SyncAsync(accessToken, refreshToken)` and throws when it reports failure (lines 216-219).
  - `ClearTokensAsync` (lines 222-240): bumps `_tokenVersion` (line 224), nulls the in-memory token, marks memory authoritative (line 228) so a logout is not undone by the connection request's cookie, clears `_sessionHeld` (line 229) so the logout itself never raises `SessionEnded`, awaits `sessionCookieSync.ClearAsync()` with its result explicitly discarded (line 233), then bumps the version a second time (line 238) and nulls the token again, so a hydrate that started during the clear and read the session being removed has its answer discarded, or dropped if it already landed.
  - `AwaitHydrateAsync(Task<string?> inFlight)` (lines 247-263): the renewal path's copy of the guarded await, clearing `_hydrateInFlight` under the lock only when it is still reference-equal to the awaited task (line 257).
  - `HydrateAsync` (lines 265-318): snapshots `_tokenVersion` (line 275), then, when the refresher is an `ISessionAwareTokenRefresher`, calls `TryAcquireAccessTokenAsync()` (line 281) and keeps the token, the `IsUnavailable` flag and the derived `definitiveNoSession` (line 284); otherwise it calls `AcquireAccessTokenAsync()` (line 288). If the version moved while the acquisition was in flight (a login or logout landed), the stale answer and its grace are discarded and the current `_accessToken` is returned (lines 291-294). Otherwise the token is cached, memory is marked authoritative (line 298), a null token with `unavailable` false starts the grace (lines 300-303), and the session-held bookkeeping runs (lines 305-315): a token marks the session held, a definitive "no session" for a held session raises `SessionEnded`. Every await on the hydrate path uses `ConfigureAwait(false)` (lines 138, 251, 281, 288), the library posture the cookie-write awaits do not take.
- **Why it's built this way**: Blazor Server's split lifecycle breaks the naive "read a token from storage" store, which would either fail during prerender (no JS) or leak the refresh token to script if it used `localStorage`. Branching on `HttpContext` presence and keeping the refresh token cookie-only resolves both. The locked single-flight is the correction of a real concurrency defect in the simpler `??=` version, and it is worth reading as a small case study in why "good enough" atomicity on a circuit is not good enough; the 401 renewal reuses that same single-flight rather than opening a second refresh path. Surfacing a failed cookie write at login, while tolerating one at logout, puts the failure where the user can still act on it. The 15-second anonymous grace trades a short staleness window for not paying a token round trip on every API call of a signed-out visitor, and it never remembers a transient failure. `SessionEnded` exists so a session that ended on the server does not leave the circuit rendering as signed in; only a definitive answer for a session the circuit actually held raises it, so neither an anonymous visitor nor a transient outage signs anyone out. See [ADR-022](https://ivanball.github.io/docs/adr/022-browser-session-cookie-auth.html).
- **Where it's used**: registered as the scoped [ITokenStorageService](#itokenstorageservice) by `AddCommonServerTokenStorage()` in the `MMCA.Common.UI.Web` [DependencyInjection](#dependencyinjection-1) (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/DependencyInjection.cs:41-50`); consumer hosts call that instead of shipping their own copy, and [BlazorWebHostExtensions](#blazorwebhostextensions) calls it for every host built with `AddMmcaBlazorWebHost` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web/Hosting/BlazorWebHostExtensions.cs:134`). The same call registers [BrowserOriginHandler](#browseroriginhandler) on the `"APIClient"` pipeline (lines 47-48). [JwtAuthenticationStateProvider](#jwtauthenticationstateprovider) subscribes to `SessionEnded` when the registered storage is session-aware (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/JwtAuthenticationStateProvider.cs:52`, handler `OnSessionEnded` at line 145) to sign the circuit out. Pinned by `ServerTokenStorageServiceTests` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Web.Tests/Services/ServerTokenStorageServiceTests.cs`).
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: the cookie names, lifetimes, and the `/auth/session/token` and `/auth/session/handoff` endpoints themselves are not in this file; they live in the `MMCA.Common.API` session-cookie plumbing and the same-origin proxy referenced by the doc comment (lines 9-47).

### AppLockInertBackground

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Components.Capabilities` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Capabilities/AppLockInertBackground.cs:15` · Level 1 · class (internal sealed)

- **What it is**: the small JS-interop helper that makes everything outside the app-lock overlay inert while [BiometricGate](#biometricgate) is locked, and lifts that again on unlock. It wraps one lazily imported module, `./_content/MMCA.Common.UI/app-lock.js` (`ModulePath`, `AppLockInertBackground.cs:18`), and remembers whether its last apply landed (`IsApplied`, `:23`).
- **Depends on**: `IJSRuntime` (primary constructor, `:15`), `ElementReference`, `IAsyncDisposable`, and the internal [LazyJsModule](#lazyjsmodule) import wrapper (`:20`). The JS side exports `inertOutside` and `release` (`wwwroot/app-lock.js:12`, `:32`).
- **Concept introduced, a modal that blocks the page behind it, not only the Tab key.** `[Rubric §21, Accessibility]` assesses whether a modal surface really is the only thing a keyboard or assistive-technology user can reach. A focus trap keeps Tab inside the panel, but programmatic focus and a screen reader's virtual cursor can still reach the page underneath; the script header (`app-lock.js:1-8`) records that the `inert` attribute removes that page from both, while leaving the lock root itself live. It also leaves an element that was already inert alone and never releases it later, so the helper never undoes someone else's `inert`.
- **Walkthrough**
  - `ApplyAsync(ElementReference lockRoot)` (`AppLockInertBackground.cs:28-44`) imports the module through `GetOrImportAsync` (`:32`), calls `inertOutside` with the overlay wrapper (`:33`) and only then sets `IsApplied` (`:34`). `JSDisconnectedException` (circuit gone) and `JSException` (the browser refused) are both swallowed (`:36-43`): the comment at `:42` notes the focus trap still holds Tab inside the panel when the inert call fails.
  - `ReleaseAsync()` (`:48-69`) returns at once when nothing was applied (`:50-53`), clears `IsApplied` before the call (`:55`), invokes `release` (`:59`) and tolerates the same two exceptions (`:61-68`).
  - `DisposeAsync()` (`:72-87`) releases, then disposes the module (`:76-77`), again tolerating a disconnected circuit or a shutdown-time interop race (`:79-86`).
- **Why it's built this way**: every call is best effort and never throws, which is what lets [BiometricGate](#biometricgate) call it from `OnAfterRenderAsync`, from unlock and sign-out, and fire and forget its disposal from a synchronous `Dispose(bool)` (`BiometricGate.razor.cs:103-108`). Keeping `IsApplied` means a release with nothing applied costs no interop call at all.
- **Where it's used**: only [BiometricGate](#biometricgate), which creates it lazily through its `InertBackground` property (`BiometricGate.razor.cs:48`); pinned through `BiometricGateTests` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Components/Capabilities/BiometricGateTests.cs`).

### InfiniteScrollObserver<TOwner>

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Components.Lists` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Lists/InfiniteScrollObserver.cs:17` · Level 1 · class (internal sealed, generic)

- **What it is**: the one place that talks to `infinite-scroll.js` for the two infinite-scroll components. It owns a per-instance observer id, a lazily imported JS module, the `DotNetObjectReference` back to its owner, and an `IsObserving` flag (lines 25-40). Its owner (a component exposing a `[JSInvokable]` callback) constructs it as `new InfiniteScrollObserver<TOwner>(JS, this)` and calls `ObserveAsync`, `UnobserveAsync` and `DisposeAsync` from its lifecycle.
- **Depends on**: `IJSRuntime`, `ElementReference`, `DotNetObjectReference<TOwner>`, `IAsyncDisposable`, and the internal `LazyJsModule` import wrapper (line 35). Nothing else first-party; consumed by [`InfiniteScrollSentinel`](#infinitescrollsentinel) and [`MobileInfiniteScrollList<TItem>`](#mobileinfinitescrolllisttitem) (the `TOwner` constraint is `class`, line 18).
- **Concept introduced, one JS-interop lifecycle shared by two components.** `[Rubric §23, Front-End Performance]` (assesses whether observers are attached on demand and detached so they stop costing anything) and `[Rubric §18, UI Architecture]`. Before the extraction each component carried its own copy of the import, attach, detach and dispose code; the helper makes a fix to one race a fix to both.
- **Walkthrough**:
  - `ObserveAsync(ElementReference sentinel)` (lines 48-78) awaits `_module.GetOrImportAsync()` (line 52), a single-flight import: Blazor does not serialize `OnAfterRenderAsync`, so a second call can start while the first import is in flight, and an unguarded `??=` would import twice and leak the overwritten instance (comment, lines 32-34). If the owner was disposed while the import was in flight, the late module is released and no observer is attached that nobody would ever detach (lines 54-62). Otherwise it creates the `DotNetObjectReference` once (line 66), calls `observe` with the reference, the element and the id (line 67), and sets `IsObserving` (line 68). `JSDisconnectedException` and `JSException` are both swallowed (lines 70-77): the list simply stops at the pages already loaded.
  - `UnobserveAsync()` (lines 82-104) returns unless the module is imported and an observer is attached (line 84), calls `unobserve` with the id (line 92), tolerates both exceptions, and clears `IsObserving` (line 103).
  - `DisposeAsync()` (lines 107-133) guards re-entry with `_disposed` (lines 109-114), unobserves and disposes the module (lines 118-119), tolerates both exceptions, and disposes the `DotNetObjectReference` in a `finally` (line 131) so the .NET side is released even if JS already went away.
- **Why it's built this way**: the observe path is where the two components had drifted apart (one tolerated `JSException`, one did not); a single internal class with the guarded import fixes the leak and the dispose-during-import race once.
- **Where it's used**: `InfiniteScrollSentinel.razor.cs` (lines 35, 59-60, 78-80) and `MobileInfiniteScrollList.razor.cs`; exercised through `InfiniteScrollSentinelTests`.

### ViewAsBanner

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Components.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/ViewAsBanner.razor.cs:23` · Level 1 · class (partial component)

- **What it is**: the banner the shared layout shows while a support user is viewing the app as another account (ADR-137, `Website/docs-src/adr/137-read-only-view-as-support-access.md`). It names the viewed account, counts down the time left on the view-as token, and ends the session when the countdown reaches zero. `MainLayout.razor:87` renders it unconditionally; it renders its content only when the principal is a view-as principal.
- **Depends on**: the cascading `Task<AuthenticationState>` (`ViewAsBanner.razor.cs:36`), `IStringLocalizer<SharedResource>` ([SharedResource](#sharedresource), `:38`), `IJSRuntime` (`:39`), the `IsViewAs` extension on [ClaimsPrincipalExtensions](group-08-auth.md#claimsprincipalextensions) (`ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:137`), and [ComponentLifetimeExtensions](#componentlifetimeextensions) for `LifetimeToken()` (`ViewAsBanner.razor.cs:104`, `:134`). Externals: `PeriodicTimer`, `CancellationTokenSource`.
- **Concept introduced, a time-boxed elevated session that ends itself.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether delegated or impersonated access is visible to the person using it and bounded in time. The banner reads the remaining lifetime straight from the token's `exp` claim, so the countdown shows the same deadline the server enforces, and it calls the end endpoint itself once that deadline passes rather than waiting for the next refused request.
- **Walkthrough**
  - `ApiPathPrefix` (`ViewAsBanner.razor.cs:34`) is the same-origin proxy prefix, `/api` when unset (`:134`).
  - `Remaining(ClaimsPrincipal?, DateTimeOffset)` (`:48-58`) is public and static, so it is testable without rendering: it parses `exp` as invariant Unix seconds (`:50-51`), returns `null` when the claim is missing or unreadable (`:53`), and clamps a past expiry to `TimeSpan.Zero` (`:56-57`).
  - `OnParametersSetAsync` (`:70-76`) sets `_viewAs` from `IsViewAs()` (`:73`), takes the display name from `Identity.Name` or the `ClaimTypes.Name` claim (`:74`), and turns the remaining time into an absolute `_expiresAt` (`:75`).
  - `OnAfterRender` (`:79-87`) starts a one-second `PeriodicTimer` on the first render, only for a view-as principal and only when `RendererInfo.IsInteractive` (`:82`); the comment (`:81`) records that a prerender shows the starting value only. `FormatRemaining` (`:89-98`) renders the time left as `mm:ss` (`:97`), never negative.
  - `TickAsync` (`:100-122`) re-renders every tick (`:106`) and, once `_expiresAt` has passed, dispatches `EndAsync` and stops (`:107-111`). Cancellation and an `ObjectDisposedException` between ticks both end the loop quietly (`:114-121`).
  - `EndAsync` (`:124-141`) is guarded by `_ending` (`:126-131`) and calls the `mmcaViewAs.end` script with `{prefix}/auth/view-as/end` (`:134`). A `JSException`, `JSDisconnectedException`, `InvalidOperationException` or `OperationCanceledException` resets `_ending` (`:136-140`): the comment records that the page is reloading or the circuit is gone and the overlay expires on its own.
  - `DisposeAsync` (`:61-67`) cancels the token source, disposes the timer and the source.
- **Why it's built this way**: computing the deadline once and re-rendering against the clock keeps the countdown honest across a slow render, and the guard on `_ending` keeps a late tick from posting the end request twice.
- **Where it's used**: the shared `MainLayout` (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Layout/MainLayout.razor:87`); pinned by `ViewAsComponentTests` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Components/Auth/ViewAsComponentTests.cs`). Its sibling [ViewAsButton](#viewasbutton) starts the session it describes.
- **Caveats / not-in-source**: where the `mmcaViewAs` script object is defined, and what it does after the end request, is not shown in this code-behind.

### ViewAsButton

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Components.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/ViewAsButton.razor.cs:23` · Level 1 · class (partial component)

- **What it is**: the admin control that starts a read-only view-as session for one account (ADR-137, `Website/docs-src/adr/137-read-only-view-as-support-access.md`). It shows only to a caller holding the view-as permission, asks for a written reason, and posts the start request through a small script that reloads the app on success.
- **Depends on**: the cascading `Task<AuthenticationState>` (`ViewAsButton.razor.cs:47`), `IStringLocalizer<SharedResource>` ([SharedResource](#sharedresource), `:49`), `IJSRuntime` (`:50`), [AdministrationPermissions](group-08-auth.md#administrationpermissions)`.ViewAsUsers` and the `HasPermissionClaim` and `IsViewAs` extensions on [ClaimsPrincipalExtensions](group-08-auth.md#claimsprincipalextensions) (`ViewAsButton.razor.cs:58`; `ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:95`, `:137`). The default route names the app's [UsersAdminControllerBase<TUserDto>](group-12-api-hosting-mapping.md#usersadmincontrollerbasetuserdto) subclass (doc comment, `ViewAsButton.razor.cs:40-44`).
- **Concept introduced, an elevated action that must state its purpose.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether privileged support access is gated by a permission and leaves an accountable trail. The button is hidden from anyone without `ViewAsUsers` and from a caller already in a view-as session (`:58`), so view-as cannot be chained; and the request carries a reason of 10 to 500 characters after trimming (`ReasonIsValid`, `:52`), which the start call refuses to send otherwise (`:76-79`).
- **Walkthrough**
  - Parameters: `UserId` is `[EditorRequired]` and typed through the `UserIdentifierType` alias (`:32-34`); `ApiPathPrefix` defaults to `/api` and `UsersRoute` to `Admin/Users` when unset (`:38`, `:45`, applied at `:85-87`).
  - `OnParametersSetAsync` (`:55-59`) computes `_canViewAs` from the permission claim and the not-already-viewing check (`:58`).
  - `Open` (`:61-65`) shows the reason form and clears any error; `Cancel` (`:67-72`) closes it and clears the reason and the error.
  - `StartAsync` (`:74-104`) returns when the reason is invalid or a start is already running (`:76-79`), builds `{prefix}/{route}/{UserId}/view-as` with an invariant `string.Create` (`:85-87`), and awaits `mmcaViewAs.start` with the trimmed reason (`:90`). The comment (`:89`) records that the script reloads the app on success, so only a refusal comes back: any status outside 2xx (`:91-94`), or a `JSException`, `JSDisconnectedException`, `InvalidOperationException` or `TaskCanceledException` (`:96-99`), shows the localized `Auth.ViewAs.Refused` text. `_starting` clears in `finally` (`:100-103`).
- **Why it's built this way**: the reload on success replaces the admin's whole client state with the viewed account's, so no cached data of the admin's session survives into the view; the component only has to handle the refusal path.
- **Where it's used**: ADC's user detail page (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.UI/Pages/Users/UserDetail/UserDetail.razor:127`); pinned by `ViewAsComponentTests` (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Components/Auth/ViewAsComponentTests.cs`) and ADC's `ViewAsTests` E2E workflow (`MMCA.ADC/Tests/E2E/MMCA.ADC.E2E.Tests/Workflows/Identity/Administration/ViewAsTests.cs`). The session it starts is shown by [ViewAsBanner](#viewasbanner).

### BiometricGate

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Components.Capabilities` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Capabilities/BiometricGate.razor.cs:18` · Level 2 · class (partial, component code-behind)

- **What it is**: a hybrid-head app-lock gate. It locks the UI behind a biometric prompt whenever the
  app returns from the background having sat there longer than `ReLockAfter`, so a device handed to
  someone else, or simply left unattended, does not reopen straight into a signed-in session. While
  locked, the page behind the overlay is made inert and focus is held on the Unlock button.
- **Depends on**: injected services resolved by the component (`AppLifecycle`'s `Resumed` event with
  [AppResumedEventArgs](group-26-device-capability-layer.md#appresumedeventargs),
  `Preferences` ([IDevicePreferences](group-26-device-capability-layer.md#idevicepreferences)) read with
  [DevicePreferenceKeys](group-26-device-capability-layer.md#devicepreferencekeys)`.AppLockEnabled`,
  `TokenStorage`, `AuthService` ([IAuthUIService](#iauthuiservice), used only to sign out), `Biometrics`,
  `Navigation`, `Logger`, `JS`, the page's localizer `L`); [AppLockInertBackground](#applockinertbackground)
  for the inert page behind the overlay (`BiometricGate.razor.cs:32`, `:48`); MudBlazor's `MudButton` for
  the focus target (`_unlockButton`, line 30).
- **Concept introduced, a discarded lifecycle task that cannot afford to throw.**
  `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses whether a re-auth control actually re-arms on every qualifying
  event, not just the first one. The class subscribes to `AppLifecycle.Resumed` on first render
  regardless of the current preference, because app lock can be switched on later in the same session
  (comment, lines 76-77), and every resume re-reads the preference. `[Rubric §18, UI Architecture &
  Component Design]` covers the handler shape itself: `OnResumed` (line 125) is a plain
  `EventHandler<AppResumedEventArgs>`, so it cannot be `async`; it fires `ReLockAsync` with an explicit
  discard, and the comment (lines 119-124) states why that discard is safe here: `ReLockAsync`
  observes its own failures with a catch-all, which avoids the async-void crash-the-process mode
  (VSTHRD100), and the catch-all comment (lines 160-161) records that nothing else would observe a
  failed re-lock.
- **Concept introduced, a precondition read that fails open before opt-in and closed after it.**
  `[Rubric §11, Security]` also assesses which way a control fails when its own inputs are unreadable.
  `ShouldLockAsync` documents both halves (lines 166-171): if the `AppLockEnabled` preference itself
  cannot be read, nothing says the owner opted in, so the gate stays open rather than forcing a
  biometric prompt on a device that may have none enrolled; if the preference reads as on but the
  stored session cannot be read, the session state is unknown and the gate locks. Either way the
  method never throws, which matters because it runs from both the first render and the resume path.
- **Concept introduced, a lock that owns focus and the page behind it.** `[Rubric §21, Accessibility]`
  assesses whether a modal surface is the only thing a keyboard or screen-reader user can reach.
  Every lock goes through `EngageLock` (lines 206-215), which sets `_locked` and queues both the
  focus move onto Unlock and the inert background, whichever path locked the gate (start-up or
  resume), so focus never stays on the page behind the overlay (field comment, lines 34-39).
- **Walkthrough**
  - `ReLockAfter` (lines 25-26) is a `[Parameter]` `TimeSpan` defaulting to 30 seconds; the comment
    (lines 20-24) explains the default is deliberately short, a device handed off is usually away from
    its owner longer than a glance at a notification.
  - State: `_lockRoot` is the overlay wrapper the inert boundary is measured from (line 31),
    `_inertBackground` the lazily created helper behind the `InertBackground` property (lines 32, 48),
    and `_focusUnlockPending` and `_inertPending` the two flags acted on after render (lines 40, 46).
  - `OnAfterRenderAsync(firstRender)` (lines 51-89): first focuses the Unlock button if
    `_focusUnlockPending` and the button reference now exists (lines 53-57), because that flag can
    only be acted on once the locked branch has actually rendered. Then, if `_inertPending` and still
    locked, it applies the inert background to `_lockRoot` (lines 59-62) and releases it again at once
    when an unlock landed while the call was in flight (lines 64-68). On `firstRender` it subscribes
    to `AppLifecycle.Resumed` (lines 78-79), then calls `ShouldLockAsync` and, if it returns true,
    calls `EngageLock` and awaits `UnlockAsync` (lines 81-88).
  - `ReLockAsync` (lines 127-164) returns early if already locked or if the background duration was
    under `ReLockAfter` (line 131), otherwise dispatches the check, `EngageLock` and unlock sequence
    through `InvokeAsync` (lines 136-146). It catches `ObjectDisposedException` and
    `InvalidOperationException` as expected teardown races (lines 148-155), and a general `Exception`
    last under a scoped `CA1031` suppression, logged rather than rethrown (lines 156-163).
  - `ShouldLockAsync` (lines 172-204) wraps the preference read in its own `try` (lines 175-185): a
    failure is logged as a warning and returns false. A preference that is off also returns false
    (lines 187-190). Otherwise a second `try` (lines 192-203) returns whether a refresh token is still
    stored, nothing to protect without a session, and a failure there is logged and returns true
    (line 202). Both catch-alls carry a scoped `CA1031` suppression naming their disposition.
  - `UnlockAsync` (lines 217-238) calls `Biometrics.AuthenticateAsync` with a localized prompt reason;
    success clears `_locked` and both pending flags and lifts the inert background through
    `ReleaseBackgroundAsync` (lines 219-224); failure re-queues `_focusUnlockPending` for the next
    render (line 234). Both paths call `StateHasChanged` under a `BL0012` suppression, because
    `UnlockAsync` also runs from `OnAfterRenderAsync` and `ReLockAsync`, where nothing re-renders
    automatically (lines 225-227, 235-237).
  - `FocusUnlockAsync` (lines 244-258) tolerates `JSDisconnectedException` (circuit gone) and
    `InvalidOperationException` (prerendering, or the element already removed).
  - `SignOutAsync` (lines 264-272) calls `AuthService.LogoutAsync()` (line 266), clears `_locked` and both pending flags, releases the inert background, and navigates to `/login`. The doc (lines 260-263) states why it is the app's own logout and never a bare token clear: clearing the tokens alone left Blazor's auth state signed in and the previous session's read cache and offline snapshots on the device.
  - `ReleaseBackgroundAsync` (lines 274-276) releases only when a helper exists, otherwise returns a
    completed task.
  - `Dispose(bool)` (lines 93-110) unsubscribes from `AppLifecycle.Resumed` if subscribed, guarded so
    it is safe to call more than once, then fires and forgets the helper's `DisposeAsync` so a gate
    torn down while locked does not leave the page behind it inert (lines 103-109); the public
    `Dispose()` (lines 113-117) forwards to it and suppresses finalization.
- **Why it's built this way**: the re-lock decision is driven entirely by wall-clock background
  duration rather than any UI state, so it behaves the same whether the app was backgrounded for a
  phone call or for the rest of the day. Catching broadly inside `ReLockAsync` but narrowly inside
  `FocusUnlockAsync` reflects the difference between an operation whose caller cannot observe a failure
  at all (the lifecycle event) and one whose failure just means "skip the focus this time". The two
  catches inside `ShouldLockAsync` resolve in opposite directions on purpose: before opt-in the safe
  default is "no lock", after opt-in it is "lock". Routing every lock through `EngageLock` keeps the
  start-up and resume paths from drifting apart on focus and inertness.
- **Where it's used**: MMCA.ADC's `DeviceUIModule`
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI/DeviceUIModule.cs`) and `App.xaml.cs`
  (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Hosts/UI/MMCA.ADC.UI/App.xaml.cs`); referenced by
  [TermsAcceptanceGate](#termsacceptancegate) (`TermsAcceptanceGate.razor.cs`); pinned by `BiometricGateTests`
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Components/Capabilities/BiometricGateTests.cs`).
  Its place in the UI module shell is described in ADR-067
  (`Website/docs-src/adr/067-ui-module-shell-composition.md`).

### InfiniteScrollSentinel

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Components.Lists` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Lists/InfiniteScrollSentinel.razor.cs:21` · Level 0 · class (partial component)

- **What it is**: a bottom-of-list marker that raises `OnVisible` when it scrolls near the viewport, so the hosting page can fetch and append its next page. It owns the IntersectionObserver and nothing else: the item markup, the fetch, and the accumulated list stay with the page.
- **Depends on**: `IJSRuntime`, `ElementReference`, and MudBlazor's `MudProgressCircular` in the markup; first-party, only [`InfiniteScrollObserver<TOwner>`](#infinitescrollobservertowner), which owns the shared JS module `_content/MMCA.Common.UI/infinite-scroll.js` (`wwwroot/infinite-scroll.js`). It is a sibling of [`MobileInfiniteScrollList<TItem>`](#mobileinfinitescrolllisttitem), which drives the same JS module.
- **Concept introduced, the observer as a child component so disposal is correct.** `[Rubric §23, Front-End Performance]` (assesses render and network cost: paging on demand instead of loading everything, and detaching observers so they stop costing anything), `[Rubric §21, Accessibility]` (assesses whether dynamic content changes are announced without hijacking focus) and `[Rubric §18, UI Architecture]`. The design point recorded in the doc comment (lines 14-19) is a lifecycle one: a page deriving from [`DataGridListPageBase<TDto>`](#datagridlistpagebasetdto) cannot hook async disposal because its `DisposeAsync` is not virtual, whereas a child component is disposed by the renderer the moment the host stops rendering it. Rendering the sentinel only while more pages exist therefore makes "detach the observer" a rendering decision rather than a bookkeeping one, and a filter reset that refills the list gets a fresh instance with a fresh observer.
- **Walkthrough**:
  - Parameters: `OnVisible` (line 26), `IsLoading` (line 29) which renders the inline progress row, and `LoadingLabel` (line 32), the localized accessible name for that row.
  - State (lines 34-41): the `_sentinelRef` element reference (line 34), the `_observer` field (line 35, an [`InfiniteScrollObserver<TOwner>`](#infinitescrollobservertowner) that now owns the observer id, the imported JS module, the `DotNetObjectReference` and the observing flag), `_wasLoading` (line 40, the previous render's `IsLoading`), and `_disposed` (line 41).
  - `OnSentinelVisible()` (lines 47-49) is the `[JSInvokable]` callback. Its name is fixed by the shared JS module, which calls it by string (lines 43-46). It returns immediately when disposed, otherwise marshals onto the renderer with `InvokeAsync` before invoking `OnVisible`.
  - `OnAfterRenderAsync` (lines 52-63) attaches the observer on the first render, and re-attaches it on the render where a load has just finished: `loadJustFinished` is `_wasLoading && !IsLoading && _observer?.IsObserving == true` (line 54), `_wasLoading` is then updated (line 55), and either condition lazily creates the observer helper (line 59) and calls `ObserveAsync(_sentinelRef)` (line 60). The reason is recorded on the field (lines 37-39): an IntersectionObserver reports threshold crossings only, so a sentinel that is still inside the viewport when the appended page arrives would never fire again and the list would stall until the user scrolled away and back. Re-observing creates a fresh observer, which delivers a fresh initial entry.
  - The module import, the `DotNetObjectReference`, the `observe`/`unobserve` calls and the swallowed `JSDisconnectedException`/`JSException` live in the shared helper, not here; see [`InfiniteScrollObserver<TOwner>`](#infinitescrollobservertowner).
  - `DisposeAsync` (lines 67-82) suppresses finalization, guards re-entry with `_disposed` (lines 71-74), and delegates teardown to `_observer.DisposeAsync()` when one was created (lines 78-80), so the detach, the module release and the `DotNetObjectReference` disposal happen in the helper.
  - The markup (`Components/InfiniteScrollSentinel.razor:4-13`) is a single `div` carrying the element reference, with the progress row rendered only while `IsLoading`. That row is `role="status" aria-live="polite" aria-busy="true"` (line 9), matching `PageLoadingState`'s politeness so a screen reader hears that more items are loading without the announcement interrupting reading.
  - The JS side is deliberately tiny: `observe` disconnects any prior observer for the id, creates an `IntersectionObserver` with `rootMargin: '200px'` and invokes `OnSentinelVisible` on intersection (`wwwroot/infinite-scroll.js:3-14`); `unobserve` disconnects and forgets the id (lines 16-22). The 200px margin is what makes the next page start loading slightly *before* the sentinel is on screen, and the disconnect-before-create step is what makes the post-load re-attach above safe to call repeatedly with the same id.
- **Why it's built this way**: extracting just the observer is what lets a page keep its own cards, empty state and error state and still get infinite scroll (lines 10-13). The alternative, folding the behavior into the list component, would force any page that wants infinite scroll to also adopt that component's layout.
- **Where it's used**: ADC's public speaker list renders it below the card grid while more pages exist, wiring `OnVisible` to its own loader and passing a localized loading label (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Conference/MMCA.ADC.Conference.UI/Pages/Public/Speakers/PublicSpeakerList.razor:144-145`, inside [`PublicSpeakerList`](group-21-conference-ui.md#publicspeakerlist)). Covered by [`InfiniteScrollSentinelTests`](group-29-testing-infrastructure.md#per-project-test-rollup).

### SignInHistoryTable

> MMCA.Common.UI · `MMCA.Common.UI.Components.Auth` · `MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Components/Auth/SignInHistoryTable.razor.cs:22` · Level 2 · class (partial component)

- **What it is**: a read-only table of an account's sign-ins, newest first, including ones that have
  ended. It takes the rows as a parameter and only formats them: a device label, an IP address, a
  status, and viewer-local times. It is the history counterpart of [UserSessionsTable](#usersessionstable),
  which shows only the live sessions (ADR-097, `Website/docs-src/adr/097-multi-device-refresh-sessions.md`).
- **Depends on**: [SignInSummaryResponse](group-08-auth.md#signinsummaryresponse) (the row shape,
  `SignInHistoryTable.razor.cs:30`), [SignInHistoryEntryKind](group-08-auth.md#signinhistoryentrykind)
  (`:72`), [SignInEndReasons](group-08-auth.md#signinendreasons) (`:82-87`),
  [ViewerTimeZone](#viewertimezone) (`:33`), [UserAgentSummary](#useragentsummary) (`:74`),
  [SharedResource](#sharedresource) for the `IStringLocalizer` (`:32`) and
  [ComponentLifetimeExtensions](#componentlifetimeextensions) for `LifetimeToken()` (`:46`).
- **Concept introduced, a status read from why a session ended.** `[Rubric §11, Security]` assesses
  whether an account holder can see suspicious access. Each row's status comes from its end reason, so
  a refresh-token reuse, a session-cap eviction or an account deletion reads differently from an
  ordinary sign-out (`DescribeStatus`, `:79-89`). A view-as row (ADR-137) shows who looked, not a
  device of the account holder's (comment `:70`, `:71-74`).
- **Walkthrough**
  - `SignIns` is an `[EditorRequired]` parameter defaulting to an empty list (`:28-30`).
  - `OnAfterRenderAsync` (`:43-50`) resolves the viewer's time zone on first render only, skips it once
    disposed, and calls `StateHasChanged` when the lookup resolved a zone (`:46-49`); the comment (`:45`)
    records that the zone is only readable once JS is available.
  - Row helpers: `DescribeDevice` returns the localized `Auth.SignIns.ViewedBySupport` text for a
    `ViewAs` row and otherwise `UserAgentSummary.Describe(signIn.Device, signIn.UserAgent, L)` (`:71-74`);
    `DescribeIpAddress` falls back to `Auth.Sessions.IpUnknown` when the address is blank (`:76-77`).
  - `DescribeStatus` (`:79-89`) maps a row with no end reason and no `EndedAt` to "Active", each
    `SignInEndReasons` constant (`SignedOut`, `ReuseDetected`, `SessionCapExceeded`, `AccountDeleted`,
    `Expired`) to its own localized text, and `ViewAsEnded` and any unknown reason to the generic
    "Ended" text (`:87-88`).
  - `FormatInstant` calls `ViewerTime.Format` (`:91`).
  - Disposal: `IDisposable` with an idempotent protected `Dispose(bool)` that cancels and disposes the
    `CancellationTokenSource` bounding the zone lookup (`:36-40`, `:54-68`).
- **Why it's built this way**: the table owns no data fetching, so the account's own sessions page and
  the admin user-detail page share it, and the default arm of the status switch keeps a reason added
  on the server later rendering as "Ended" instead of blank.
- **Where it's used**: the shared `Sessions` page
  (`MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/Sessions.razor:125`) and ADC's user detail
  page (`MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.UI/Pages/Users/UserDetail/UserDetail.razor:136`);
  pinned by `SignInHistoryTableTests`
  (`MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Tests/Components/Auth/SignInHistoryTableTests.cs`) and
  ADC's `UserDetailTests`.
